chunks.text: Pleonasm · الحشو · Using superfluous or redundant words. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Reflected meaning
chunks.text: Reflected meaning · المعنى المنعكس · When one sense of a polysemous word colours how its other senses are understood. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Reinforcement
chunks.text: Reinforcement · التعزيز · Adding a target-language item that strengthens a source item: ‘among the group’, مِنْ ضِمْنِ الفِرْقة. The opposite is condensation. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Theme and rheme
chunks.text: Theme and rheme · المبتدأ والخبر (الموضوع والمحمول) The theme is what a clause is about, usually placed first; the rheme is what is said about it (also topic and comment). Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Root repetition
chunks.text: Root repetition · الجناس الاشتقاقي · Arabic device of placing words from the same root close together: تخليص الإبريز في تلخيص باريز. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Semantic repetition
chunks.text: Semantic repetition · الترادف التوكيدي · Using near-synonyms together, common in Arabic (المَحْل والمَجاعة والمَسْغَبة), but in English mostly kept to fixed pairs like ‘last will and testament’. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Slang
chunks.text: Slang · اللغة العامية الدارجة · A variety differing from the standard in grammar and vocabulary, used by one section of a speech community. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Social meaning
chunks.text: Social meaning · المعنى الاجتماعي · What words show about relationships and roles, such as the Arabic plural ‘you’ used as a mark of respect. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Sociolect
chunks.text: Sociolect · اللهجة الاجتماعية · The variety shared by a social group, such as ‘the Queen’s English’. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Stative verb
chunks.text: Stative verb · فعل الحالة · A verb that names a state, such as know or remain, and is not normally used in progressive forms. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Tautology
chunks.text: Tautology · تحصيل الحاصل · Repeating the same idea in different words. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Text function
chunks.text: Text function · وظيفة النص · What a text is for (to sell, instruct, inform); it should be specified when a translation is commissioned. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Thematic meaning
chunks.text: Thematic meaning · المعنى الموضوعاتي · Meaning that comes from the order in which information is presented. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Translation loss
chunks.text: Translation loss · الفقد في الترجمة · Anything of the source that does not survive in the translation, at grammatical, semantic, cultural or intertextual level. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Translation by omission
chunks.text: Translation by omission · الترجمة بالحذف · Leaving source elements out of the translation; also called concentration or economy. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Translation by addition
chunks.text: Translation by addition · الترجمة بالإضافة · Including elements not in the source; also called dissolution or amplification. Husni & Newman (2015), Glossary

chunks.title: Anuvad
chunks.text: Anuvad · أنوفاد · The Sanskrit word for translation, still used in modern Indian languages: ‘saying after’, a temporal image rather than the spatial ‘carrying across’ (Trivedi). Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Invariant core
chunks.text: Invariant core · النواة الثابتة · What all translations of a work have in common: its stable semantic elements, as opposed to the variants of expression (Popovič). Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Semiotic transformation
chunks.text: Semiotic transformation · التحويل السيميائي · Replacing the signs of a message with signs of another code while keeping its invariant information (Ludskanov). Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Linguistic untranslatability
chunks.text: Linguistic untranslatability · استحالة الترجمة اللغوية · When the target language has no lexical or syntactic substitute for a source item; usually solved by restructuring (Catford). Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Cultural untranslatability
chunks.text: Cultural untranslatability · استحالة الترجمة الثقافية · When the target culture lacks a feature of the source situation, such as a Finnish or Japanese ‘bathroom’ (Catford). Bassnett argues it is present in every translation. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Loss and gain
chunks.text: Loss and gain · الفقد والكسب · Some meaning is always lost in translation, but a translator can also enrich or clarify a text. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Metaphrase
chunks.text: Metaphrase · الترجمة الحرفية (درايدن) Dryden’s term for turning an author word by word and line by line. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Paraphrase (Dryden)
chunks.text: Paraphrase (Dryden) الترجمة بتصرف · Dryden’s ‘translation with latitude’, sense for sense: his preferred middle way. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Imitation (Dryden)
chunks.text: Imitation (Dryden) المحاكاة · Dryden’s term for a translation that departs from the original as the translator sees fit. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Sense-for-sense translation
chunks.text: Sense-for-sense translation · الترجمة بالمعنى · Rendering meaning rather than words: Cicero and Horace’s non verbum de verbo, followed by St Jerome. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Vertical and horizontal translation
chunks.text: Vertical and horizontal translation · الترجمة الرأسية والأفقية · Translation from a prestige language such as Latin into the vernacular (vertical) versus between languages of equal standing (horizontal) (Folena). Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Visibility
chunks.text: Visibility · ظهور المترجم · Venuti’s term: fluent translation hides the translator, while foreignizing translation makes their work visible. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Rewriting
chunks.text: Rewriting · إعادة الكتابة · Lefevere’s view of translation, alongside criticism, anthologies and adaptation, as one of the ways most readers meet literature. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Cultural turn
chunks.text: Cultural turn · المنعطف الثقافي · Bassnett and Lefevere’s 1990 shift of attention to the context, history and conventions surrounding translation. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Polysystem theory
chunks.text: Polysystem theory · نظرية الأنظمة المتعددة · Even-Zohar’s idea that cultures translate according to need: young or unsettled literatures translate more, established ones less. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Ostranenie (making strange)
chunks.text: Ostranenie (making strange) التغريب الأسلوبي · The Russian Formalist device of deliberately ‘thickening’ language to sharpen perception. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Translation unit
chunks.text: Translation unit · وحدة الترجمة · The stretch of text a translator works with at one time; the whole text is the prime unit. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Performability
chunks.text: Performability · قابلية الأداء · In theatre translation, keeping the rhythms and ‘gestural text’ an actor needs, not just the words. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Minimax
chunks.text: Minimax · مبدأ الحد الأدنى والأقصى · Levý’s principle that translators choose the solution giving the most effect for the least effort. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Pure language
chunks.text: Pure language · اللغة الخالصة · Benjamin’s idea that translation brings out a hidden language that echoes the original. Bassnett (2014)

chunks.title: Common Law
chunks.text: Common Law · القانون العام (الأنجلوسكسوني) A legal system built from judges’ decisions and precedent (England, the USA, Canada, Australia; Oman’s system has roots in it). Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Civil Law
chunks.text: Civil Law · القانون المدني (اللاتيني) A legal system based on codified statutes, rooted in Roman law (continental Europe; Algeria, Morocco, Syria and Tunisia alongside Islamic law). Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Court of Cassation
chunks.text: Court of Cassation · محكمة التمييز / النقض / التعقيب · The highest court in several Arab states (a French calque): Kuwait, Jordan and the UAE say التمييز, Egypt and Syria النقض, Tunisia التعقيب. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Court of First Instance
chunks.text: Court of First Instance · المحكمة الابتدائية · The court that first hears a case; Jordan says محكمة البداية, Lebanon محكمة الدرجة الأولى. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Power of attorney
chunks.text: Power of attorney · سَنَد التوكيل · A document authorizing someone (an attorney-in-fact, وكيل) to act for another. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Notary public
chunks.text: Notary public · كاتب العدل · An official who certifies documents; in the Maghreb a عَدْل does similar work. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Affidavit
chunks.text: Affidavit · إقرار مشفوع باليمين · A written statement sworn to be true; a declarative legal text. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Prescriptive legal text
chunks.text: Prescriptive legal text · النص القانوني المُلزِم · A text that imposes obligations with sanctions: constitutions, treaties, laws, contracts. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Metalegal text
chunks.text: Metalegal text · النص الواصف للقانون · A text about the law (textbooks, articles) that is not itself a legal instrument. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Doublet (legal)
chunks.text: Doublet (legal) الثنائيات القانونية · A fixed legal pair of near-synonyms (null and void; terms and conditions), usually one word in Arabic (باطل; شروط). Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Shall (legal)
chunks.text: Shall (legal) صيغة الإلزام · In legal English, an obligation (like must), never a future; Arabic often uses a plain imperfect. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Performative do
chunks.text: Performative do · فعل الأداء · The non-emphatic ‘do’ of legal English (‘We the People … do ordain’); not translated into Arabic. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Recognized translation
chunks.text: Recognized translation · الترجمة المعتمدة · An official translation that later texts must follow, such as Oman’s ‘Ministry of Legal Affairs’ for وزارة الشؤون القانونية. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Whereas clause
chunks.text: Whereas clause · «لمّا كان» A preamble clause giving the grounds for a legal act; Arabic opens each with لمّا كان / ولمّا كان. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: In compliance with
chunks.text: In compliance with · عملاً بـ · The usual Arabic rendering of this legal phrase, not any of the dictionary verbs for ‘comply’. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Waqf / habs
chunks.text: Waqf / habs · وقف / حبس · A religious endowment: وقف in the Mashriq, حبس in North Africa; often borrowed as waqf. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Idda
chunks.text: Idda · العِدّة · The legally prescribed waiting period before a woman may remarry; paraphrased or borrowed in translation. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

chunks.title: Mahr
chunks.text: Mahr · المَهْر · The dowry paid to the bride in an Islamic marriage contract. Husni & Newman (2015), ch. 3

human · BAS · HN15 · What a translator really does · دور المترجم · A translator reads, interprets, decides and then writes. Three published cases show the job better than any definition. للّه دَرُّه! His milk is due to God. Every word of the literal version is in the dictionary, yet the meaning is lost. The book calls it “a mock-exoticism”. Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 1. Bon appétit, said by a father to break the silence after a bitter family quarrel. Good appetite means nothing in English. The translator must weigh who speaks, to whom, and what the moment means. Bassnett, 2014, pp. 30–33. A Lebanese wedding planner speaks Lebanese Arabic among Saudi characters (بنات الرياض) Arab readers hear the dialect; English readers cannot, so the translator adds four words. “The translator explicated what is implicit.” Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 82–83. Translation is “a process of negotiation between texts and between cultures … mediated by the figure of the translator” — and the translator “has a clear moral responsibility to the TL readers”. Bassnett, 2014, pp. 6, 33 · Three kinds of translation · أنواع الترجمة الثلاثة · Roman Jakobson distinguishes three types (Bassnett, 2014, pp. 25–26):Intralingual: rewording in the same language.Interlingual: translation between two languages, “translation proper”.Intersemiotic: from words into another sign system, such as music, dance, cinema or painting.Even apparent synonyms are never perfect equivalents: each word carries “non-transferable associations and connotations”. Language lives inside culture · اللغة والثقافة

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: Bassnett compares language to the heart within the body of culture: just as a surgeon cannot neglect the body, “the translator treats the text in isolation from the culture at his or her peril” (2014, p. 25). butter (British English) A perfect dictionary match, but in Britain butter is spread on bread and carries high status; in Italy it is mainly for cooking. Same word, different value. Bassnett, 2014, pp. 29–30 · patient owl · In the West the owl stands for wisdom; in Arab culture it is “the night crow” (غراب الليل), a bad omen. Drop the owl or use an Arabic animal with the same quality. Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 19. Languages divide the world differently: Finnish has many words for snow, “in Arabic for aspects of camel behaviour”. Bassnett, 2014, p. 40 · Formal and dynamic equivalence · التكافؤ الشكلي والديناميكي · Eugene Nida separates two kinds of equivalence (as cited in Bassnett, 2014, p. 36):Formal equivalence “focuses attention on the message itself, in both form and content”.Dynamic equivalence aims at equivalent effect: the new reader should respond as the original reader did.Equivalent effect can go too far. One Bible translation turned “greeting with a holy kiss” into “give one another a hearty handshake all round” — “what seems to be a piece of inadequate translation in poor taste”. Loss and gain · الفقد والكسب

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: Since two languages never match exactly, something is always lost. But the translator “can at times enrich or clarify the SL text as a direct result of the translation process”, and what is lost in one place can be made up elsewhere (Bassnett, 2014, p. 39). This making-up is called compensation. اشتغل على كتابه ليلَ نهار · He worked on his book day and night. The pair is dropped and its emphasis is carried by every single. Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 22 · Domestication and foreignisation · التوطين والتغريب · Schleiermacher (1813) contrasted a translation that reads as if written in the target language with one that keeps the foreign visible. Lawrence Venuti took this up: “Domestication conforms to the expectations, values and norms of the target culture, while foreignization challenges readers by making them aware that they are encountering texts from outside their known parameters.” Bassnett, 2014, pp. 46–47Neither is always right. The brief, the readers and the purpose decide. Purpose decides: Skopos · نظرية الغاية · Reiss and Vermeer called it skopos, Greek for “purpose”. Vermeer’s rule: “Translate/interpret/speak/write in a way that enables your text/translation to function in the situation in which it is used and with the people who want to use it and precisely in the way they want it to function.” Bassnett, 2014, p. 84So a professional letter, an instruction manual or a recipe may be restructured in the target language, from word-for-word to a complete rewrite, depending on what it must do.

colloc · HN15 · The company a word keeps · التلازم اللفظي · Collocation is “the company that words keep”, and it often defies logic: we make a mistake but do an exercise. Each language chooses its own partners (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 1). thundering applause · Arabic applause is a storm. p. 1 · an indifferent reception · Arabic makes it tepid. p. 1 · Free, restricted and bound · أنواع المتلازمات · Free: each word combines freely, as in red car.Restricted: one word takes a small set of partners. To perpetrate and ارتكب both go with crime: ارتكب جريمة (p. 3). So do مصادر مطّلعة and جمهور غفير (p. 4).Bound: one word appears with only one partner: حربٌ ضروس fierce war, أمٌّ رؤوم doting mother, عقبةٌ كؤود insurmountable obstacle (p. 5).Arabic has many more bound collocations than English. As early as the eleventh century, al-Thaʿālibī collected them in Fiqh al-Lugha (p. 5). One word, many partners · كلمة واحدة وشركاء كثر · English heavy has about thirty Arabic equivalents, depending on the noun (Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 16–17): English · Arabic · heavy rain · مطر غزير · heavy fog · ضباب كثيف · heavy sleep · سبات عميق · heavy seas · بحار هائجة · heavy smoker · مدخّن مفرط · heavy industry · صناعة ثقيلة · heavy losses · خسائر هائلة · heavy responsibility · مسؤولية عظيمة · heavy bombing · قصف عنيف · It works the other way too: أدّى واجبه to do one’s duty, أدّى يميناً to swear an oath; ضرب خيمة to pitch a tent, ضرب رقماً قياسياً to break a record, ضرب مثلاً to give an example (pp. 17–18). Don’t trust the dictionary alone · فخّ المعنى المعجمي

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: Translating each word by its dictionary meaning gives Arabic that is understandable but not what native speakers say (Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 15–16): English · Word by word · What Arabic says · electrically charged · مشحون بالكهرباء · مشبّع بالكهرباء · imminent danger · خطر قريب · خطر مُحدِق · unexpected danger · خطر غير متوقّع · خطر داهم · warm reception · استقبال ساخن · استقبال حارّ · Use a collocations dictionary and a corpus. A corpus shows at once that شعواء goes only with حرب, and that حريق goes with شبّ and التهم (p. 24). Translating a collocation · ترجمة المتلازمات · Husni and Newman list the options (2015, pp. 20–21):Equivalent collocation: to shed tears ذرف دموعاً; to shed leaves أسقط ورقاً.Paraphrase: to hose down نظّف بالماء.Functional equivalent: to shed blood قتل.Borrowing: the Cold War الحرب الباردة.Some calques are now ordinary Arabic: وقع في الحب, كذبة بيضاء, خط ساخن (p. 20). The choice depends on text type, register and audience (p. 21). Idioms grow from culture · التعابير الاصطلاحية · An idiom’s meaning “is not the sum of the meaning of its parts” (quoted in Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 26), and its words are frozen: بين المطرقة والسندان, never بين السندان والمطرقة (p. 27). heart-warming · A language born in desert heat finds comfort in coolness; the easy life is عيش بارد, a “cold life”. p. 28 · apples and oranges · Opposites are “fat and fire” in Arabic. p. 28 · False friends · الأصدقاء المخادعون · Some idioms look alike and mean different things (Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 29–31): Arabic · Looks like · Actually means · فقد أعصابه

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: to lose one’s nerve (courage) to lose one’s temper · من أجل عينيك · for your eyes only (secret) for your sake · سحب ذيله · tail between one’s legs (shame) to strut · عضّ أنامله · nail-biting (anxiety) anger · شدّ حزامه · to tighten one’s belt · also: to prepare oneself · “The translator has to guard against imposing SL meanings on TL idioms, irrespective of formal similarities.” p. 31 · Seven ways to translate an idiom · استراتيجيات ترجمة التعبير · In order of preference (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 33):Same meaning and form: an iron fist in a velvet glove قبضة حديدية في قفاز مخملي; the lion’s share نصيب الأسد.Same meaning, different form: a drop in the ocean غيض من فيض; to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds لعب على الحبلين.Paraphrase keeping some culture: to back the wrong horse راهن على الجواد الخاسر.Functional equivalent: dark horse شخص غامض.Omission: it really got his hackles up → استشاط غضباً.Addition: to shrug one’s shoulders هزّ كتفيه / هزّ كتفيه لامبالاةً.Borrowing: to have green fingers يده خضراء.For it’s raining cats and dogs the book lists the borrowing تمطر الدنيا قططاً وكلاباً, idioms such as إنّ الدنيا تمطر كأفواه القرب, and the plain إنّ الدنيا تمطر بغزارة: register and audience decide (pp. 34–35). Similes · التشبيه

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: Similes are bound to culture. Rendering as strong as a horse as قوي مثل فرس “would provoke ridicule from most Arabic speakers” (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 35). The options (p. 36):Same form and meaning: as strong as a lion قوي كالأسد.Same meaning, different form: as patient as Job صبر أيوب.Omission with compensation: as thin as a matchstick في غاية الرقة.Literal, signposted: as fast as a bullet سريع كرصاصة (كما يقال بالإنكليزية). Proverbs · الأمثال · Proverbs carry folk wisdom, resist any change, and hold a high place in Arabic at every social level (Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 36–37). عصفورٌ في اليد خيرٌ من عشرةٍ على الشجرة · Equivalent proverb, same form. p. 38 · إذا كثُر الربابنةُ غرقت السفينة · Same meaning, different image. p. 39 · غابت السباعُ ولعبت الضباع · p. 39 · مَن حفر حفرةً لأخيه وقع فيها · An equivalent idiom conveying the result. p. 39 · Patience is a virtue. Arabic proverbs use religious language far more often. p. 38 · الكلابُ تنبح والقافلةُ تسير · Borrowed, with a clear rendering. p. 39 · Word pairs · المزاوجة · Both languages join near-synonyms into fixed pairs: null and void, first and foremost; الصالح والطالح, لا يُعدّ ولا يُحصى (Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 5–6). Arabic still creates them freely. The book’s strategies (pp. 21–22): الجنّة والنار · A similar pair. فتّش عن موظف جديد على السهل والوعر · Another pair. بلا قيدٍ أو شرط · One word for the pair. قلباً وقالباً · Functional equivalent. Phrasal verbs and compounds · الأفعال العبارية والمركّبات

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: Phrasal verbs are “one of the black spots” of learning and translation (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 9). Take off alone is خلع (clothes), أقلع (a plane), قلّد (imitate), نجح (succeed), بتر (amputate) and خفّض (deduct) (p. 10).English builds compounds freely; Arabic usually uses an إضافة or a phrase: bedroom غرفة نوم, real-estate agency وكالة عقارية, fire drill تدريب على إطفاء الحريق — keep the preposition (pp. 48–49).Into English, avoid turning every إضافة into of: مطار القاهرة is Cairo airport, صانع القرار is decision-maker (pp. 50–51).

revise · HN15 · HN13 · Dialect, register, idiolect · اللهجة والمستوى اللغوي · A dialect differs in pronunciation, grammar and words; an accent only in pronunciation. Register is the level of formality, and getting it wrong causes comic or confusing effects: nobody in a fight says “I say, old fellow, will you kindly desist from hitting me?” Each person also has an idiolect, a personal way of speaking. Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 56–57 · Diglossia · الازدواجية اللغوية · Arabic has a standard variety (الفصحى) beside many spoken dialects (العامية). The dialect is the mother tongue; the standard is learned at school. Charles Ferguson (1959) described a “high” variety for sermons, lectures and news and a “low” one for family and friends; real speech moves along a continuum between them. Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 58–62The word diglossia was first used by Ioannis Psicharis for Greek; William Marçais applied it to Arabic (p. 58). Standard Arabic varies too · تنوّع الفصحى · Modern Standard Arabic is not identical across the Arab world (Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 64–71):mobile phone: جوّال، نقّال، محمول، خلوي، هاتف متحرّك, by country.January: كانون الثاني (Levant), جانفي (Tunisia, Algeria), يناير (Egypt, Morocco).إجازة is a degree in Lebanon and a holiday in Egypt; تدّعي على means “to sue” in Lebanese usage and “to accuse falsely” in Egyptian usage.For readers across the Arab world, choose a neutral word: قابلية الأكل rather than the regional صلاحية or صلوحية (p. 71). Dialogue into English · ترجمة الحوار إلى الإنجليزية

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: Arabic novels often write dialogue in formal Arabic, so the translator must decide how the character really sounds (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 77): ماذا تقولين يا أمّي؟ — a thirteen-year-old boy · What are you saying, oh mother? Natural speech for the speaker. p. 77 · Beware the Victorian “pseudo-biblical, neo-gothic, mock-Elizabethan, bogus Oriental style”. Bernard Lewis, as cited in Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 73 · Dialect into Arabic · ترجمة اللهجة إلى العربية · Which dialect would you choose? Any one may exclude readers elsewhere. The same English line (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 79): Variety · That should not be a problem. Standard Arabic · لا ينبغي أن يكون ذلك بمشكلة · Kuwaiti · مافي أي مشكلة · Egyptian · مش مشكلة، مفيش مشكلة · Algerian · ما فيها باس · The book suggests a middle way (pp. 81–82): Standard Arabic with spoken features most readers recognise — اللي, subject–verb–object order, ـوا for ـون, ما for لم. Compare الكشافون الذين يلعبون بكرة القدم with الكشافين اللي يلعبوا بكرة القدم.Without such choices, voices flatten: one Arabic Sherlock Holmes gives a London policeman the same formal Arabic as Holmes, “a pragmatic and a cultural loss” (p. 86). A published commentary · تعليق منشور

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: Husni and Newman comment on their own English translation of Yūsuf Idrīs’s story حكاية مصرية جدًا (2015, pp. 87–89):يا أسطى → guv’: a British term used in similar situations; “teacher” or “sir” would sound wrong.عسكري → cop: “In keeping with the register, ‘cop’ is preferable here to something formal like ‘police officer’.”مترو → train, not metro: Cairo’s underground did not exist when the story was written.Each note names the problem, gives the solution and justifies it — the shape of a good commentary. Punctuation · علامات الترقيم · Western-style punctuation in Arabic is essentially a twentieth-century development and is often inconsistent. Writers may stack marks for intensity; in English, “these must be reduced” (Husni & Newman, 2013, entry “Punctuation”): مَن المسؤول: الشرطة أم المتظاهرون؟! Arabic suspension points (…) at the end of a list are usually omitted or replaced by a comma. Writing Arabic names in English · النقل الحرفي · Transliteration maps letter to letter; transcription renders the sound. نجيب محفوظ is Najīb Maḥfūẓ for scholars but Naguib Mahfouz in everyday English; محمد may be Muhammad, Mohammed or Mohamed. Don’t write Saeed and Aziz in one line: the same Arabic letter spelled two ways. Choose the system for the audience, and keep naturalised spellings such as imam. Husni & Newman, 2013, entry “Transliteration and transcription”

revise · HN15 · HN13 · Legal texts follow a legal system · الترجمة القانونية · Legal translation is tied to a legal system, not just a language: in the US to table a proposal means to shelve it, in the UK to submit it for discussion (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 98). The translator must understand “what legal effect it is supposed to have, and how to achieve that legal effect in the other language” (quoted on p. 99). Legal shall · shall في النصوص القانونية · In legal English shall expresses obligation, not the future (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 138). Arabic legal texts often use the present tense (المضارع), not سوف: Each State Party shall adopt such measures as may be necessary. UN convention text. p. 140 · The employee shall be deemed to have been appointed under probation for three months. Husni & Newman, 2013, entry “Will/shall” The passive · المبني للمجهول · Legal English uses the passive far more than Arabic does. Arabic translations often use an active verb or a verbal noun (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 137): The proposed budget shall be reviewed by the Committee. p. 137 · The truce was broken by the government. تمّ اختراق الهدنة من جانب الحكومة · A named doer with من قبل / من طرف / من جانب is “not considered normative usage” and is “frowned upon by careful users of Arabic”. Husni & Newman, 2013, entry “The passive” Translation memory · ذاكرة الترجمة

chunks.title: #1 (cont.)
chunks.text: Translation memory tools store your past translations and suggest them for new segments; they save the most time for translators who work in one field. But remember “Rubbish in – Rubbish out”: a memory is only as good as what was stored, and it can repeat old errors (Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 165–167). Online dictionaries and forums · القواميس الإلكترونية · Many free online dictionaries have fewer entries than good printed ones, are updated less often, give few collocations and examples, and often name no author, sources or method. Most translators would not accept a term from a stranger in the street, yet many accept one from a stranger on a forum. Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 168–169 · Machine translation · الترجمة الآلية · The Georgetown experiment (1954) translated over sixty Russian sentences automatically, and its makers expected the problem to be solved within years. Yehoshua Bar-Hillel answered with “The box was in the pen”: a machine cannot tell a playpen from a writing pen (Husni & Newman, 2015, pp. 169–170). اشترت أختي سيارة جديدة الأسبوع الماضي · Sisters car of the new week last bought. Two online systems tested in the book produced the broken version; an Arabic legal sentence defeated every system. Complex syntax was the main stumbling block. pp. 171–172. Note: today’s systems are far more fluent than those tested in 2015, but a fluent sentence is not always an accurate one. Always post-edit.

chunks.title: Borrowing
chunks.text: Borrowing · الاِقتِراض · Take the foreign word into the target language unchanged, and let it naturalise. No term exists yet in the target language · The foreignness is part of the meaning · A brand, a proper name, a dish · Borrowing when the target language already has a perfectly good word. Arabic has حاسوب; reaching for كمبيوتر out of habit is laziness, not a procedure. computer · Borrowed and now fully naturalised — it takes Arabic plurals and adjectives. تُرجُمان · Borrowing runs both ways. English took the Ottoman court interpreter's title straight from Arabic. الجَبْر · So did algorithm, alcohol, cipher. Half of English mathematics is borrowed Arabic.

chunks.title: Calque
chunks.text: Calque · النَّسْخ · Translate the source expression piece by piece to build a new expression in the target language. Coining a term the language needs · The image survives the crossing · Technical and institutional vocabulary · Most calques fail. A successful one enters the dictionary; a failed one reads as a mistranslation. You cannot tell in advance — you have to check whether it is already in use. skyscraper · A calque that won. It is now the only Arabic word for it, and no reader hears the English underneath. cold war · Another success — the metaphor crossed intact and became standard. the elephant in the room · الفيل في الغُرفة · A calque that fails. No Arabic reader decodes it, so describe the thing instead.

chunks.title: Literal translation
chunks.text: Literal translation · التَّرجَمة الحَرفيّة · Word for word, structure for structure — when the two languages happen to agree. Concrete, unmarked, everyday statements · The syntax lines up without strain · Legal text where nothing may shift · Treating this as the default and the other six as decoration. Literal translation is one tool among seven, and between Arabic and English it is the one that fits least often. I left my book on the table. Nothing is gained by intervening. When literal works, use it and move on. The meeting begins at nine. Same. Resist the urge to embellish neutral text. It's raining cats and dogs. تُمطِر قِططاً وكِلاباً · And here it collapses. The test is not grammar — it is whether the reader receives what the source reader received.

chunks.title: Transposition
chunks.text: Transposition · الإبدال · Change the part of speech without changing the meaning. The target language prefers a different grammatical shape. Arabic prefers verbs where English prefers nouns · Unpacking an English noun-stack · Carrying English nominalisation into Arabic. English says after his return; Arabic says بعد أن عاد — a verb. Keeping the noun produces stiff, translated-sounding Arabic. He is a fast runner. هو عَدّاء سَريع. Adjective + noun becomes verb + adverb. Arabic would rather do than be. after his return from Cairo · بعد عَودَته من القاهِرة · The literal is grammatical and still reads as a translation. The verb reads as Arabic. زادَ الطَّلَبُ زِيادةً كبيرة. The demand increased a large increase. Arabic's absolute object (المفعول المطلق) has no English form — it becomes an adverb.

chunks.title: Modulation
chunks.text: Modulation · التَّطويع · Change the point of view — say the same thing from the other side. The literal is correct but reads oddly · Negation in one language is affirmation in the other · Cause and effect swap places · Modulating when nothing required it. This procedure is for when the direct route produces awkward target text, not a licence to rewrite. It is not difficult. ليس صعباً. Litotes in English, plain statement in Arabic. Both are available — pick the one the context wants. Don't forget to call. لا تَنسَ أن تتّصِل. Negative to positive. Arabic often prefers the affirmative instruction. ما تقصّر. You do not fall short. The same flip in the other direction — Arabic denies a fault, English states a virtue.

chunks.title: Equivalence
chunks.text: Equivalence · التَّكافُؤ · Replace a whole fixed expression with the target language's own fixed expression for that situation. Proverbs, idioms, set phrases · Formulaic politeness · Anything the source reader recognised as a unit. Translating the words inside the unit. A proverb is one item of vocabulary, not a sentence to be parsed. Once upon a time… مرّة واحدة على وقت… Both open a story. Neither is a translation of the other, and that is the point. يد واحدة لا تصفّق. One hand does not clap. Same claim, different image, equal recognisability. That is equivalence. تسلم إيدك. May your hand be safe. And here the procedure runs out: English has no fixed expression for this moment, so there is nothing to swap in. The function — praise plus thanks — has to be stated instead.

chunks.title: Adaptation
chunks.text: Adaptation · التَّكييف · Change the cultural reference itself, because the original refers to something the target reader does not have. Culture-bound objects, foods, holidays, institutions · Marketing and localisation · Children's literature · Over-adapting. If the source culture is what the reader came for — a novel set in Kansas — erasing it is a betrayal, not a service. Adapt the reference only when the reference is a vehicle, not the cargo. as American as apple pie · أمريكي كفطيرة التفّاح · Keep the shape of the comparison, swap the object for one the reader actually loves. Break a leg! اِكسِر ساقك! The English is superstition dressed as an insult. Arabic has no theatre superstition, so only the function crosses. a Thanksgiving dinner · عَشاء عيد الشُّكر · Sometimes the right adaptation is none: keep the foreign reference and footnote it, rather than turning it into عيد الفطر and losing the setting.

chunks.title: Journalistic
chunks.text: Journalistic · صَحافيّ · News is the highest-volume translation work in the Arab world and the fastest. An agency desk may rebuild a wire story in eight minutes. What you are handling is not prose but a structure: an inverted pyramid with the whole story in sentence one, a headline that obeys its own grammar in each language, and a set of house formulas that repeat across every story a newsroom publishes. الترجمة الصحفيّة أكثر أنواع الترجمة انتشاراً وأسرعها إيقاعاً. والنصّ الخبريّ ليس نصّاً أدبيّاً بل بنية ثابتة: الخبر كلّه في الجملة الأولى، والعنوان له قواعده الخاصّة في كلّ لغة، والصياغات مكرّرة معروفة في كلّ غرفة أخبار. فمهمّتك أن تنقل البنية لا الكلمات. Read the whole story before translating a word — the lead often needs reordering. Translate the body first and the headline last. Your headline summarises your Arabic, not the English headline. Turn the headline into a nominal sentence — a verbal noun (ارتفاع، اجتياح), no finite verb. Flatten the reporting verbs: أكّد، أشار، أوضح all become said unless the source truly means more. Use the target newsroom's own stock formulas, not translations of the source's. Verify every name, number, date and place against a second source. Mistakes here are corrections, not style notes. News prose is built to be scanned. The first sentence carries the whole story, verbs stay neutral, and the headline plays by its own grammar in each language. Front-load the information — who, what, where, in sentence one. Keep reporting verbs flat: said, not confirmed or revealed. Match the target language's headline grammar, not the source's

chunks.title: Journalistic (cont.)
chunks.text: English headlines are verbal and drop articles; Arabic headlines are nominal (جملة اسمية). Translating an English headline word-for-word produces something no Arabic newsdesk would print. Aid convoy turned back at border as talks stall. قافلة المساعدات أُعيدت من الحدود بينما تتعثّر المحادثات. Every verb became a verbal noun and the conjunction shrank to a bare و. The literal is grammatical Arabic — it is simply not headline Arabic, and no desk in the region would run it. أكّد المتحدّث أنّ القوّات لم تدخل المدينة. The spokesman confirmed that the forces had not entered the city. One word, and the story changes. Confirmed tells the reader the claim is established; أكّد is simply the ordinary Arabic verb for said. This one habit has put corrections on the wires more often than any other error in the genre. The minister, who had returned from Cairo only hours earlier and was speaking to reporters outside the ministry, said the agreement would be signed within weeks. قال الوزير، الذي كان قد عاد من القاهرة قبل ساعات فقط وكان يتحدّث إلى الصحفيين خارج الوزارة، إنّ الاتّفاق سيُوقَّع في غضون أسابيع. English buries the news in the middle of a thirty-word sentence. Arabic news style puts it first and pushes the circumstances into a second sentence. Same facts, opposite architecture — and no amount of care at word level gets you there.

chunks.title: Political & Diplomatic
chunks.text: Political & Diplomatic · سِياسيّ ودِبلوماسيّ · In political translation the vocabulary is the argument. Two renderings can both be accurate and carry opposite claims, so the choice of a word is the choice of a position — and you are making it whether you notice or not. Professionals handle this by not deciding alone: they work to a style guide, flag contested terms upward, and keep the source's attributions and hedges exactly where they were. في النصّ السياسيّ يكون اختيار المفردة هو الموقف نفسه. فقد تكون ترجمتان صحيحتين لغويّاً وتحملان معنيين متعارضين. ولهذا لا يقرّر المترجم وحده: يلتزم بدليل التحرير، ويشير إلى المصطلحات الخلافيّة ليقرّرها المحرّر، ويحافظ على النسبة والتحوّط كما وردا في الأصل دون تقوية أو تخفيف. Establish who is publishing this and for whom before you settle a single term. Get the outlet's style guide or glossary. If none exists, ask for one in writing. Mark every contested term and query it — never resolve it silently. Preserve attributions and hedges word for word: alleged, reportedly, according to, وُصِف بأنّه. Use the official rendering for institutions, treaties and titles; coining a new one implies a different document. Reread your Arabic asking one question: does it assert anything the English only reported? In political text the word choice is the content. Two accurate renderings can carry opposite framings, and the translator does not get to be neutral by accident — only on purpose. Know that a lexical choice is a framing choice, and make it consciously. Follow the client's or outlet's style guide; do not improvise terminology

chunks.title: Political & Diplomatic (cont.)
chunks.text: Preserve hedges and attributions exactly — alleged, reportedly, according to. Silently picking one side's vocabulary because it came first to mind. When a term is contested, flag it for the editor rather than deciding alone. austerity measures · إجراءات التقشُّف · Both name the identical policy. The first is what its critics call it; the second is what its authors call it. There is no neutral option here — only a chosen one, and the choice belongs to the editor, not to you. undocumented migrants · مهاجرون غير شَرعيّين · The English deliberately avoids illegal. Rendering it غير شرعيّين reverses that decision and takes a position the source refused to take. Here the literal is not the neutral choice — it is an edit. Witnesses said the vehicle appeared to have been struck from the air. المركبة أُصيبت من الجوّ. The English carries two layers of distance — witnesses said and appeared to. The literal deletes both and turns an unverified account into the newspaper's own finding. This is the most consequential mistake available in political translation.

chunks.title: Legal
chunks.text: Legal · قانونيّ · Legal text is read by someone looking for a loophole. Its virtues are the opposite of good writing: repetition instead of variation, rigidity instead of flow, length instead of economy. You are not producing a readable document — you are producing one that cannot be argued into a second meaning. Everything you would normally improve, here you must leave alone. النصّ القانونيّ يقرؤه من يبحث عن ثغرة، وفضائله عكس فضائل الكتابة الجيّدة: التكرار لا التنويع، والجمود لا السلاسة، والإطناب لا الاختصار. أنت لا تنتج نصّاً سهل القراءة بل نصّاً لا يمكن تحويله إلى معنى ثانٍ. وكلّ ما تودّ تحسينه في نصّ آخر يجب أن تتركه هنا كما هو. Read the definitions clause first and build your glossary out of it. Render each defined term one way everywhere — including inside quotations and headings. Keep the numbering, the clause boundaries and every cross-reference untouched. Translate modal force, not tense: shall = يجب/يلتزم, may = يجوز, must = يتعيّن. Never سوف. Keep doublets (باطل ولاغٍ) and keep the passive wherever the source uses it to avoid naming an actor. Never fix the source. If a clause is ambiguous in English it stays ambiguous in Arabic — flag it to counsel. Legal translation is the one place where elegance is a defect. Nothing may be added, nothing lost, nothing smoothed. The reader is a court. One defined term, one rendering, throughout the entire instrument. Keep doublets and archaisms — legal Arabic has its own. Preserve sentence boundaries and numbering; do not tidy the syntax

chunks.title: Legal (cont.)
chunks.text: Shall is not سوف. In legal English shall imposes an obligation — يجب / يلتزم / يتعيّن. Reading it as a future tense changes a duty into a prediction. The Contractor shall indemnify the Client against all claims. المُتعَهِّد سوف يُعوِّض العميل عن جميع المطالبات. Shall is not the future here — it is a duty. سوف converts a binding obligation into a prediction about what the contractor will probably do, which no court can enforce. The single most expensive word in legal translation. Time is of the essence. الوقت من الجوهر. Four English words become fourteen Arabic ones — because the phrase is not a description, it is a term of art that makes lateness a material breach. The literal is elegant and says nothing a court can act on. including, but not limited to, the following: متضمّناً، لكن ليس محدوداً بـ، ما يلي: Legal Arabic already owns this formula, and it is the only version a court reads as non-exhaustive. The literal reads as a translator's improvisation and invites exactly the argument the clause exists to prevent.

chunks.title: Technical
chunks.text: Technical · تِقنيّ · Technical text is followed, not read. Someone has a machine or a screen in front of them and your sentence tells them what to press next. Consistency is not a stylistic preference here — it is the entire product. Two words for one thing means the reader concludes there are two things, and then the procedure fails. النصّ التقنيّ يُتَّبع ولا يُقرأ. فأمام القارئ جهاز أو شاشة، وجملتك تخبره بما يضغط تالياً. والاتّساق هنا ليس ذوقاً بل هو المنتج نفسه: كلمتان لشيء واحد تعنيان أنّ القارئ سيظنّ أنّهما شيئان، فيفشل الإجراء. اختر المصطلح مرّة والتزم به إلى آخر الملفّ. Build the glossary before translating, from the client's terminology and the shipped interface. Work in a CAT tool with a termbase so drift is caught mechanically instead of by memory. Match UI strings to the actual localised interface, character for character — including the buttons. Keep instructions imperative and short: one action per sentence. Gloss a borrowed term once in parentheses — الذّاكِرة المُؤقَّتة (cache) — then commit to one form. Finish with a terminology-only pass, searching the file for every glossary entry. Technical translation rewards consistency over beauty. The same term must appear the same way on page 1 and page 400, because the reader is following a procedure and a synonym reads as a different thing. Build a glossary before you translate a single line, and obey it. Never vary a term for style — variation is an error here. Match the product's own UI strings; do not translate a button freshly

chunks.title: Technical (cont.)
chunks.text: Elegant variation. In literary work, repeating a word is a weakness; in technical work, not repeating it is a bug. user account password reset request form · مستخدم حساب كلمة مرور إعادة تعيين طلب نموذج · English stacks five nouns left to right; Arabic chains them right to left as an إضافة, so the entire order reverses. Translate this one word at a time and you produce a string no reader can parse — the classic signature of machine output. Restore default settings — the same command, three times in one manual. استعادة الإعدادات التلقائيّة … استعادة الإعدادات الافتراضيّة … استرجاع الضبط المبدئيّ. All three renderings are defensible Arabic. Together they tell the reader there are three different features. In technical work the error is not the word choice; it is the variation. Click Save. اِضغط «حِفظ». — while the shipped button actually reads «تخزين» The manual must name the button that exists, not the button you would have named. A flawless translation of the wrong label is a support ticket with your name on it.

chunks.title: Medical
chunks.text: Medical · طِبّيّ · Medical text splits by reader before it splits by language. One drug generates a regulatory dossier, a clinician's summary and a patient leaflet, and all three use different words for the same condition. Getting the level wrong is not awkward writing; it is a leaflet the patient cannot act on. Accuracy here includes being understood. الترجمة الطبّيّة تتفرّع بحسب القارئ قبل أن تتفرّع بحسب اللغة. فالدواء الواحد له ملفّ تنظيميّ وملخّص للطبيب ونشرة للمريض، وثلاثتها تستخدم ألفاظاً مختلفة للحالة نفسها. والخطأ في المستوى اللغويّ ليس عيباً في الأسلوب بل نشرة لا يستطيع المريض العمل بها. فالدقّة هنا تشمل أن تُفهَم. Establish the audience from the brief first: regulator, clinician, or patient. Use the established Arabic term — the Unified Medical Dictionary or the client's glossary. Never coin one. Keep numbers, units, frequencies and time windows absolutely literal. Daily and 24 hours are different windows. Preserve every negation and every warning. Never compress a contraindication to save space. For patient material, read it aloud to a non-specialist. If they stumble, rewrite it. Have a clinician review anything touching dosage, diagnosis or interactions before delivery. Medical text splits by audience before it splits by language. The same condition has one name for a clinician and another for the patient holding the leaflet, and mixing them is a safety problem, not a style one. Identify the reader first — clinician, patient, or regulator. Use the established term, never a fresh coinage. Keep dosage, units and negations absolutely literal

chunks.title: Medical (cont.)
chunks.text: Levelling the register. A patient information leaflet written in clinician Arabic is not a translation — it is a document nobody can act on. Your test result is negative. نتيجة تحليلك سَلبيّة. In everyday Arabic سلبيّة means bad. Patients have read a clean result as a diagnosis and acted on it. A clinician's summary keeps سلبيّة; a patient leaflet must say what it means. Same word, two documents, one of them dangerous. Do not take more than 4 tablets in 24 hours. لا تأخذ أكثر من ٤ حبّات يوميّاً. Daily resets at midnight; 24 hours is a rolling window. A patient who takes four at eleven at night and four at one in the morning has obeyed the literal translation exactly — and taken a double dose. side effects · adverse events · الأعراض الجانبيّة for both · Not synonyms in regulatory writing. An adverse event is anything that happened during treatment; a side effect is one attributed to the drug. Collapsing them changes what the document reports to a regulator.

chunks.title: Literary
chunks.text: Literary · أدبيّ · Literary translation is the only kind where the shape of the sentence is part of what it says. You are handed an effect built out of one language's materials and asked to rebuild it out of another's. So the question is never what does this mean — it is what does this do, and how do I make Arabic do it. الترجمة الأدبيّة هي النوع الوحيد الذي يكون شكل الجملة فيه جزءاً من معناها. يُسلَّم إليك أثرٌ بُني بموادّ لغة، ويُطلب منك أن تعيد بناءه من موادّ لغة أخرى. ولذلك ليس السؤال «ما معنى هذا؟» بل «ما الذي يفعله هذا، وكيف أجعل العربيّة تفعله؟». وما تخسره، اخسره بقرار لا بغفلة. Read the whole work before you translate a line. Voice is a pattern; one page cannot reveal it. Fix each character's register early and hold it to the last page. When something must be lost, choose which deliberately — and write the choice down. Leave every ambiguity ambiguous. Resist the urge to help the reader. Read your Arabic aloud. Rhythm and sentence length carry pace, and the ear catches what the eye misses. Add a translator's note for what you sacrificed. That is scholarship, not apology. Literary translation is the only kind where the form is part of the message. You are not moving information; you are rebuilding an effect out of different materials. Preserve voice — a character's register is characterisation. Keep what the author left ambiguous ambiguous. Match rhythm and sentence length; they carry pace

chunks.title: Literary (cont.)
chunks.text: Explaining. When a translator resolves an ambiguity, fills a silence, or unpacks a metaphor, the reader loses the experience the author built. Trust the reader as much as the author did. يا ليلُ طُلْ، ويا نَومُ زُلْ. O night, lengthen; O sleep, depart. The Arabic rhymes طُلْ with زُلْ, and that rhyme is the line's entire music. The literal keeps the meaning and throws the poem away; the rendering rebuilds a music of its own out of English stress. Form is content here. ولم يقل شيئاً حين رآها. And he said nothing when he saw her — because he still loved her. The Arabic refuses to say why. The 'helpful' version answers a question the author spent a chapter not answering. Explaining is the cardinal sin of the genre, and it is almost always committed with good intentions. شنو تسوّي هني؟ — spoken by a street character in a Kuwaiti novel · What are you doing here? The Arabic is dialect, and dialect in fiction is characterisation. A rendering in clean standard English silently promotes the character two social classes and erases the author's reason for writing him that way.

chunks.title: Marketing & Transcreation
chunks.text: Marketing & Transcreation · تَسويقيّ وإبداعيّ · Advertising is the genre where you are often paid not to translate. What the client owns is an effect — a feeling, a decision to buy — and the English sentence that produced it is disposable scaffolding. The deliverable is a new Arabic line that does the same job. That is a different service with its own name: transcreation, التَّرجَمة الإبداعيّة, and it is billed differently for good reason. الإعلان هو النوع الذي قد يُدفع لك فيه كي لا تترجم. فما يملكه العميل هو الأثر — شعور، أو قرار شراء — والجملة الإنجليزيّة التي أنتجته مجرّد سقالة تُهدَم بعد البناء. والمطلوب سطر عربيّ جديد يؤدّي الوظيفة نفسها، وهذه خدمة أخرى لها اسمها: الترجمة الإبداعيّة. Ask for the creative brief and the campaign's single message. Translate that, not the copy. Write three or four Arabic options, never one. The client is choosing, not receiving. Say every option out loud in the target dialect and listen for accidental meanings. Check the line and the product name against existing brands and slang in that market. Name the technique you used for each option — adaptation, discursive creation, compensation — so the client is choosing between arguments, not guesses. Return the options with one line of rationale each, so the client can judge the effect, not the wording. Advertising is the one genre where you are often asked not to translate at all. The deliverable is the emotion the campaign produces, and the sentence is disposable. Work from the creative brief, not the source sentence. Check the new line for unintended readings out loud, in dialect

chunks.title: Marketing & Transcreation (cont.)
chunks.text: Know which of the three you are being paid for: translation, adaptation, or transcreation. Translating a slogan. A slogan is a piece of engineering tuned to one language's sounds and puns; carried across word-for-word it arrives dead. What you owe the client is a new slogan with the same job. Just do it. اِفعَلها فقط. The English works because of three flat stresses and a refusal to explain itself. The literal Arabic has neither, and reads like an instruction from a manual. This is transcreation, التَّرجَمة الإبداعيّة, and it is a different service billed at a different rate. Sleep on it. — a mattress campaign · نَم عليه. The English fires on two meanings at once: lie on this mattress, and take your time deciding. No Arabic word does both jobs, so the pun cannot be translated at all — it has to be replaced by an Arabic pun that lands just as hard. Anything less loses half the ad. a campaign built around the Christmas dinner table · حملة عن عشاء عيد الميلاد · Nothing in the brief was about Christmas. It was about a loaded table and a crowded family, and in this market that table is set at sunset in Ramadan. Adapt the vehicle, deliver the cargo.

chunks.title: Localisation
chunks.text: Localisation · الأَقلَمة · Localisation is not a genre — it is a process, and the text is only part of what goes through it. A product is being moved into a market, and the words travel with dates, currencies, units, name fields, address forms, sort orders, images, colours, legal notices and the direction the interface runs in. The translator here works inside strings, not paragraphs, and often cannot see where a string will land. الأَقلَمة ليست نوعًا نصّيًّا بل عمليّة، والنصّ جزء ممّا يمرّ بها. فالمنتَج يُنقَل إلى سوق جديدة، وتسافر معه التواريخ والعملات والوحدات وحقول الأسماء وصِيَغ العناوين والصور والألوان والإشعارات القانونيّة واتّجاه الواجهة نفسها. Ask for context before you translate a string: where does it appear, what is the character limit, what can replace the placeholder? Never reorder or invent placeholders. {count} and %s are code; moving them is a bug, not a style choice. Translate the interface into Arabic and mirror it: the layout flips to right-to-left, not just the text alignment. Convert what has to convert — dates, times, currencies, units, number formats, week start — and flag what must not, such as version numbers and product names. Check that a name field, an address form and an alphabetical sort still work for the target market. Review images, icons, colours and examples for things that do not travel: hand gestures, flags, holidays, sample names and addresses. Plan for expansion: Arabic and English do not occupy the same width, and a button is a fixed box.

chunks.title: Localisation (cont.)
chunks.text: A process, not a genre: the product is being moved into a market, and the words are only one of the things that have to change. Context for every string before it is translated. Placeholders and markup carried through untouched. True right-to-left layout, not right-aligned English layout. Dates, units, currencies and sort orders converted, product names and versions left alone. Treating the string list as a text. Strings arrive out of order and out of context, so the same English word becomes a button, a heading and an error message in three different places. Translating the list top to bottom without asking where each one lands produces an interface that is correct line by line and incoherent as a whole. You have {count} new messages · لديك {count} رسائل جديدة · Arabic counts in singular, dual, and several plural shapes, so one sentence with one placeholder cannot be right for 1, 2, 3 and 11. This is a plural rule, not a translation choice, and it has to be handled in the localisation framework rather than patched in the string. 03/04/2026 · ٤ مارس ٢٠٢٦ — or 3 April 2026 · Nothing in the source says which number is the month. Rendering it either way is a guess with a one-in-two chance of being wrong, and in an invoice or a medical record that is not a small error. Raise it; do not translate it. an interface with a back arrow pointing left · واجهة عربيّة يشير سهم الرجوع فيها إلى اليمين

chunks.title: Localisation (cont.)
chunks.text: Progress bars, carousels, sliders, breadcrumbs and back arrows all reverse in a right-to-left interface, because they encode direction of travel. Right-aligning Arabic inside a left-to-right layout leaves an interface that reads correctly and behaves backwards.

chunks.title: Audiovisual Translation
chunks.text: Audiovisual Translation · التَّرجَمة السَّمعيّة البَصَريّة · Subtitling is translation with a ruler and a stopwatch. You have roughly 37 to 42 characters per line, two lines at most, and a viewer who reads about 17 characters a second while also watching the picture. Most of the work is deciding what to leave out, because the image and the actor's voice have already delivered half the meaning before your words arrive. الترجمة السمعيّة البصريّة ترجمة بمسطرة وساعة. لديك نحو ٣٧ إلى ٤٢ حرفاً في السطر، وسطران على الأكثر، ومشاهدٌ يقرأ نحو ١٧ حرفاً في الثانية وهو يتابع الصورة. وأكثر عملك أن تقرّر ما تحذفه، لأنّ الصورة ونبرة الممثّل أدّتا نصف المعنى قبل أن تصل كلماتك. Watch the scene before writing. The picture decides what you are allowed to cut. Spot the timings first, then write into the space you actually have — not the other way round. Cut vocatives, greetings, hesitations, repetitions, and names the viewer can already see. Break lines at grammatical joints, and never carry one subtitle across a shot change. One idea per subtitle. Split a long sentence rather than shrinking the text. Read every subtitle at playback speed. If you cannot finish it, neither can the viewer. Subtitling is translation under a stopwatch and a ruler. You have a character limit, a reading-speed limit, and a picture that already told the audience half of it. Respect the character limit and the reading speed — roughly 17 characters per second. Cut what the image, the tone or the context already carries · Never split a subtitle across a shot change

chunks.title: Audiovisual Translation (cont.)
chunks.text: Translating everything. Names, greetings, repetitions and hesitations usually go. A subtitle the viewer cannot finish reading has failed even if every word is right. واللّه ما كنت أدري إنّك جاي اليوم، لو دريت لجهّزت لك شي. — 98 characters. By God, I did not know that you were coming today; had I known, I would have prepared something for you. — 104 characters. A seventy-per-cent cut, and nothing the viewer needed is gone: the apology is already on the actor's face. In this genre compression is accuracy, because a subtitle nobody can finish reading has translated nothing. تسلم إيدك يا غالي، واللّه ما تقصّر أبداً، اللّه يعطيك العافية. May your hands be safe, dear one; by God, you never fall short; may God give you health. Three layered Gulf courtesies — seventy-nine characters — become nineteen. The warmth is carried by the voice and the face; the subtitle's only job is not to contradict them. a three-second shot carrying a fourteen-word English line. all fourteen words — 78 characters on screen for three seconds. At roughly seventeen characters a second, a three-second subtitle holds about fifty-one. Anything longer is not a subtitle the viewer read — it is one they saw. The ruler decides, not your judgement.

chunks.title: Academic
chunks.text: Academic · أكاديميّ · Scholarly prose is cautious on purpose. Its hedges, qualifiers and citations are claims about how certain the author is, and that certainty is part of the finding. A translator who tightens suggests into proves has not improved the paper — they have published a result the authors did not obtain. النصّ الأكاديميّ حذر بقصد. فتحوّطاته وقيوده وإحالاته دعاوى عن درجة يقين الباحث، ودرجة اليقين جزء من النتيجة. والمترجم الذي يحوّل «تشير» إلى «تُثبت» لم يحسّن البحث بل نشر نتيجة لم يتوصّل إليها أصحابه. فالأمانة هنا أن تنقل الشكّ كما نقلت الخبر. Identify the field and adopt its established Arabic terminology, not a rendering of your own. Keep every hedge, and count them: two hedges in the English need two in the Arabic. Do not merge or split the author's sentences. Argument structure is content. Follow the target journal's conventions for quotations, titles and references. Check every technical term that is also an everyday word — significant, control, subject, population. Flag anything you suspect is an error in the source. Never silently correct a published claim. Scholarly prose is careful on purpose. Its hedges, qualifications and citations are claims about certainty, and strengthening them is falsification. Preserve every hedge exactly — suggests, may indicate, appears to. Keep terminology aligned with the field's established Arabic, not your own. Reproduce citation and reference conventions of the target journal. Upgrading certainty. The data suggest is not the data prove, and a translator who tightens it has changed the paper's finding.

chunks.title: Academic (cont.)
chunks.text: These preliminary findings may indicate a possible association. تُثبِت هذه النتائج وجود عَلاقة. The English hedges four times — preliminary, may, indicate, possible. The literal deletes all four and publishes a finding the authors did not make. Count the hedges in the source, then count them again in your Arabic. The difference was significant (p .05). كان الفرق مُهِمّاً. A false friend with a technical meaning. In a results section significant means statistically significant — a defined threshold — not important. مُهِمّ makes a claim about consequence that the statistic does not support. The sample comprised 41 participants (see Table 2). — where Table 2 lists 43. silently corrected to ٤٣ so the text matches the table. You found a real error, and it is not yours to fix. Translating the discrepancy faithfully and flagging it is the professional act; correcting it quietly makes you the author of a claim you cannot defend.

chunks.title: Word-for-Word vs. Sense-for-Sense
chunks.text: 46 BCE · c. 395 CE · Historical debate · Word-for-Word vs. Sense-for-Sense · Cicero · St. Jerome · Word for word · Sense for sense · Fidelity · Literal translation · Should the translator reproduce the words and formal structure of the source, or its meaning, force and effect? One of the oldest debates in Western translation thought. Cicero described translating Greek oratory into Latin without rendering each word mechanically, keeping the force of the rhetoric instead. St. Jerome later defended translating sense for sense rather than word for word. هو كسر حاجز الصمت. Word-oriented · He broke the barrier of silence. Sense-oriented · He broke the silence. Explaining why a literal translation is not automatically a faithful one. Cicero, De Optimo Genere Oratorum (46 BCE) St. Jerome, Letter 57, to Pammachius, on the Best Method of Translating (c. 395)

chunks.text: 1813 · Theory · Schleiermacher: Two Methods of Translating · Friedrich Schleiermacher · Moving the reader · Moving the author · Foreignness · Do you bring the author to the reader, or the reader to the author? In “On the Different Methods of Translating” Schleiermacher set out two fundamental directions: move the author towards the reader, or move the reader towards the author. This later became the basis of the domestication / foreignization debate. اجتمع الضيوف في الديوانية بعد صلاة المغرب. Taber · Formal equivalence · Dynamic equivalence · Functional equivalence · Receptor response · Naturalness · Should the translation keep the form, or produce the same response in its readers? chunks.text: 1984 · Theory · Berman: The Ethics of the Foreign · Antoine Berman · The foreign · Deforming tendencies · Rationalization · Clarification · Expansion · Ennoblement · Does the translation respect the foreignness of the text? Berman warns against reducing foreign texts too far to target-language norms. He lists deforming tendencies: rationalization, clarification, expansion, ennoblement, impoverishment, destruction of rhythm, of linguistic patterning, and of vernacular features. كانت الدنيا تضيق به شيئاً فشيئاً. Flattened · He became increasingly distressed. Text-sensitive · The world seemed to close in around him, little by little. Literary translation and translation ethics. Berman, L’Épreuve de l’étranger (1984); English: The Experience of the Foreign (1992)

chunks.title: Derrida: Deconstruction
chunks.text: 1985 · Theory · Derrida: Deconstruction · Jacques Derrida · Différance · Instability of meaning · Untranslatability · Does a text have one stable meaning to transfer? Deconstruction challenges the idea of a single stable meaning that can move intact into another language. Translation depends on difference and exposes the instability of absolute equivalence. عين · Possible senses · eye · spring · source · spy · essence · Puns, ambiguity, untranslatability. Derrida, “Des Tours de Babel” (1985)

chunks.title: Eco: Translation as Negotiation
chunks.text: 2003 · Theory · Eco: Translation as Negotiation · Umberto Eco · Negotiation · Loss and gain · Reader expectations · What does the translator trade off against what? Translation is negotiation under constraints — among meanings, cultural conventions, style, reader expectations and the text itself. It is rarely one-to-one substitution. حياك الله · Possible · Welcome. · Glad to have you. · May God bless you. Everyday decisions where several renderings are possible. Eco, Mouse or Rat? Translation as Negotiation (2003)

chunks.title: Feminist Translation Theory
chunks.text: 1996 · 1997 · Approach · Feminist Translation Theory · Sherry Simon · Luise von Flotow · Gender · Visibility · Intervention · Linguistic sexism · Who is represented, how, and who holds linguistic power? Feminist approaches examine translation and gender, identity, authorship, linguistic sexism and visibility. Simon describes feminist translation as a cultural intervention that can create new meanings. English source · Every student must submit his assignment. Neutral rendering · Every student must submit their assignment. Gendered language; representation. Simon, Gender in Translation (1996) von Flotow, Translation and Gender (1997; later edition)

chunks.title: Postcolonial Approaches to Translation
chunks.text: 1992 · 1999 · Approach · Postcolonial Approaches to Translation · Key scholars include Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, Susan Bassnett, Harish Trivedi, Tejaswini Niranjana and Maria Tymoczko · Power · Representation · Language hierarchy · Resistance · Whose categories does the translation reproduce? Not one theory with founders but a tradition of approaches. They read translation through colonial history, power, language hierarchy, identity, resistance and representation, and ask how translation has served — and can resist — unequal relations between cultures. بدو · Common rendering · Bedouins · Historical, political and ethnographic texts. Spivak, “The Politics of Translation” (1992) Bassnett & Trivedi (eds), Post-Colonial Translation: Theory and Practice (1999)

chunks.title: Sociological Approaches
chunks.text: 1998 · 2016 · Approach · Sociological Approaches · Building on Pierre Bourdieu · Field · Habitus · Capital · Agency · What social environment made this choice likely? Translation as social practice, shaped by field, habitus, capital, institutions, publishers, clients and norms. Sameh Hanna’s study of Shakespeare translation in Egypt applies this to Arabic. Explaining why, not only what. Simeoni, “The Pivotal Status of the Translator’s Habitus” (1998) Hanna, Bourdieu in Translation Studies (2016)

chunks.title: Narrative Theory
chunks.text: 2006 · Theory · Narrative Theory · Mona Baker · Narrative · Framing · Selective appropriation · Relabelling · Repositioning · Which story does the translation help to tell? Translators and interpreters circulate, reinforce or contest narratives through framing, selective appropriation, relabelling and repositioning of participants. مقاتلون · Choices · fighters · combatants · militants · armed groups. Political translation, journalism, conflict and human-rights texts. Baker, Translation and Conflict: A Narrative Account (2006)

chunks.title: Cognitive Translation Studies
chunks.text: 1980s – today · Research paradigm · Cognitive Translation Studies · Translation Process Research · Process · Think-aloud · Keystroke logging · Eye tracking · Decision-making · What happens in the translator’s mind? Studies comprehension, problem-solving, attention, memory, decision-making and revision, using think-aloud reports, keystroke logging, eye tracking and screen recording. Comprehension · Problem · Research · Decision · Draft · Revision · مجلس الأمة · CAT tools, machine translation, post-editing, training. Krings, Was in den Köpfen von Übersetzern vorgeht (1986)

chunks.title: Corpus-Based Translation Studies
chunks.text: 1993 – today · Research paradigm · Corpus-Based Translation Studies · Mona Baker · Corpus · Parallel corpus · Comparable corpus · Collocation · What patterns appear across thousands of translations? Large collections of texts are used to study translated language, terminology, collocation, style and translator behaviour — moving from single examples to empirical patterns. Terminology, style and research. Baker, “Corpus Linguistics and Translation Studies” (1993)

chunks.title: Translation Universals
chunks.text: 1993 – today · Hypotheses · Translation Universals · Corpus researchers · Explicitation · Simplification · Normalization · Levelling-out · Do translations share tendencies whatever the languages? A family of hypotheses, not laws: explicitation, simplification, normalization and levelling-out. Corpus research has tested them repeatedly; scholars disagree on how universal they are. Treat them as tendencies. وصل متأخراً، لذلك اعتذر. Explicitation · He arrived late, so he apologized. Reviewing your own drafts for habits. Baker, “Corpus Linguistics and Translation Studies” (1993)

chunks.title: Eco-Translatology
chunks.text: 2000s · Approach · Eco-Translatology · Hu Gengshen · Adaptation · Selection · Translational eco-environment · How does a translation adapt to its environment? A more recent and less established framework, using an ecological metaphor: adaptation, selection, environment and balance between linguistic, cultural and communicative dimensions. Contemporary research; read alongside the established theories, not instead of them. Hu Gengshen, An Approach to Translation as Adaptation and Selection (2004)

chunks.title: Audiovisual Translation
chunks.text: 1990s – today · Field · Audiovisual Translation · A field, not one theory · Subtitling · Dubbing · Voice-over · Captioning · Reading speed · How do you translate for the screen? Subtitling (time, space, reading speed, segmentation), dubbing (timing, rhythm, lip synchrony), voice-over and captioning for deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers. Connects to Skopos, functionalism, relevance, multimodality and discourse analysis. Film, TV, online video, accessibility. Díaz Cintas & Remael, Audiovisual Translation: Subtitling (2007)

chunks.title: Gile’s Effort Models
chunks.text: 1995 · Model · Gile’s Effort Models · Daniel Gile · Listening effort · Memory effort · Production effort · Coordination · Processing capacity · Why do interpreters make errors even when they know the language? Interpreting draws on limited processing capacity shared between listening, production, memory and coordination. When demand exceeds capacity: errors, omissions and delays. Listening · Memory · Production · Coordination · وقد أكدت الحكومة، في الوقت ذاته، أنها لن تتراجع عن موقفها، رغم الضغوط الدولية المتزايدة… Interpreting training. Gile, Basic Concepts and Models for Interpreter and Translator Training (1995; later editions)

chunks.title: Word-for-Word vs. Sense-for-Sense
chunks.text: A translation can follow the source’s words or its meaning — and the two often pull apart. Gives students the most basic vocabulary for any translation decision. Shows that literal is not the same as faithful · Too binary: most real translations mix both · Says nothing about purpose, audience or culture. You render هو كسر حاجز الصمت as “He broke the silence.” Which side of the debate is this? Answer: Sense for sense · The image of a “barrier” is dropped because English expresses the same meaning naturally without it: meaning is kept, words are not.

chunks.title: Schleiermacher: Two Methods of Translating
chunks.text: Either move the author towards the reader, or move the reader towards the author. Names the basic cultural choice every translator faces. The root of Venuti’s domestication and foreignization. Presents two poles where most translations sit in between. Written about literary and philosophical texts, not all genres. You keep “diwaniya” in English with a short gloss. Which direction is that? Answer: Bringing the reader to the author · The reader is asked to meet an Arabic cultural term on its own terms, which moves the reader towards the source.

chunks.title: Vinay & Darbelnet: Comparative Stylistics
chunks.text: Translators move between languages through a small set of nameable procedures. Gives precise names for what you did to a phrase · Very practical for training and commentary · Procedures, not a theory of why you choose one. Built on French–English; some categories overlap. بعد وصول الوفد → “after the delegation arrived”. Which procedure changed the noun into a verb? Answer: Transposition · Transposition changes the word class (noun → verb) while keeping the meaning.

chunks.title: Jakobson: Three Kinds of Translation
chunks.text: Translation happens within a language, between languages, and between sign systems. Widens what counts as translation · Links translation to interpretation and semiotics · A classification, not a method · Says little about how to translate well · A novel is adapted into a film. Which kind of translation is that? Answer: Intersemiotic · Moving from words to images and sound is translation between sign systems: intersemiotic.

chunks.title: Nida: Formal and Dynamic Equivalence
chunks.text: A translation can keep the form of the source, or aim for the same response in its new readers. Puts the reader’s understanding at the centre. Explains why natural target-language renderings are often more faithful · “Same response” is hard to measure · Grew out of Bible translation with a missionary purpose; later criticised for that. ألف مبروك! → “Congratulations!” Which kind of equivalence is that? Answer: Dynamic · The number “a thousand” is dropped, but the effect — warm congratulations — is reproduced.

chunks.title: Catford: A Linguistic Theory of Translation
chunks.text: Translation is replacing textual material in one language with equivalent material in another, with predictable shifts. Precise vocabulary for grammatical changes · Useful for Arabic nominal style → English verbal style · Works mostly at sentence level · Leaves out context, culture and purpose · وصول (noun) becomes “arrived” (verb). Which shift is that in Catford’s terms? Answer: Class shift · The word class changes from noun to verb: a class shift, one of Catford’s category shifts.

chunks.title: Koller: Five Kinds of Equivalence
chunks.text: Equivalence is not one thing: a translation can be equivalent in one respect and not another. Lets you name exactly what was kept and what was lost. Very useful for poetry, advertising and wordplay · Does not tell you which kind to prioritise · Can feel like a checklist rather than a method. A translated contract is rewritten to sound like an English contract. Which equivalence is prioritised? Answer: Text-normative · Following the conventions of the target text type is text-normative equivalence.

chunks.title: Newmark: Semantic and Communicative Translation
chunks.text: Semantic translation serves the author; communicative translation serves the reader. Clear, teachable method for a whole text · Matches text types: expressive texts lean semantic, informative ones communicative · The two methods overlap in practice · Prescriptive: tells you what to do more than why. الوقت كالسيف إن لم تقطعه قطعك → “Time waits for no one.” Which method? Answer: Communicative · The image is replaced with a natural English proverb that carries the message: communicative translation.

chunks.title: Baker: Equivalence at Multiple Levels
chunks.text: Equivalence can be achieved or lost at the level of the word, the phrase, the grammar, the text or the pragmatics. Diagnoses exactly where a problem sits · Strong bridge between theory and practice · A framework for analysis rather than a single theory. Less about ideology (Baker addresses that elsewhere) هل يمكنك إغلاق الباب؟ → “Could you close the door?” At which level is equivalence achieved? Answer: Pragmatic · The translation reproduces the speech act — a polite request — not a question about ability: pragmatic equivalence.

chunks.title: Reiss: Text Types
chunks.text: How you translate depends on what the whole text is for: informing, expressing or persuading. Sets priorities before translating · Gives criteria for judging a translation · Many texts mix types · The categories can be too neat for real texts. You translate a fundraising appeal. Which text type, and what is the priority? Answer: Operative — the reader’s response · An appeal is meant to make readers act: operative, so the response matters most.

chunks.title: Skopos Theory
chunks.text: The purpose the translation must serve in its target context decides how it is translated. Explains why one text can have several correct translations. Fits professional work with clients and briefs. Can seem to justify any change if “the purpose” demands it. Raises questions about the translator’s duty to the source — which Nord’s “loyalty” answers. You translate a Kuwaiti government announcement for an international audience. What does Skopos theory ask you to establish first? Answer: The purpose and audience of the translation. Every decision follows from the skopos — the purpose and audience of the target text — so it comes first.

chunks.title: Holz-Mänttäri: Translational Action
chunks.text: Translation is a professional action involving many participants, not just words moving between languages. Matches how professional translation actually works · Gives the translator an expert role · Abstract terminology · Moves attention away from the source text · Who is the “commissioner” in a translation job? Answer: The person or body that orders it · The commissioner orders the translation and sets its conditions; the reader is the target audience.

chunks.title: Nord: Function Plus Loyalty
chunks.text: A translation serves its purpose, but the translator stays loyal to everyone in the communication. Adds ethics to functionalism · Gives a detailed text-analysis model for students · “Loyalty” can be hard to define in practice · The analysis model is long to apply · A client asks you to make an accusation in a statement stronger.
