What does loyalty require? Answer: Separate translation from rewriting, and make the change visible to the client. Loyalty means not misleading any party: an ideological change must be named as adaptation, not passed off as translation.

chunks.title: House: Overt and Covert Translation
chunks.text: Some translations openly remain translations; others are made to work as original target-culture texts. A full model for assessing quality · Explains why some texts need a “cultural filter” Detailed and time-consuming to apply · The line between overt and covert is not always clear. A ministry announcement is rewritten as “Online scholarship applications are now open.” Which kind of translation? Answer: Covert · It reads like an original English institutional notice, not a visible translation: covert.

chunks.title: Hatim & Mason: Discourse and the Translator
chunks.text: Meaning depends on context: who is speaking to whom, in which genre, with what intention. Brings register, genre and pragmatics into translation · Draws heavily on Arabic–English examples · Demanding analysis for every text · Less about the act of choosing a single word · In Hatim & Mason’s register analysis, “tenor” refers to… Answer: The relationship between the participants. Field is what is happening, tenor who is talking to whom, mode the channel.

chunks.title: Gutt: Relevance Theory
chunks.text: Readers infer meaning from words plus context; a translation should make the intended meaning recoverable. Explains implicit meaning, irony and indirectness · Grounded in cognitive pragmatics · Hard to apply as a step-by-step method · Predicting readers’ context is difficult · Why does Gutt say translators cannot simply decode words? Answer: Because meaning is partly inferred from context. Communication is inferential: words + context + inference. The translator must infer, then make it inferable.

chunks.title: Polysystem Theory
chunks.text: Translated literature holds a position in a culture’s literary system, and that position shapes how it is translated. Explains why translations differ across cultures and periods · Links translation to literary history · Mostly about literature · Abstract; says little about individual decisions. When translated literature is “central” in a culture, translations tend to… Answer: Introduce new forms and models · In a central position, translation is innovative and brings new forms in; in a peripheral one it conforms.

chunks.title: The Manipulation School and Rewriting
chunks.text: Translation is a form of rewriting shaped by ideology, poetics and patronage. Explains censorship, retitling and framing · Shows that translations shape reputations · Can make every translation sound like manipulation · Focused on literary systems · A publisher cuts politically sensitive passages from a translated novel. Which of Lefevere’s factors is most at work? Answer: Patronage and ideology · Those who control publication (patronage) apply ideological limits to what may appear.

chunks.title: Descriptive Translation Studies
chunks.text: Study what translators actually do, and the norms that explain it, before judging it. Makes translation studies empirical · Explains patterns across many translations · Describes rather than guides a translator · Norms can be hard to prove · Which question is typical of Descriptive Translation Studies? Answer: What do translators of press releases actually do, and why? DTS describes real behaviour and the norms behind it, rather than prescribing.

chunks.title: The Cultural Turn
chunks.text: Translation moves between cultures, not just languages, and carries power, identity and ideology with it. Brings culture and power into the field · Explains choices that equivalence cannot · A broad movement rather than a method · Can lose sight of the linguistic detail · Rendering فريج as “fareej”, “old neighbourhood” or “traditional quarter” — what does the cultural turn ask? Answer: What cultural meaning each one carries and what disappears. Each option transmits a different cultural meaning; the cultural turn makes that the question.

chunks.title: Venuti: Domestication and Foreignization
chunks.text: A translation can make the foreign familiar (domestication) or let it stay visibly foreign (foreignization) — and that choice is political. Makes the translator visible · Connects small choices to cultural power · Foreignization can make texts hard to read · The two terms are a spectrum, not a switch · “Time waits for no one” for الوقت كالسيف… — which strategy? Answer: Domestication · A familiar English proverb replaces the Arabic image: domestication. Keeping the sword image would be foreignization.

chunks.title: Benjamin: The Task of the Translator
chunks.text: Translation is not passing on information; it reveals the relationship between languages. Takes form and language seriously · Central to literary translation thinking · Philosophical and difficult · Offers no practical method · What does Benjamin reject? Answer: The idea that translation only transmits information. For Benjamin a translation that only passes on information is a bad one; form matters.

chunks.title: Steiner: The Hermeneutic Motion
chunks.text: Translation is interpretation in four moves: trust, aggression, incorporation, restitution. Describes the translator’s experience of understanding · Useful for metaphor and literary texts · Metaphorical language · Hard to test or apply step by step · In Steiner’s motion, which stage tries to compensate for what translation has taken? Answer: Restitution · Restitution restores balance after the translator has taken from the source.

chunks.title: Berman: The Ethics of the Foreign
chunks.text: A good translation respects the foreignness of the text instead of smoothing it away. Lists concrete “deforming tendencies” to check a draft against. Strong ethical voice for literary translation · Can be hard to apply to practical texts · Values the source very strongly over the reader. Turning كانت الدنيا تضيق به شيئاً فشيئاً into “He became increasingly distressed” is which deforming tendency? Answer: Rationalization / clarification · The image is explained away into plain meaning — clarification that destroys the figure.

chunks.title: Derrida: Deconstruction
chunks.text: No text has one stable meaning that translation could carry across intact. Takes ambiguity and untranslatability seriously · Challenges simple ideas of equivalence · Very abstract · Gives little practical guidance · عين can mean eye, spring, source or spy. What does deconstruction highlight? Answer: That meaning is unstable and translation must choose. Instability of meaning is central, not a nuisance: translation always selects.

chunks.title: Eco: Translation as Negotiation
chunks.text: Translation is negotiation: the translator trades off meaning, style, culture and readability. Realistic picture of everyday decisions · Accessible, with many examples · Describes the process more than guiding it · حياك الله → “Welcome.” / “Glad to have you.” / “May God bless you.” What is Eco’s point? Answer: The translator negotiates literal meaning, function and politeness. There is rarely one-to-one substitution; the choice is a negotiation among constraints.

chunks.title: Feminist Translation Theory
chunks.text: Translation can reproduce or challenge how gender is represented, so the translator’s choices are never neutral. Makes gendered language and representation visible · Recognises the translator as an agent · Interventions can be seen as unfaithful · Not a single unified method · What is a feminist translation approach most concerned with? Answer: Who is represented, how, and who holds linguistic power. It examines representation, visibility and power, not only grammatical gender.

chunks.title: Postcolonial Approaches to Translation
chunks.text: Translation happens between unequal languages and cultures, and can reproduce or resist colonial ways of seeing. Shows the power behind naming and representing · Essential for historical and political texts · A family of approaches, not one theory · Can be hard to turn into concrete choices · A historical source uses بدو. What would a postcolonial approach ask first? Answer: Who named this group, and whose categories the translation reproduces. The question is power and representation: whose labels are being carried into English.

chunks.title: Sociological Approaches
chunks.text: Translations are shaped by the social world of the translator: institutions, clients, status and norms. Explains why, not only what · Applies well to Arabic translation history · Can push the text itself into the background · Needs research data to apply · The same text is translated for a university press and for a commercial publisher. Sociology of translation asks… Answer: What social environment made each choice likely. It looks at field, habitus and capital: the social conditions behind decisions.

chunks.title: Narrative Theory
chunks.text: Translators help tell stories about the world, and their choices can frame, reinforce or contest them. Powerful for political, media and conflict texts · Shows how one word frames events · Focused on ideology more than craft · Easy to over-read intention · مقاتلون → “fighters”, “militants” or “armed groups”. What does narrative theory call this choice? Answer: Framing by relabelling · Choosing a label positions the actors and frames the story: relabelling.

chunks.title: Cognitive Translation Studies
chunks.text: Study what happens in the translator’s mind while translating, not only the final text. Measurable data (keystrokes, eye movements) Directly useful for training and tools · Experiments are artificial · Data is hard to interpret · Which method belongs to cognitive translation research? Answer: Keystroke logging and eye tracking · Process research observes the translator at work through keystrokes, gaze and think-aloud.

chunks.title: Corpus-Based Translation Studies
chunks.text: Large collections of texts reveal patterns in translated language that single examples cannot. Evidence instead of anecdote · Useful for terminology and style · Shows patterns, not causes · Depends on the corpus chosen · What makes a study “corpus-based”? Answer: It analyses large collections of texts. Corpus studies work from large, searchable collections of texts.

chunks.title: Translation Universals
chunks.text: Translations may share tendencies — explicitation, simplification, normalization — whatever the languages. Helps you notice your own habits · Testable with corpora · Hypotheses, not laws · Scholars disagree how universal they are · Adding “so” to make وصل متأخراً، لذلك اعتذر explicit in English is an example of… Answer: Explicitation · Making a logical link explicit is explicitation.

chunks.title: Eco-Translatology
chunks.text: Translation as adaptation and selection within a linguistic, cultural and communicative environment. A recent framework from Chinese translation studies. Holistic view of the translator’s environment · Less established than the classic theories · Ecological metaphor can be vague · How should a student treat eco-translatology? Answer: As a newer, less established framework. It is recent and still debated; read it alongside the established theories.

chunks.title: Audiovisual Translation
chunks.text: Translating for the screen adds time, space, sound and image as constraints. Highly relevant to modern work · Connects theory to practical constraints · A field, not a single theory · Which is a constraint specific to subtitling? Answer: Reading speed and line length · Subtitles must be read in time and fit the screen; lip synchrony is a dubbing constraint.

chunks.title: Gile’s Effort Models
chunks.text: Interpreting draws on limited mental capacity shared between listening, memory, production and coordination. Explains errors even in skilled interpreters · Very practical for training · A model, not a full theory of meaning · Capacity is hard to measure directly · An interpreter starts omitting details when the speaker speeds up. Gile would explain this as… Answer: Processing demand exceeding available capacity. When the efforts together need more capacity than is available, errors and omissions appear.

chunks.title: Cicero
chunks.text: Cicero · 106 – 43 BCE · Roman · Orator, statesman and translator · Rome’s greatest orator translated Greek speeches into Latin and described doing it as an orator, not as an interpreter: keeping the force of the argument rather than counting words. His remark is the oldest statement of the word-for-word vs. sense-for-sense debate. Word-for-Word vs. Sense-for-Sense

chunks.title: St. Jerome
chunks.text: St. Jerome · c. 347 – 420 · Roman Christian · Bible translator · Translator of the Latin Bible later known as the Vulgate. In his Letter 57 he defended translating sense for sense, except in scripture — a defence that framed Western thinking about translation for over a thousand years. Word-for-Word vs. Sense-for-Sense

chunks.title: Friedrich Schleiermacher
chunks.text: Friedrich Schleiermacher · 1768 – 1834 · German · Theologian and philosopher · Theologian, philosopher and translator of Plato. His 1813 lecture set out the two directions a translator can take — bring the author to the reader, or the reader to the author — the root of today’s domestication and foreignization debate. Schleiermacher: Two Methods of Translating

chunks.title: Walter Benjamin
chunks.text: Walter Benjamin · 1892 – 1940 · German · Philosopher and critic · Philosopher and literary critic who translated Baudelaire. His preface “The Task of the Translator” argued that translation is not about passing on information but about the relationship between languages. Benjamin: The Task of the Translator

chunks.title: Roman Jakobson
chunks.text: Roman Jakobson · 1896 – 1982 · Russian-American · Linguist · One of the founders of modern linguistics and semiotics. His short 1959 essay named three kinds of translation — intralingual, interlingual and intersemiotic — and is still a starting point for the field. Jakobson: Three Kinds of Translation

chunks.title: Jean-Paul Vinay
chunks.text: Jean-Paul Vinay · 1910 – 1999 · French, worked in Canada · Linguist · Linguist who, with Jean Darbelnet, compared French and English and catalogued the seven procedures a translator can use, from borrowing to adaptation. Their framework is still how translators name what they did to a phrase. Vinay & Darbelnet: Comparative Stylistics

chunks.title: Jean Darbelnet
chunks.text: Jean Darbelnet · 1904 – 1990 · French, worked in Canada · Linguist · Co-author, with Jean-Paul Vinay, of Comparative Stylistics of French and English and its seven translation procedures. Vinay & Darbelnet: Comparative Stylistics

chunks.title: Eugene A. Nida
chunks.text: Eugene A. Nida · 1914 – 2011 · American · Linguist and Bible translator · Linguist at the American Bible Society who led Bible translation projects across many languages. He made the reader’s response central to translation with his distinction between formal and dynamic equivalence. Nida: Formal and Dynamic Equivalence

chunks.title: J. C. Catford
chunks.text: J. C. Catford · 1917 – 2009 · Scottish · Linguist and phonetician · Phonetician and linguist who treated translation as an operation between language systems. He gave the field the term “translation shifts”. Catford: A Linguistic Theory of Translation

chunks.title: Werner Koller
chunks.text: Werner Koller · German-language scholar · Translation scholar · Split the single idea of equivalence into five kinds — denotative, connotative, text-normative, pragmatic and formal-aesthetic — so a translator can say exactly what was kept and what was given up. Koller: Five Kinds of Equivalence

chunks.title: Peter Newmark
chunks.text: Peter Newmark · 1916 – 2011 · British, born in Czechoslovakia · Translation teacher · One of the most influential teachers of translation. His distinction between semantic and communicative translation, and his Textbook of Translation, shaped translator training worldwide. Newmark: Semantic and Communicative Translation

chunks.title: Katharina Reiss
chunks.text: Katharina Reiss · 1923 – 2018 · German · Translation scholar · Linked translation decisions to the type and function of the whole text, and co-wrote the founding book of Skopos theory with Hans Vermeer. Reiss: Text Types · Skopos Theory

chunks.title: Hans J. Vermeer
chunks.text: Hans J. Vermeer · 1930 – 2010 · German · Linguist and translation scholar · Founder of Skopos theory: the purpose of a translation decides how it is made. Skopos Theory

chunks.title: Justa Holz-Mänttäri
chunks.text: Justa Holz-Mänttäri · German-born, worked in Finland · Translation scholar · Described translation as a professional action involving initiators, commissioners, translators and audiences — not just a transfer of words. Holz-Mänttäri: Translational Action

chunks.title: Christiane Nord
chunks.text: Christiane Nord · German · Translation scholar · Developed functionalism into a teachable method with a detailed model of translation-oriented text analysis, and added the ethical principle of loyalty. Nord: Function Plus Loyalty

chunks.title: Juliane House
chunks.text: Juliane House · German · Linguist and translation scholar · Built one of the best-known models of translation quality assessment and the distinction between overt and covert translation. House: Overt and Covert Translation

chunks.title: Basil Hatim
chunks.text: Basil Hatim · Arab-British · Translation scholar · Brought discourse analysis, register and pragmatics into translation studies with Ian Mason. His work draws extensively on Arabic–English translation. Hatim & Mason: Discourse and the Translator

chunks.title: Ian Mason
chunks.text: Ian Mason · British · Translation and interpreting scholar · Co-author, with Basil Hatim, of Discourse and the Translator and The Translator as Communicator. Hatim & Mason: Discourse and the Translator

chunks.title: Ernst-August Gutt
chunks.text: Ernst-August Gutt · German · Linguist · Applied relevance theory from cognitive pragmatics to translation, treating it as interpretive use of language. Gutt: Relevance Theory

chunks.title: Itamar Even-Zohar
chunks.text: Itamar Even-Zohar · b. 1939 · Israeli · Cultural researcher · Created polysystem theory, which studies the position translated literature holds within a culture’s literary system. Polysystem Theory

chunks.title: Theo Hermans
chunks.text: Theo Hermans · Belgian · Translation scholar · Edited The Manipulation of Literature, which gave its name to the school that sees translation as a form of rewriting. The Manipulation School and Rewriting

chunks.title: André Lefevere
chunks.text: André Lefevere · 1945 – 1996 · Belgian · Translation scholar · Showed how ideology, poetics and patronage shape translations, and with Susan Bassnett led the cultural turn. The Manipulation School and Rewriting · The Cultural Turn

chunks.title: Gideon Toury
chunks.text: Gideon Toury · 1942 – 2016 · Israeli · Translation scholar · Founder of Descriptive Translation Studies: study what translators actually do, and the norms behind it. Descriptive Translation Studies

chunks.title: Susan Bassnett
chunks.text: Susan Bassnett · b. 1945 · British · Translation and comparative literature scholar. Author of the classic introduction Translation Studies, and a leading voice of the cultural turn and of postcolonial translation studies. The Cultural Turn · Postcolonial Approaches to Translation

chunks.title: Lawrence Venuti
chunks.text: Lawrence Venuti · b. 1953 · American · Translator and theorist · Translator from Italian, French and Catalan. Named the translator’s invisibility and set domestication against foreignization. Venuti: Domestication and Foreignization

chunks.title: George Steiner
chunks.text: George Steiner · 1929 – 2020 · Born in Paris; British and American careers · Critic and philosopher · Literary critic whose After Babel describes translation as a four-stage act of interpretation. Steiner: The Hermeneutic Motion

chunks.title: Antoine Berman
chunks.text: Antoine Berman · 1942 – 1991 · French · Translator and theorist · Translator and theorist who argued for an ethics that respects the foreignness of the text, and listed the deforming tendencies that erase it. Berman: The Ethics of the Foreign

chunks.title: Jacques Derrida
chunks.text: Jacques Derrida · 1930 – 2004 · French, born in Algeria · Philosopher · Founder of deconstruction, who questioned whether any text has a single stable meaning that translation could carry intact. Derrida: Deconstruction

chunks.title: Umberto Eco
chunks.text: Umberto Eco · 1932 – 2016 · Italian · Novelist and semiotician · Semiotician and novelist who worked closely with his own translators, and described translation as negotiation. Eco: Translation as Negotiation

chunks.title: Sherry Simon
chunks.text: Sherry Simon · Canadian · Translation scholar · Author of Gender in Translation, which describes feminist translation as a cultural intervention that can create new meanings. Feminist Translation Theory

chunks.title: Luise von Flotow
chunks.text: Luise von Flotow · Canadian · Translation scholar · Author of Translation and Gender, one of the founding overviews of feminist translation studies. Feminist Translation Theory

chunks.title: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
chunks.text: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak · b. 1942 · Indian · Literary theorist and translator · Postcolonial theorist and translator of Derrida and Mahasweta Devi, whose essay “The Politics of Translation” questions whose voice survives. Postcolonial Approaches to Translation

chunks.title: Pierre Bourdieu
chunks.text: Pierre Bourdieu · 1930 – 2002 · French · Sociologist · Not a translation scholar, but his concepts of field, habitus and capital became the basis of the sociology of translation. Sociological Approaches

chunks.title: Mona Baker
chunks.text: Mona Baker · b. 1953 · Egyptian-born British · Translation scholar · Author of In Other Words, pioneer of corpus-based translation studies and of narrative theory in translation. Baker: Equivalence at Multiple Levels · Narrative Theory · Corpus-Based Translation Studies · Translation Universals

chunks.title: Daniel Gile
chunks.text: Daniel Gile · French · Interpreting scholar · Conference interpreter and researcher whose Effort Models explain why interpreting is cognitively demanding. Gile’s Effort Models

chunks.title: Hu Gengshen
chunks.text: Hu Gengshen · Chinese · Translation scholar · Proposed eco-translatology, which views translation as adaptation and selection within an environment. Eco-Translatology

chunks.title: Jerome
chunks.text: Jerome · c. 347 – 420 · Bethlehem · Hebrew & Greek to Latin · Not word for word, but sense for sense. He produced the Vulgate, the Latin Bible that Western Europe read for more than a thousand years. In his letter to Pammachius he wrote that he translates not word for word but sense for sense - the sentence the whole profession still quotes at itself. He also insisted on going back to the Hebrew rather than working from the Greek. He is the patron saint of translators, and his feast day is International Translation Day. One root, chosen wrong, for a thousand years · Hebrew (Exodus 34:29) קָרַן (q-r-n) The other reading · the same three consonants also spell qeren, "horn" — and that is the one he took · What he wrote · cornuta esset facies sua — "his face was horned", where the sense is that it sent out rays of light. The consonants carry both shone and horn, and the vowels that would separate them are not written. His choice put horns on Moses in European art for a thousand years, Michelangelo's included. The man who wrote not word for word but sense for sense is also the standing proof of how far one root-choice travels.

chunks.title: Ibn al-Muqaffa
chunks.text: Ibn al-Muqaffa · c. 724 – 759 · Basra · Middle Persian to Arabic · One translation seeded a thousand years of European storytelling. He rendered the Pahlavi Kalila wa-Dimna - the Indian animal fables - into Arabic prose so good that it became the original everyone worked from. From his Arabic the book passed into Hebrew, Latin, Castilian and eventually every European language; La Fontaine's fables descend from it. He did not preserve a text, he relaunched one - the most travelled book in the world moves through his sentences. A title that could travel · Sanskrit, through Middle Persian · Karataka & Damanaka (the two jackals) Word for word · the names transliterated — sounds an Arabic reader could not hold on to · What he wrote · كليلة ودمنة (Kalīla wa-Dimna) He reshaped the names to Arabic until the book could be named in Arabic — and it is that title, not the Sanskrit one, that went on into Hebrew, Latin, Castilian and French. He also opened it with a chapter of his own, widely credited to him rather than the Pahlavi: the translator added material, and the addition stayed for a thousand years.

chunks.title: Al-Jahiz
chunks.text: Al-Jahiz · c. 776 – 869 · Basra & Baghdad · wrote the first theory · The first person to say out loud that poetry does not translate. In the Book of Animals he set down the earliest serious argument about what translation cannot do. He held that a translator must command both languages equally or he will damage both - and that poetry cannot cross at all, because its metre, its sound and its rhetorical shape are its meaning, so all that survives is information. Every argument about untranslatability since is a footnote to him. His claim, demonstrated · Arabic (Imru' al-Qays, before Islam) وَلَيْلٍ كَمَوْجِ البَحْرِ أَرْخَى سُدُولَهُ · What crosses · "And a night like the sea's waves let down its curtains over me" What does not · the ṭawīl metre, the rhyme, the archaic diction — every part of it that was doing the work. Al-Jahiz translated nothing; this is his argument worked out, not his rendering. In the Book of Animals he held that poetry cannot cross, because metre, sound-shape and rhetorical figure are not decoration on the meaning — they are part of it, so all that arrives is the report. He also insisted a translator must be equally strong in both tongues, or he will damage both.

chunks.title: Hunayn ibn Ishaq
chunks.text: Hunayn ibn Ishaq · 809 – 873 · Baghdad · Greek & Syriac to Arabic · Sense before words - eleven centuries before anyone gave it that name. He ran the translation bureau of the House of Wisdom and turned the whole Greek medical corpus - Galen, Hippocrates, Dioscorides - into Arabic. He refused to work word for word. He hunted down every manuscript of a text he could find, collated them into one reliable original, and only then carried the sense across. That is still the method. His Galen kept medicine alive for seven hundred years, and when Europe wanted Greek medicine back it had to translate his Arabic to get it. Building the vocabulary as he went · Greek · χυμός (chymos) — "juice, sap" Word for word · "juice" — or the Greek sound carried straight over, which told an Arabic physician nothing · What he wrote · خِلْط (khilṭ) — "a mixture" Arabic had no word for a bodily humour. Instead of importing the Greek sound he took an ordinary Arabic word for a mixture and made it the technical term — أخلاط is still the Arabic for the four humours. Translating Galen meant building the language that could hold Galen, and a great deal of Arabic medical vocabulary is his.

chunks.title: Qusta ibn Luqa
chunks.text: Qusta ibn Luqa · c. 820 – 912 · Baalbek, then Baghdad · Greek to Arabic · Three languages, and the sciences in all of them. A physician and scientist from Baalbek who worked in Greek, Syriac and Arabic. He translated Greek mathematical and mechanical works into Arabic and wrote his own treatises on medicine and the sciences. He belongs to the generation that had to build a technical Arabic while using it. Translating mechanics or medicine meant deciding what a term would mean in Arabic from then on, and then writing original work in the vocabulary he had just settled. When the translation becomes the original · The Greek · Hero of Alexandria, Mechanics, and four books of Diophantus’ Arithmetica · What survives of it · nothing — the Greek of both is lost · What we read instead · his Arabic, Fī raf’ al-ashyā’ al-thaqīla and the Arabic Arithmetica, which are now the text. Hero’s Mechanics reaches us only through Qusta’s Arabic, and four books of Diophantus known from no Greek manuscript survive in an Arabic version transmitted under his name. Every modern edition and every translation into a European language is made from the translation. It is the plainest answer to anyone who calls the work secondary: where the source is gone, the translator’s sentences are all the evidence there is.

chunks.title: Thabit ibn Qurra
chunks.text: Thabit ibn Qurra · c. 826 – 901 · Harran, then Baghdad · Greek & Syriac to Arabic · He corrected translations because he could do the mathematics. A mathematician and astronomer from Harran who translated Greek scientific works into Arabic and revised translations already in circulation, among them Euclid and Ptolemy, alongside his own work in mathematics and astronomy. He is the argument against treating translation and subject knowledge as separate trades. Revising a mathematical text means being able to follow the proof; where he changed a rendering, he changed it because he knew what the mathematics had to say. The only revision with its reviser’s name on the spine · What he was handed · the Arabic Elements of Euclid as Ishaq ibn Hunayn had rendered it · The usual fate of a reviser · corrections absorbed into someone else’s text, and the reviser forgotten · What the manuscripts call it · the Ishaq–Thabit version — the standard name scholars still use for that Euclid. The Arabic Euclid that circulated for centuries is catalogued as Ishaq’s translation in Thabit’s revision, and he worked over the Almagest the same way. Revision is a stage of the job, not a favour done at the end of it; here it is a stage recorded in the title, because the person doing it could follow the proof.

chunks.title: Ishaq ibn Hunayn
chunks.text: Ishaq ibn Hunayn · c. 830 – 910 · Baghdad · Greek & Syriac to Arabic · The second generation - carrying a method, not just a post. He translated Greek philosophy and science into Arabic - works of Aristotle, Euclid's Elements, and a version of Ptolemy's Almagest - and practised as a physician at the Abbasid court, as his father had before him. A method only survives if someone inherits it. He worked the way Hunayn worked: gather every manuscript, settle what the text actually says, and only then carry the sense across. The Arabic Aristotle that later philosophers argued over, and that Europe eventually read through Latin, came in large part through the translations of his generation. Two Greek words, two opposite decisions · Greek (Aristotle) ὕλη (hylē) εἶδος (eidos) — matter and form · One route · carry the Greek sound over and let the reader learn a new word · What the Arabic settled on · هَيُولَى — the Greek sound kept صُورة — an ordinary Arabic word given a technical job. Two terms from the same sentence of the same philosopher, handled in opposite ways, and both choices stuck: هيولى is still the Arabic for Aristotelian matter and صورة still its form. Borrow or build is decided term by term, not once for the whole book — and whatever this generation decided, later Arabic philosophy had to argue inside it.

chunks.title: Martin Luther
chunks.text: Martin Luther · 1483 – 1546 · Wittenberg · Greek, Hebrew & Latin to German · He translated for people who had never been asked what German sounded like. He translated the New Testament into German in 1522 and the complete Bible by 1534, and in 1530 wrote an open letter on translating that defended the choices he had made against critics who wanted the Latin followed word by word. He argued that the test of a rendering was whether ordinary German speakers recognised their own language in it - so he listened to how people actually spoke and wrote that, rather than tracking the Latin. The result carried far beyond religion: it is one of the texts that shaped written German itself. One word that is not in the original · Latin (Romans 3:28) arbitramur hominem iustificari fide absque operibus legis · Word for word · "we hold that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law" — and there is no alone anywhere in it · What he wrote · durch den Glauben allein — "by faith alone"

chunks.title: Martin Luther (cont.)
chunks.text: His critics counted the words and found one too many. In the Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen of 1530 he answered that German puts allein in when a denial is followed by what replaces it — nicht dies, sondern allein das — and that a translator who leaves it out has written Latin in German letters. The test he set there is the famous one: go and listen to the mother in the house, the children in the street, the common man in the market, and translate so they know you are speaking to them. The word was also doing theological work, and he knew it: this is where a translator’s idiom and a translator’s conviction are hardest to tell apart.

chunks.title: William Tyndale
chunks.text: William Tyndale · c. 1494 – 1536 · Antwerp · Greek & Hebrew to English · He was executed for it, and then everyone quoted him. He translated the New Testament into English from the Greek, printed it abroad, and was strangled and burned for doing it. Roughly four fifths of the King James Version is his wording, untouched. The salt of the earth, the powers that be, a law unto themselves - his phrases. He did not only translate into English; he shaped the English the rest of us inherited. Three words he refused to use · Greek · ἐκκλησία πρεσβύτερος ἀγάπη · What was expected · "church" "priest" "charity" — the Latin-descended words already in place · What he wrote · "congregation" "elder" "love" Not a matter of taste. Each choice removed a word that held up an institution and put a plain English one where it stood, which is a large part of why the books were burned and then so was he. Where English had nothing he made it: Passover, scapegoat, atonement, mercy seat are his coinages, and roughly four fifths of the King James New Testament is his wording untouched.

chunks.title: John Dryden
chunks.text: John Dryden · 1631 – 1700 · London · Latin & Greek to English · Three ways to carry a poem across, and a warning about two of them. A poet and critic who translated Virgil, Ovid and others into English, and who in his preface to Ovid's Epistles in 1680 named three ways of doing it: metaphrase, word by word; paraphrase, sense for sense with the author kept in view; and imitation, where the translator departs from the original at will. Naming the three made it possible to argue about which one a given text deserved. He preferred the middle way and distrusted the extremes - and translators have been arguing along that same line ever since, usually without knowing whose terms they are using. His own middle way, caught in the act · Latin (Virgil, Aeneid I.1–4) Arma virumque cano, Troiae qui primus ab oris saevae memorem Iunonis ob iram · Metaphrase — word by word · "Arms and the man I sing, who first from the shores of Troy on account of the mindful anger of cruel Juno" Paraphrase — what he published in 1697 · "Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc’d by Fate, / And haughty Juno’s unrelenting hate, / Expell’d and exil’d, left the Trojan shore."

chunks.title: John Dryden (cont.)
chunks.text: Juno’s anger is Virgil’s, three lines later; Dryden pulls it forward into the opening sentence and gives it an English couplet to live in. Nothing is invented and nothing is tracked word for word — which is exactly the middle term he had named seventeen years earlier in the preface to Ovid’s Epistles. There he warned against both ends: metaphrase is "dancing on ropes with fettered legs", and imitation, which he allowed Cowley in the Pindaric odes, is the greatest wrong to the memory of the dead.

chunks.title: Friedrich Schleiermacher
chunks.text: Friedrich Schleiermacher · 1768 – 1834 · Berlin · Greek to German · Move the reader toward the writer, or the writer toward the reader. A philosopher and theologian who translated Plato into German, and who in an 1813 lecture on the different methods of translating set out the choice a translator cannot avoid: leave the writer in place and move the reader toward him, or leave the reader in place and move the writer toward him. Almost every later theory argues with that lecture. It is often flattened into the pair foreignisation and domestication - terms that came later, from Venuti - and the flattening loses the point, which was not that one path is right and the other wrong, but that a translator must choose one and stay with it. The fork he says you cannot stand in the middle of · Arabic · إن شاء الله · Move the reader toward the writer · "God willing" — or in shā’ Allāh left standing in the English, so the reader knows whose sentence this is · Move the writer toward the reader · "all being well" — what an English speaker would have said in that spot, with the origin gone

chunks.title: Friedrich Schleiermacher (cont.)
chunks.text: Schleiermacher translated Plato, not Arabic; the pairing above is his argument applied to a phrase this site actually has to translate. His 1813 lecture puts it as two roads and no third: either the translator leaves the writer in peace as much as possible and moves the reader toward him, or he leaves the reader in peace and moves the writer toward him. Mixing them, he warns, leaves writer and reader who never meet at all. He also separated Dolmetschen, the interpreting of business, from Übersetzen, the translation of art and scholarship — a distinction the profession still runs on.

chunks.title: Rifaa al-Tahtawi
chunks.text: Rifaa al-Tahtawi · 1801 – 1873 · Tahta, Paris, Cairo · French to Arabic · He did not translate a shelf of books. He built the school that did. Sent to Paris in 1826 as imam to an Egyptian student mission, he learned French, translated, and wrote an account of the city and its institutions, Takhlis al-Ibriz fi Talkhis Bariz. Back in Cairo he led the School of Languages, Madrasat al-Alsun, which trained translators and produced translations across law, geography, history and the sciences. Institutions outlast individuals. The school turned translation in Egypt into a trained profession rather than a personal gift, and a great deal of modern Arabic technical vocabulary was settled by the work that came out of it. A word with no Arabic to land in · French (the Charter of 1814, which he set out in Arabic) libert · The Arabic word that was there · حُرِّيَّة — at that time the opposite of slavery, a condition of persons, with no political sense attached to it · How he made it carry the new sense · he told his readers that what the French call libert is what we mean by justice and equity, العدل والإنصاف, because it means every man standing equal before the law

chunks.title: Rifaa al-Tahtawi (cont.)
chunks.text: This is from Takhlīṣ al-Ibrīz fī Talkhīṣ Bārīz, his account of Paris. Confronted with a term Arabic had no political use for, he did not coin a word and he did not transliterate: he explained the foreign concept through a value his readers already held, and let the old word grow into the new job. حرية in its modern political sense comes down through that generation’s work. Later translators would call this an explanatory equivalent; he was inventing the manoeuvre because a whole vocabulary of politics, law and science had to be brought across, and he then built Madrasat al-Alsun so it would not depend on one man’s judgement.

chunks.title: Eugene A. Nida
chunks.text: Eugene A. Nida · 1914 – 2011 · United States · Translation theory · Bible translation · He tried to make translation something you could study, not only practise. A linguist who spent his career on Bible translation across many languages, and wrote the books that turned translating into an object of systematic study - among them Toward a Science of Translating and, with Charles Taber, The Theory and Practice of Translation. He set formal correspondence, which follows the shape of the original, against what he called dynamic or functional equivalence, which aims for an effect on the reader like the effect the original had on its own. The pair is often reduced to equivalence means natural-sounding, which is not what he argued: his framework is about the whole relationship between text, receptor and context. The same verse under each of his two settings · Greek (Romans 16:16) ἀσπάσασθε ἀλλήλους ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ · Formal correspondence · "greet one another with a holy kiss" — the shape of the original kept, and a gesture most readers have never performed · Dynamic equivalence · "give one another a hearty handshake all around" — the reading Nida’s own project put into the Good News Bible

chunks.title: Eugene A. Nida (cont.)
chunks.text: His argument is not that the second is nicer English. It is that the first reproduces the form and the second reproduces the effect on the receptor — a greeting that lands as a greeting — and that a translator must know which of the two the job calls for. Notice the cost as well: the handshake has quietly deleted a first-century practice from the text. Venuti, last in this lineage, uses this very rendering as his example of what domestication does.

chunks.title: Gregory Rabassa
chunks.text: Gregory Rabassa · 1922 – 2016 · New York · Spanish & Portuguese to English · The author said the translation beat the original. He translated One Hundred Years of Solitude, Hopscotch, and much of the Latin American boom into English. Garcia Marquez waited three years for him, then said the English was better than the Spanish. Rabassa's account of how was disarmingly plain: he did not study the book first, he read it as he translated, because he wanted the English to move at the speed of a reader meeting it. Functional equivalence, practised at the top of the craft. One verb, and the whole first sentence turns on it · Spanish · aquella tarde remota en que su padre lo llevó a conocer el hielo. Word for word · that distant afternoon when his father took him to know ice. What he wrote · that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice. Conocer is to know, to meet, to be acquainted with. "Know" is dead on the page in English and "see" throws the wonder away; discover is a child meeting the thing for the first time, which is what the Spanish actually does. García Márquez waited three years for him and then said the English was better than the Spanish.

chunks.title: Salma Khadra Jayyusi
chunks.text: Salma Khadra Jayyusi · 1926 – 2023 · Palestine & the US · Arabic to English · She built the shelf that modern Arabic literature stands on in English. A poet and scholar who founded PROTA, the project that translated modern Arabic literature into English at scale - more than thirty volumes of it. Before her an English reader could barely find modern Arabic poetry or fiction; after her there was a library. She also proved something about the job: she commissioned, edited and argued the work into existence, because translation at that scale is institution-building, not only writing. Two hands on every poem · Stage one · a close, literal draft by a translator who has the Arabic · Left there · accurate, and not a poem in English — information about a poem · Stage two · an English-language poet works that draft until it is poetry in English, with her editing between them. This was PROTA's house method, and she treated the second stage as non-optional — which is why she kept co-translating with poets rather than publishing the literal drafts. Her other lesson is the unglamorous one: she commissioned, edited, funded and argued more than thirty volumes into print, because at that scale translation is institution-building.

chunks.title: Lawrence Venuti
chunks.text: Lawrence Venuti · born 1953 · United States · Italian to English · theory · Whose voice disappears when a translation reads smoothly? A translator from Italian and a theorist who argued that English-language publishing prizes translations that read as though they were never translated, leaving the translator invisible - and who set out the case in The Translator's Invisibility and The Scandals of Translation. He gave the argument its current vocabulary: domestication, which smooths a text into the target culture, and foreignisation, which keeps the reader aware that they are reading from elsewhere. Neither is simply the good one. They are choices with consequences - for the writer, for the reader, and for whose literature gets to sound like itself. The compliment that proves his point · What reviewers praise · "fluent" "seamless" "reads as though it had been written in English" What is being praised · that no reader can feel the other language under the page — the translator has succeeded by leaving no trace of having been there · What he asks instead · a translation you can see: the strangeness left where it was, and a name on the cover that belongs to somebody

chunks.title: Lawrence Venuti (cont.)
chunks.text: The Translator’s Invisibility builds the case out of the reviews themselves, where fluency is the only thing consistently praised and the translator is usually not named. His objection runs past style to the contract and the copyright page, and past those to the traffic: English publishes very little in translation and expects what it does publish to sound like English, so the smoothing is also a direction of travel. Nida’s "hearty handshake" is one of his examples — domestication, he argues, is not neutral service to the reader but an ethnocentric reduction of the foreign text. He does not claim foreignizing is always right; he claims the choice is never innocent, and the reader should be told it was made.

chunks.title: Scripture, and the first argument
chunks.text: Scripture, and the first argument · النقل الأول والجدل حول الحرف · 3rd century BC – 5th century AD · The word-for-word question is older than every theory that answers it. lede · Translation has no beginning — wherever two languages met, somebody translated. What has a beginning is the argument about how, and it starts with a religious text and a practical problem. card · The Septuagint, and the first authoritative translation. In third-century-BC Alexandria the Hebrew Bible was put into Greek for a Jewish community that no longer read Hebrew. The legend says seventy-two translators worked separately and produced identical texts.The legend matters more than the history. It is the first claim that a translation can carry the authority of its original — and every argument since about whether a translation can be scripture, or law, or evidence, is a continuation of it. card · Cicero, 46 BC · Translating Greek speeches into Latin, Cicero writes that he did not render verbum pro verbo — word for word — but kept the force and the figures. Horace repeats the advice a few years later.That single phrase sets the terms for the next two thousand years. Everything in this guide is, in one way or another, an answer to it. card · Jerome, and the exception he made

chunks.title: Scripture, and the first argument (cont.)
chunks.text: In his letter to Pammachius (c. 395) Jerome takes Cicero's side outright: not word for word but sense for sense.Then he exempts scripture, where even the order of the words is a mystery. Note what has happened: the first person to state the rule clearly also states that it does not apply to the most important text he will ever translate. Text type decides the method — the idea arrives at the same moment the method does.

chunks.title: Baghdad, and the translation movement
chunks.text: Baghdad, and the translation movement · حركة الترجمة في بغداد · 8th – 10th century · Two centuries of funded, professional, systematic translation — and the first method. lede · Under the Abbasids, Greek science, medicine and philosophy were translated into Arabic on a scale nothing in history had attempted — often through Syriac, over roughly two hundred years, paid for by caliphs, viziers and private families. It is the point at which translation becomes a funded profession with a method. card · Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, and translation as rewriting. Earlier and from a different direction: Kalīla wa-Dimna came into Arabic from Middle Persian, itself from Sanskrit.He did not transfer it, he rebuilt it — adding, framing, shaping Arabic literary prose in the act. The result is a founding text of Arabic literature that is also a translation, which is a fact worth sitting with. card · Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq's method · Ḥunayn described how he worked, and it is recognisably modern scholarship: collect every manuscript you can find, collate them, establish a sound text, and only then translate.He also revised his own earlier versions when better manuscripts turned up. Textual criticism as a precondition of translation — in the ninth century. card · Al-Jāḥiẓ's objection

chunks.title: Baghdad, and the translation movement (cont.)
chunks.text: Against all of this, al-Jāḥiẓ argued that the translator must be the equal of the author in knowledge of the subject, not merely of the language — and that poetry cannot be translated at all, because what makes it poetry does not survive.The first is now the uncontroversial basis of specialised translation. The second is still being argued about. card · What it was for · Patronage, prestige, and use. Physicians needed Galen; astronomers needed Ptolemy; the state needed administration.Translation here is not a literary hobby. It is infrastructure — and the works translated in Baghdad are the ones Europe will later translate out of Arabic, in the next era.

chunks.title: Toledo, and the road back west
chunks.text: Toledo, and the road back west · مدرسة طليطلة · 11th – 13th century · Europe recovered its own Greek inheritance through Arabic. lede · In Spain and Sicily, Arabic works — including the Arabic versions of Greek texts made in Baghdad — were translated into Latin. Gerard of Cremona went to Toledo to find a copy of Ptolemy's Almagest, learned Arabic, stayed, and is credited with some seventy works. card · How it was actually done · Often in pairs, and through a third language. A Jewish or Mozarab collaborator read the Arabic aloud in Castilian; a Latin-writing cleric wrote it down in Latin.The intermediate language was spoken and left no text. Relay translation, team translation and the interpreter's role all appear here at once — and so do their characteristic errors. list · What crossed, and what it left in English · The route is still visible in the vocabulary: Almagest — Ptolemy's astronomy, from المجسطي, an Arabic mangling of a Greek superlative. Europe took the book back under an Arabic name. Algebra, from الجبر; algorithm, from al-Khwārizmī's own name. Alcohol, alkali, cipher, zenith, nadir — the definite article ال fossilised into the English word. Ibn Sīnā's Canon of Medicine, which was a European medical textbook into the seventeenth century. card · The point a student should take from it

chunks.title: Toledo, and the road back west (cont.)
chunks.text: The transmission is not one culture generously handing knowledge to another. It is a two-way chain of translations, each step lossy, each step necessary.And nobody in Toledo was translating for the pleasure of it. They were translating because the texts were better than anything available in Latin.

chunks.title: The Bible in the vernacular
chunks.text: The Bible in the vernacular · الكتاب بلغة الناس · 16th century · Translation as a capital offence — and as the making of two national languages. lede · Putting scripture into the language people actually spoke was, for a time, a crime. Tyndale was strangled and burned in 1536 for having done it. Luther had a prince protecting him and survived. card · Luther's rule · In the Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen (1530) Luther answers his critics: you do not ask the Latin letters how to speak German, you look at the mouth of the common man in the marketplace and ask how he says it.It is the target-language-bias argument, four centuries before anyone called it communicative translation. card · What it actually changed · Far more than religion. These translations fixed the shape of modern German and modern English.Tyndale's phrasings passed almost unaltered into the King James Version and from there into ordinary speech: the powers that be, the salt of the earth, a law unto themselves, fight the good fight. Most English speakers quote a sixteenth-century translator every week without knowing it. card · Why the authorities were right to be frightened. A text only the clergy can read is a text only the clergy can interpret. Translation moved the authority to interpret.Keep this in view for the ideology unit of 284: the claim that translation is a neutral technical service has never once been true, and here it is not even pretending.

chunks.title: The age of the rules
chunks.text: The age of the rules · عصر القواعد · 17th – 18th century · Translators stop defending themselves anecdotally and start classifying. lede · English writers begin to set out what the options actually are, rather than arguing case by case. It is the first move towards a systematic account, and it is made by practising poets rather than scholars. list · Dryden's three, 1680 · In the preface to his Ovid's Epistles, Dryden divides translation into three: Metaphrase — word by word and line by line. He compares it to dancing on a rope with fettered legs. Paraphrase — sense for sense, the author kept in view but the words free. He recommends this one. Imitation — the translator takes liberties not only with the words but with the sense, writing what the author might have written. He mistrusts it, and does it anyway. card · Tytler's three laws, 1790 · Alexander Fraser Tytler's Essay on the Principles of Translation is the first book-length treatment in English. His laws: a translation should give a complete transcript of the idea of the original, its style and manner should be of the same character, and it should have all the ease of original composition.The three pull against each other, and he knows it. Deciding which to sacrifice is still the job. card · Why this era matters to you · Dryden's middle term is the ancestor of every later three-way scheme: literal, communicative and free; formal and dynamic; foreignising and domesticating.The categories have changed names several times. The decision underneath has not changed at all.

chunks.title: Two paths, and the Nahḍa
chunks.text: Two paths, and the Nahḍa · الرومانسية والنهضة · 19th century · Move the reader to the author, or the author to the reader — and Cairo builds an institution. lede · The nineteenth century produces the sharpest statement of the central choice, and, at the other end of the Mediterranean, the first modern state translation institution in Arabic. card · Schleiermacher, 1813 · In a lecture in Berlin he says there are only two paths: either the translator leaves the author in peace and moves the reader towards him, or leaves the reader in peace and moves the author towards him.Any mixture, he says, produces something unreliable. He prefers the first, because it enlarges the reader's own language. Venuti will rename these foreignising and domesticating in 1995, and credit him. card · Al-Ṭahṭāwī, Paris and Cairo · Sent to Paris in 1826 as imam to a student mission, he learned French, read the Enlightenment, and wrote an account of France for Arabic readers. Back in Cairo he founded the School of Languages — مدرسة الألسن — in 1835.Hundreds of works into Arabic: law, engineering, geography, military science. And with them the modern Arabic vocabulary for constitution, citizenship, public opinion and the rest — a case of translation making the terms a language would then argue in. card · The same century, the opposite problem

chunks.title: Two paths, and the Nahḍa (cont.)
chunks.text: Schleiermacher is arguing about how to keep the foreign foreign, for a culture confident enough to be enlarged by it.Al-Ṭahṭāwī is building the means to acquire what a different power already had. Both are translation policy; they are answering different questions, and reading them together is more instructive than reading either alone.

chunks.title: The machine, and the model
chunks.text: The machine, and the model · قرن الآلة والنموذج · 20th century · Translation is declared a decoding problem, solved in five years, and abandoned in seventeen. lede · Two things happen at once: engineers try to automate translation, and linguists try to describe it. The first fails publicly. The second produces most of the vocabulary this course uses. list · The machine, in four dates · 1949. Warren Weaver's memorandum proposes treating translation as decoding: a Russian text is English in a strange code. 1954. The Georgetown–IBM demonstration translates forty-nine selected Russian sentences and claims the problem will be solved within five years. 1966. The ALPAC report finds machine translation slower, less accurate and more expensive than a human. American funding collapses for two decades. 1990s onward. Statistical methods, then neural ones from 2016, then large language models. The failure was never arithmetic — it was that meaning is not in the code. card · Nida, and equivalence · Out of Bible-translation practice, Eugene Nida distinguishes formal equivalence — stay close to the form of the source — from dynamic equivalence — produce on the new reader the effect the original had on its own.The phrase effect on the receptor is his, and Newmark's communicative translation descends directly from it. So does most of 284. card · And the literary proof

chunks.title: The machine, and the model (cont.)
chunks.text: Gregory Rabassa's English One Hundred Years of Solitude (1970) is the translation García Márquez said he preferred to his own Spanish.Rabassa's own account of how he did it: he read it as he translated it, without finishing it first. Worth holding against every process model on this site — including the one in 180.

chunks.title: Where it stands now
chunks.text: Where it stands now · الحاضر · 1990s – today · The translator becomes visible, and the machine comes back. lede · Two arguments run at the same time and hardly talk to each other: one about the translator's position and power, one about what the software has made of the job. card · Visibility · Venuti's The Translator's Invisibility (1995) points out that Anglo-American publishing prizes a translation that reads as though it were not one — and that this fluency is not neutral. It erases both the translator and the foreignness of the text.Whether you agree or not, the question it forces is a real one: who is served by a translation that hides its own existence? card · Institutions, not single books · Salma Khadra Jayyusi's PROTA did not translate a book; it built the apparatus by which Arabic literature could exist in English at all — commissioning, editing, anthologising, finding publishers.A reminder that what gets translated is decided long before any translator opens the file, and usually by someone else. list · And the work itself has changed shape · Post-editing. A large share of commercial translation is now correcting machine output rather than producing a first draft — a different skill, and often worse paid. Audiovisual. Subtitling and dubbing, with constraints (characters per line, reading speed, lip-sync) that no literary theory anticipated. Localisation. Software, games and interfaces, where the text is fragments without context and the product is adapted, not translated.

chunks.title: Where it stands now (cont.)
chunks.text: Community and crisis translation. Volunteers, fansubbers, and translators in emergencies — unpaid, unregulated, and often the only version anyone reads. card · The ALPAC question, returning · In 1966 a committee asked whether the machine was actually cheaper than a person, and the answer was no.The question is open again, and this time the honest answer depends entirely on the text type, which is where 180 began and where this guide ends.

chunks.title: 1972, and a name
chunks.text: 1972, and a name · الاسم والخريطة · The paper the field dates itself from. lede · James Holmes, The Name and Nature of Translation Studies, 1972. Before it, translation was studied inside comparative literature, inside contrastive linguistics, inside workshops — never on its own terms, and without an agreed name. list · What the map contains · Holmes divides the field in two, and then divides again: Pure — theoretical (what translation is and how it works) and descriptive (what translations actually are, in the world). Descriptive splits three ways: product-oriented (this translation, compared with that one), process-oriented (what happens in the translator's head), function-oriented (what the translation did in its receiving culture). Applied — training, tools and aids, criticism, and policy. card · Why a map was the useful thing to produce · Not because it settled anything, but because it showed people working on unrelated-looking problems that they were in the same field.Almost every branch on it has since grown into a subfield with its own journals. The one Holmes could not have drawn is the computational one.

chunks.title: Jakobson's three kinds
chunks.text: Jakobson's three kinds · أنواع الترجمة الثلاثة · 1959, and still the cleanest definition in the subject. list · The division · Roman Jakobson separates three things the one word covers: Intralingual — within a language. Paraphrase, summary, putting a contract into plain Arabic. Interlingual — between two languages. Translation proper, in his phrase, and what the profession sells. Intersemiotic — between sign systems. A novel into a film, speech into subtitle, a warning into a pictogram. card · What the third one is for · It is not a curiosity. Subtitling is interlingual and intersemiotic at once — speech into writing and one language into another, under a character limit.Kuwaiti Sign Language interpreting is the same: no writing system, a different modality, and a different language. Jakobson's third category is the one that has grown fastest.

chunks.title: The linguistic phase
chunks.text: The linguistic phase · المرحلة اللسانية · Translation described as an operation on language, with a vocabulary for its moves. list · Three accounts, roughly a decade apart · Vinay & Darbelnet, 1958. Seven procedures — borrowing, calque, literal translation, transposition, modulation, equivalence, adaptation. The Compass's own guide works all seven in Arabic and English. Catford, 1965. Shifts: the small obligatory departures from formal correspondence that the target language's grammar forces on you — level shifts and category shifts. Nida, 1964. Formal against dynamic equivalence — the form of the source, or the effect on the receptor. card · What this phase got right, and what it missed. Right: a shared vocabulary for describing what a translator actually did to a sentence. Almost everything on this site that lets you say here is the move I made comes from here.Missed: why the translator chose that move. The texts were treated as though they had no commissioner, no deadline, no publisher and no politics.

chunks.title: Skopos: the purpose decides
chunks.text: Skopos: the purpose decides · نظرية الغرض · The brief outranks the source text. lede · Hans Vermeer (1978), then Reiss and Vermeer together (1984): a translation is an action, actions have purposes, and the purpose of the target text — the skopos — determines the method. card · The consequence people find uncomfortable · The same source text, commissioned for two purposes, yields two translations, and both are correct. Fidelity is demoted: it becomes one possible requirement of a brief, not the definition of the job.If you have ever translated a document one way for a court and another way for a press release, you have already agreed with Vermeer. card · Where it is strongest, and where it is weakest. Strongest on commercial and technical work, where there really is a brief and a client.Weakest on literature, where the purpose is not given in advance and the translator is usually the one deciding it. Critics also object that it licenses too much: a sufficiently bold brief can justify almost any intervention.

chunks.title: Describe, don't prescribe
chunks.text: Describe, don't prescribe · الدراسات الوصفية · Polysystem theory and descriptive translation studies. card · Even-Zohar, and where translations sit · Polysystem theory (1970s) treats a literature as a system of systems, with a centre and a periphery, and asks where translated literature sits in it.His answer: usually the periphery — but at the centre when a literature is young, or in crisis, or peripheral itself. At those moments translation changes the receiving literature rather than conforming to it. Read the Nahḍa against this and it stops looking like borrowing. card · Toury, and norms · Gideon Toury turns the subject around: stop asking what translators should do, and describe what they demonstrably did, then infer the norms they were working under.Norms are not rules; they are what a community at a given moment treats as acceptable. This is why a translation from 1880 and one from 2020 can both be competent and look nothing alike.

chunks.title: The cultural turn
chunks.text: The cultural turn · المنعطف الثقافي · 1990: the unit of study stops being the sentence. lede · Bassnett and Lefevere's Translation, History and Culture (1990) names the shift: translation is rewriting, rewriting is done under patronage and ideology, and the interesting questions are about power rather than equivalence. list · What grew out of it · Postcolonial translation studies — translation as an instrument of empire, and as a means of answering back. Who translates whom, and in which direction, is not an accident. Feminist translation — the translator's interventions made deliberate and visible rather than hidden. Ideology and censorship — what gets translated, what does not, and what is quietly altered on the way. This is 284's last two units, and it comes from here. Translation and conflict — interpreters in war and asylum, and the position they are placed in. card · The standing objection · That the turn moved so far from the text that it stopped being about translation.Worth taking seriously. The defence is that the sentence-level account could not explain why two competent translators, given the same text, produce systematically different books — and it could not.

chunks.title: Invisibility
chunks.text: Invisibility · احتجاب المترجم · Venuti, 1995 — and Schleiermacher's two paths, renamed. lede · Lawrence Venuti argues that Anglo-American publishing rewards the translation that reads as though it were written in English — and that this fluency is an ideology, not a standard. It makes the translator disappear and the foreign text look domestic. split · The two strategies · Domesticating · التوطين · Bring the text to the reader. Fluent, transparent, no friction — and the reader never learns that anything was ever strange. Foreignising · التغريب · Take the reader to the text. Keep the resistance, let the target language be marked by the encounter — at the cost of ease, and sometimes of sales. card · What to do with it in practice · Venuti is not saying domestication is always wrong. He is saying it is a choice that is usually made invisibly, by an industry rather than by a translator.The usable form of the argument, and the one 284 ends on: know which you did, and be able to say why.

chunks.title: Where the research is now
chunks.text: Where the research is now · اتجاهات البحث الحالية · Corpora, cognition, sociology — and the argument with the machine. list · Four live areas · Corpus translation studies. Mona Baker (1993 onward) uses large electronic corpora to test claims empirically — including the recurring finding that translations tend to be more explicit, more conventional and more standardised than originals. Cognitive and process research. Keystroke logging, eye-tracking and think-aloud protocols, filling in Holmes's process-oriented branch with evidence rather than introspection. Sociology of translation. The translator as a worker: status, rates, unions, the agency model, and who actually captures the value. Machine translation and post-editing. Quality estimation, the measurable degradation of post-edited style, and what happens to a language when most of its incoming text arrives through one model. card · And the question underneath all four · Every one of them is a version of Holmes's original problem: this is an activity everybody uses and almost nobody examines.The reason to know the history is not reverence. It is that each of these debates has been had before in other words, and knowing which ones were settled — and which only went quiet — is the difference between a practitioner and a technician.

chunks.title: Translation Minor
chunks.text: Translation Minor · مساند الترجمة · 24 credits · ٢٤ وحدة دراسية · Entry prerequisite 142 · take all four compulsory courses, and two from each elective group. المتطلب السابق: ١٤٢ — أربعة مقررات إجبارية، ومقرران من كل مجموعة اختيارية. Compulsory · المقررات الإجبارية · Take all four · أربعة مقررات، ١٢ وحدة دراسية · Compulsory · 180 · Principles of Translation · مبادئ الترجمة · 142 · What translation is, before you are any good at it. The foundation course, and the prerequisite for everything else in the minor. It separates form from meaning — the shape a language happens to use, and the thing being said — and shows that keeping one usually costs you the other.From there come the choices a translator actually makes: literal or free, and which of the procedures the sentence in front of you needs. The course's real subject is that these are decisions, made by a person, for reasons that can be stated. Every course above it · Any first commission · The basis of a commentary · That you stop translating words and start translating messages — and that you can say afterwards what you did, and why. procedures · toolkit · What translation is not · ما ليست الترجمة · Ten things everybody believes, and why the course begins by clearing them away. lede · Almost everyone arrives with the same set of beliefs about this work, and almost all of them are wrong. They are worth stating plainly, because each one, left in place, produces a specific kind of bad translation. split · The first confusion, and the one that matters most · Translation · الترجمة التحريرية

chunks.title: Translation Minor (cont.)
chunks.text: Written text into written text. You can stop, look something up, change your mind, and revise. Interpreting · الترجمة الشفوية · Speech into speech, in real time, often while the speaker is still talking. There is no second pass. list · The rest of them · Each is stated as people state it, with what is actually true underneath: It is an exchange of words. Languages differ in vocabulary, grammar and structure, so what moves across is the sense, not the words. Some things have no counterpart at all and must be conveyed another way. Any bilingual can do it. Two languages is the entry requirement, not the qualification. The work needs training, command of both written registers, and knowledge of the subject. Machines have made it unnecessary. Machine output is a draft. It does not know the subject and does not read the culture. Someone has to be able to tell when it is wrong — which takes more skill than translating, not less. The need is shrinking. It is not. The market has grown, not contracted, alongside the tools. A translator covers every field. Almost nobody does. Legal, medical and financial translation are separate trades with separate vocabularies. Translators work in many languages. Most work in two. The depth required in each is the reason. You need not understand the material. You cannot translate what you have not understood. It is the one thing with no shortcut. Culture is optional. It is not separable from the language. Idiom, reference and what may be said at all are cultural facts.

chunks.title: Translation Minor (cont.)
chunks.text: It can be free. Free tools translate phrases. Documents that carry consequences are paid work, for the same reason the consequences exist. card · Why start here · Every one of these produces a recognisable fault. Believing it is word-exchange produces the word-for-word rendering. Believing bilingualism is enough produces fluent text that is wrong about the subject. Believing culture is optional produces the sentence that is accurate and unsayable.The rest of the course is, in a sense, these errors taken one at a time. One sentence, and the belief it exposes · English · The bill was tabled. Word by word · وُضِع مشروع القانون على الطاولة · What it actually says · أُرجئ النظر في مشروع القانون · In British usage to table a bill is to bring it forward; in American usage it is to shelve it. No dictionary lookup of the individual words reaches this. You need to know which parliament you are in — which is the myth about understanding the material, in one sentence. Do this before the next unit · Take any news paragraph in English and translate it into Arabic twice: once trying to keep the word order, once ignoring it entirely.Put them side by side. The second is almost certainly better. Write one sentence saying what the first one lost — that sentence is the whole subject of this course. Translation Studies · دراسات الترجمة · The practice is ancient. The discipline is about fifty years old. lede

chunks.title: Translation Minor (cont.)
chunks.text: People have translated for as long as there have been neighbours who spoke differently. Studying translation as a subject in its own right is recent — and for most of the twentieth century the academy treated it as a language-teaching exercise rather than a field. card · 1972, and a map · James Holmes set out a map of what a discipline of translation would actually contain, and that paper is usually taken as the point where the field began to be one. Before it, translation was studied inside comparative literature, inside contrastive linguistics, inside workshops — never on its own terms.It is now interdisciplinary by nature: linguistics, literature, culture, and increasingly computing all have a claim on it. list · Jakobson's three kinds · Roman Jakobson divided translation into three, and the division still holds: Intralingual — within one language. Rewording, paraphrase, summary, simplifying a contract into plain Arabic. Interlingual — between two languages. What is usually meant by the word, and the subject of this course. Intersemiotic — between sign systems. A novel into a film, a warning into a pictogram, speech into subtitle. list · Translation as a process, not an act · The word names both the process and its product. As a process it has stages, and skipping any of them shows in the result: Read the source until you understand it, and find out what you do not know. Establish its message, intent, form, type and audience. Draft, holding that message and intent, for the audience the target text will actually have.

chunks.title: Translation Minor (cont.)
chunks.text: Conform to the norms of the target language rather than the shape of the source. Revise and check. The same content, three kinds of translation · Source · No unauthorised entry. Intralingual · Only staff may go past this point — same language, different words · Interlingual · ممنوع الدخول لغير المصرَّح لهم · And intersemiotic: the red circle with a bar through it that says the same thing to somebody who reads neither language. All three are translation under Jakobson; only the middle one is what the profession sells. Do this before the next unit · Find a short legal or official sentence in Arabic — a clause from a contract, a notice on a government site. Do all three of Jakobson's kinds on it: reword it in plain Arabic, translate it into English, and describe the sign or icon that would carry it.Note which was hardest. For most people it is the first, which is the useful surprise. Where the work came from · لمحة تاريخية · Four moments, and what each of them moved. lede · The history matters here for one reason: in every period, translation is what carried knowledge across a border it could not otherwise cross. The technique changed. That function did not. card · The ancient world · Egypt, Greece and Rome all ran on translation — for trade, for governance, for law. The Rosetta Stone is the emblem: the same decree in three scripts, which is why Egyptian writing could be read again at all. What moved was science, philosophy and literature, and it moved because somebody carried it. card · The Middle Ages

chunks.title: Translation Minor (cont.)
chunks.text: Latin was the language of scholarship, so Greek and Roman work survived in Europe largely by being translated into it, in monasteries, by hand.The Compass's own Translators in History holds the other half of this period, the one the standard account often leaves out: the Arabic translation movement, and the scholars who preserved and advanced the same inheritance. card · The Renaissance · The classics were translated out of Latin and Greek into the languages people actually spoke. That single move — into the vernacular — put ancient learning in front of a wide readership for the first time, and the consequences were not literary but historical. card · The twentieth century · Translation became a subject. Eugene Nida, working on Bible translation, brought a systematic account of equivalence to it; Holmes gave the field its map; journals, departments and research centres followed.That is the short answer to why this course exists and why it has a reading list. Why the vernacular move was not a small one · Latin · Vulgus vult decipi. Kept in Latin · readable by perhaps two people in a hundred · Into the spoken language · الناس تحب أن تُخدَع · Nothing about the sentence changed except who could read it — and that is the entire content of the Renaissance as far as translation is concerned. Access is not a side effect of translation. It is the point of it. Do this before the next unit

chunks.title: Translation Minor (cont.)
chunks.text: Pick one translator from Translators in History in this site and answer, in three sentences: what did they move, from where to where, and what would not exist if they had not?Keep the answer. You will be asked to write commentary like this for your own work later in the minor. Equivalence at word level · التكافؤ على مستوى الكلمة · There is no such thing as one word for one word. This unit says exactly why. lede · Mona Baker's account of equivalence starts at the smallest unit and works upward, and this is the bottom of it. The finding is blunt: there is no one-to-one correspondence between words and units of meaning — not even within a single language. card · Words are not the smallest unit · Rebuild is one word carrying two pieces of meaning. Unbreakable is one word carrying three. The piece that cannot be cut further is the morpheme, not the word.So a count of words tells you nothing. English happiness is one word and so is Arabic سعادة; English tennis player is two words and Turkish tenisçi is one. Nothing follows from the counting. list · The four kinds of lexical meaning · Baker separates what a word carries into four. Most translation arguments are really disagreements about which of these is being preserved: Propositional — what it refers to in the world.
