A term without a source is a guess, however confident it sounds.

chunks.where: Learn › Translation Minor › ENGL 180 Principles of Translation
chunks.title: Localisation
chunks.text: Localisation · الأقلمة · Translation is one part of it. The rest is everything else the product assumes about you. lede · Localisation is adapting a product, service or piece of content so that it is linguistically and culturally right for a particular market — software, websites, manuals, multimedia, games. card · Locale · The technical term for what you are adapting to. A locale is the set of features of a user's environment that depend on language, country or region, and cultural convention.It settles sort order, keyboard layout, and the formats for date, time, number and currency. None of that is translation, and all of it is wrong if you ignore it. card · Where translation sits · Translation is the linguistic aspect of localisation — a subset of the activities, not the whole of it. Its goal within that process is the same as everywhere else in this course: equivalence of meaning, idiomatic, lexical and conceptual.The rest of localisation is layout that survives right-to-left, images that make sense locally, forms that accept local addresses, and defaults that assume the right things. card · The test · A localised product should not read as a translated one. The user should not be able to tell that it was made somewhere else — which is a higher standard than accuracy, and a different one.It is also the clearest case in the course of a translation being judged by its effect on its reader rather than by its correspondence to its source. The same interface, two locales · English build · Payment due 03/04/2026 $1,250.00 · Translated only

chunks.where: Learn › Translation Minor › ENGL 180 Principles of Translation
chunks.title: Localisation (cont.)
chunks.text: الدفعة مستحقة 03/04/2026 · $1,250.00 — every word rendered, and the date is now ambiguous and the currency foreign · Localised · الدفعة مستحقة في ٣ أبريل ٢٠٢٦ ١٬٢٥٠٫٠٠ د.ك · Nothing here is a translation problem. Date order, numeral form, decimal and thousands marks and currency are all locale conventions — and getting them wrong on an invoice is more consequential than any wording choice on the screen. The last one · Take one screen of an app or website you use in English and localise it into Arabic — not just translate it.List everything you had to change that was not a word: direction, alignment, date and number formats, currency, icons, the example names in the form fields. That list is the difference between translation and localisation, and it is the last thing this course has to teach you.

chunks.title: What terminology is
chunks.text: What terminology is · ما علم المصطلح؟ A discipline nobody quite agrees on, and why it had to exist. lede · There is no settled agreement on what terminology is, and the reason is historical: it borrowed from older fields — semantics, lexicology, lexicography — and each of them left a different idea of what the subject is for. card · Why it appeared when it did · Two pressures, both recent. Science and technology pushed the frontier back in genetics, space, information science, telecommunications — and every new concept needs a name.And contact between language communities. The need for terms is real in one language; it multiplies when two or more are in contact, because for every concept named in one, an equivalent has to be found in the others. list · Why practitioners disagree · The disagreement is not academic point-scoring. Each position produces a different kind of work: Those who fear that a flood of new terms will impede communication see terminology as a means of standardising. Many linguists and lexicologists treat it as technical lexicography and nothing more. Some schools set out to produce exhaustive word lists — without defining the terms or classifying the concepts. split · The word has two meanings, and they are not the same size · The terms themselves · المصطلحات · The technical terms and expressions used in an art, a science or a specialised subject. Still the ordinary English sense. The study of them · علم المصطلح

chunks.title: What terminology is (cont.)
chunks.text: The systematic research and identification of the terms specific to a subject field, and of the concepts they represent. The sense this course means. card · The definition to know · A discipline aimed at systematically identifying specialised terms in the context in which they are used, analysing the concepts they represent in that context, and creating and standardising terms, if need be, to meet the user's need for means of expression.It is a linguistic discipline with theoretical guidelines and defined work methods. That is what separates it from collecting vocabulary. list · The four work methods · The whole course is these four, taken in turn: Term identification — finding the terms peculiar to a field: simple, complex and phrasal. Contextual analysis — determining each term's meaning from the context it sits in. Term creation — filling a genuine gap, and only after every source has been searched. Standardisation — settling which term may carry the concept, and recording it. The order matters: identify before you create · The temptation · No Arabic term comes to mind, so coin one. What the discipline says · The terminologist's role is first and foremost to identify existing terms, not to invent new ones. When coining is warranted · Only when every available source has been researched and the evidence shows no term exists in the target language for that concept.

chunks.title: What terminology is (cont.)
chunks.text: This is the single most common error a beginner makes, and it is expensive: a coined term that duplicates an existing one splits the field's usage in two, and both halves then have to be reconciled by somebody later. Do this before the next unit · Pick a field you know a little — banking, aviation, nursing. Write down ten of its terms in English.Now mark each one: is it a term peculiar to that field, or a general-language word you have assumed belongs to it? Most people find three or four of the ten are general words. Those four are not terminology, and knowing the difference is where this subject starts.

chunks.title: Specialized terms and the user
chunks.text: Specialized terms and the user · المصطلحات المتخصصة والمستفيد · Who the work is for, and why context decides everything. lede · Almost every field of human endeavour has its own special language — the arts, science, business, economics, law, medicine. The lexicon of a special language holds both general-language words and terms with special reference, and terminology is concerned only with the second. split · Two kinds of context, two levels of difficulty · Situational · السياق الموقفي · The term is connected to the concrete thing it refers to. You can see the object. The meaning becomes clear. Written · السياق النصي · Nothing to point at. You analyse the context, identify the semantic features it contains, and build the concept from those. card · Why this matters most in two languages · In bilingual and multilingual work you must find enough information on the source term's meaning in context to go and research its target-language equivalent in context.Equivalence of semantic features across the two contexts is called textual correspondence, and it is what establishes that two terms are equivalent. Not a dictionary line: matching features in matching contexts. card · The user decides the job · Terminologists work to the user's communication needs, and those vary enormously — an advertiser's needs are not a scientist's.But every user, whoever they are and whatever language they speak, arrives with the same question: what is this called, or what do I call this? Everything else is method. list · Where the findings go · Research has to end somewhere it can be used and changed:

chunks.title: Specialized terms and the user (cont.)
chunks.text: Records, once on paper and now in computerized databases. Multiple access to the same information without reproducing it, huge capacity, very fast retrieval. Vocabularies — for a wide audience or users unfamiliar with terminological method. Alphabetical: source entry, target equivalents, a concise definition, the subfield. Glossaries — an alphabetical list of terms specific to a discipline with their target-language equivalents. Why usage, not correctness, is the test · The rule · Terminologists must be aware of current usage. What happens if they are not · Their work would serve no purpose were they to give the user depreciated or rare terminology. How usage is established · By researching terms in context — not by preference, authority, or what the dictionary printed twenty years ago. A term that is defensible and unused is a failure. This is the point where terminology parts company with prescriptive grammar: the question is never what people ought to say, but what the field actually says now. Do this before the next unit · Take one English term from a specialised field and find it in three different written contexts — not three dictionaries, three real texts.For each, list the semantic features the context supplies. Then compare your three lists. Where they agree you have the concept; where they differ you have either a second sense or a sloppy source, and telling those apart is the work.

chunks.title: Semantics and lexicography
chunks.text: Semantics and lexicography · علم الدلالة وصناعة المعجم · The two disciplines terminology is mistaken for, and the direction that separates them. lede · Terminology is regularly confused with the other disciplines that deal with the lexicon. It is worth being able to say exactly how it differs, because the difference is not a matter of degree — it is a matter of which end you start from. card · What the semanticist does · Semantics studies the relationship between the linguistic sign and the object it refers to — why a chair is called a chair. Two approaches:Diachronic, the historical one: fish from Old English fisc and Old Frisian fisk, and then how that first meaning branched — the flesh of the fish, a piece of hard wood strengthening a ship's mast, a cold person.Synchronic, the descriptive one: meanings as a system, where one meaning can have several signs and one sign several meanings, and the dates are irrelevant because old and new survive side by side as polysemy. card · What the terminologist does with the same word. Begins with the context, not the etymology. Researching in biology, the terminologist establishes that a cold-blooded aquatic vertebrate with gills is called a fish.That the word means other things in other fields is interesting and not the point. The semanticist wants the whole semantic range; the terminologist wants the features that fix one label to one concept in one field. split · And the direction of travel · The lexicographer · صانع المعجم

chunks.title: Semantics and lexicography (cont.)
chunks.text: Starts from the sign and investigates the concept or concepts it represents. Researches the entire lexicon. The reader is decoding — they met a word and need its meaning. The terminologist · أخصائي المصطلح · Starts from the concept and researches its sign. Researches only the stock specific to a field. The user is encoding — they have a meaning and need the word for it. list · Three places that difference shows · Nomenclature. The lexicographer takes every word and every meaning in every situation. The terminologist takes the terms of one subject within a stated framework — and takes all its means of expression: simple, complex and phrasal. Analysis. Lexicographical analysis builds a word's complete semantic profile. Terminological analysis determines the characteristics of one concept, so the term can be linked to it and an equivalent found in another language. Definition. A lexicographer's definition covers all accepted uses. A terminologist's condenses the semantic features of the term as used in one real situation. One word, two disciplines, two right answers · The word · fish · The semanticist's answer · Every meaning it has carried — the animal, the flesh, the mast timber, the cold person — literal and figurative, concrete and abstract, together making its semantic range in modern English. The terminologist's answer, in biology · سمكة — a cold-blooded aquatic vertebrate with gills. The rest exists and is not the question being asked.

chunks.title: Semantics and lexicography (cont.)
chunks.text: Neither is wrong. They are answers to different questions, and a translator who reaches for the wrong one brings back either far too much or the wrong sense entirely. Do this before the next unit · Take a polysemous English word that also works as a term — cell, bond, charge, current.Write the lexicographer's entry: every sense you can find. Then pick one field and write the terminologist's: the single concept, its features, and the Arabic term for it. Notice that the second is shorter and much harder.

chunks.title: Term and concept
chunks.text: Term and concept · المصطلح والمفهوم · What counts as a term, and what makes a concept that term's own. lede · Terminological inquiry has to make the relation between a term and its concept explicit — between the signifier, a word in the language, and the signified, the object in the world. They are joined through the concept in the mind, and it is the concept that terminology works on. list · Three shapes a term can take · A term designates a concept specific to a subject field. The examples below are all from television production: Simple — one word: a stem with or without affixes. To coproduce, commentator, monochrome. Still simple though they hold several morphemes, because co-, -ator and mono- cannot stand alone as terms. Complex — two or more words in a grammatical relationship: captive audience, laughmeter, director-producer, closeup, ultrawide-angle lens, to lip sync. Phrasal — a group of words with a higher syntactic function: request for copyright clearance, to preempt a program, filmed on location, on the air. card · One concept, whatever the shape · All three represent a single concept in the field. That is the test, not the word count.And it has a consequence: remove any one element of a complex term and the concept changes. Ultrawide-angle lens is not a long way of saying lens. card · Essential characteristics

chunks.title: Term and concept (cont.)
chunks.text: A concept is described by the sum of its essential characteristics. Take watch: having a face and hands, being used to tell time, having a movement driven in one of several ways.All true — and not enough, because they do not separate a watch from every other timepiece. Add designed to be worn on a wristband, pin or chain and now they do. The characteristics that are both necessary and sufficient to distinguish a concept from all others are its essential characteristics. They need not come in any particular order. card · A term belongs to its field, not to the language. General-language words are constantly borrowed by disciplines to name new concepts. Their meaning is broadened, narrowed or otherwise changed — they take on a new semantic load.Furniture in the urban-planning term street furniture does not mean what it means at home. Highway in information highway is not a road. Investigate the term in the field it belongs to, or you will translate the wrong concept confidently. Borrowed word, new semantic load · English term · street furniture · The general-language reading · أثاث الشارع — furniture, outdoors. Grammatical, and not what an urban planner means. The concept · عناصر تأثيث الشارع — benches, bollards, lamp posts, shelters: the fixed public fittings of a street. The English word was borrowed from the general language and given a new load. The Arabic has to carry the concept, not the borrowed word — which is why the equivalent is longer and why the literal version tells the reader nothing. Do this before the next unit

chunks.title: Term and concept (cont.)
chunks.text: Find five terms in one field and sort them: simple, complex, phrasal.Then take the complex ones and delete one element from each. Write what the remainder now means. In every case it should be a different concept, not a vaguer version of the same one — if it is only vaguer, what you had was probably not a term.

chunks.title: Subject-field research
chunks.text: Subject-field research · البحث في مجال متخصص · The long kind: exhaustive, systematic, and six stages before you extract a single term. lede · Research carried out on the terms and concepts of a whole subject is subject-field research. It is relatively exhaustive, runs over a long period, and therefore demands a thorough and systematic approach — most of which happens before any term is written down. list · Six stages, all preliminary · Every one of these is completed before scanning for and extracting terms begins: Determining the research objectives · Estimating the necessary resources · Becoming familiar with the subject field · Selecting the documentation · Locating the documentation · Evaluating the documentation · card · 1 · Objectives — settled with the client · Three things: purpose, target audience, scope.Purpose varies from filling a total gap to revising and enlarging what exists. Audience runs from layman to specialist — a company manager, a language professional, an enthusiast. And scope follows the need: the basic terminology of a field is a few hundred concepts; the complete terminology of a field or major subfield is a few thousand. list · 2 · Resources — also settled with the client · Three kinds, and the questions to ask about each: Human. How many terminologists? Is there support staff to key in the data? Can one or more subject-field specialists take part?

chunks.title: Subject-field research (cont.)
chunks.text: Documentary. Are there original documents — not translations — in both languages? Vocabularies or glossaries in the field or related ones? Bibliographic databases? Does any term bank already hold material on it? Financial. What is required, and is it available? card · Why this front-loading is not bureaucracy · A few hundred concepts and a few thousand are not the same job with a different deadline; they are different jobs. Agreeing the scope after starting means discovering halfway that the work was aimed at the wrong audience, at the wrong depth, from documentation that cannot support it.And the documentary question does the most work: original documents, not translations. Research a term from a translated source and you may be researching the previous translator's guess. The same field, two different assignments · Client A · “We need our staff to understand the basics of Islamic banking in English.” What that is · A few hundred concepts. A vocabulary. Audience: non-specialist. Documentation: introductory and regulatory. Client B · “We are drafting contracts and need the complete terminology.” — a few thousand concepts, specialist audience, original contracts and standards as sources. Same subject field, same two languages, and almost nothing else in common. Determining the objective is not a formality before the work — it is the decision that shapes every stage after it. Do this before the next unit

chunks.title: Subject-field research (cont.)
chunks.text: Choose a field and write a one-page research plan through all six stages: purpose, audience, scope in number of concepts, the three resource questions, and a named list of documentation.For the documentation, mark each source original or translated. If more than half your list is translated, the plan is not yet viable — and finding that out now is the point of writing it.

chunks.title: Term research
chunks.text: Term research · البحث في مصطلح مفرد · The short kind: one term, one client, and often an answer needed today. lede · Research on individual terms or concepts is term research, and it is most of the terminological work done in private organisations and government agencies — answering the questions of everybody from the layman to the expert. card · Why it exists at all · Ideally subject-field research would be done in every field. It would take time and money, both usually scarce — and even with both, it could never keep pace: there would always be new concepts to name, new problems, new users.Term research is what covers the gap, and it is not second-best. It is the form of the work most people actually encounter. list · Six steps · Discussion with the client · Checking the concept · Consulting a specialist · Researching the solution · Checking the solution · Presenting the solution · card · The best training there is · Clients ask about almost any topic and usually need an answer within four to forty-eight hours. That pressure is the training.You work directly with the user, so you learn what users actually need. You sharpen the habit of assimilating a subject fast. And you come to know your documentation so well that you develop a sense of which source is likely to hold this particular answer — which is a skill no reading list can give you. card · Note the second step

chunks.title: Term research (cont.)
chunks.text: Checking the concept comes before consulting anyone or researching anything.Clients ask for a word. What they have is a concept they cannot name, and it is frequently not the concept their question implies. Establish what they actually mean first, or the following four steps research the wrong thing efficiently. The question asked, and the question meant · The client asks · “What is the English for تعثر?” Answered straight · stumbling, faltering, default — three terms from three fields, offered blind · After checking the concept · It is a loan agreement. The concept is a borrower failing to meet an obligation, so the term is default — and the file says so, with the context it came from. One question to the client turned three guesses into one sourced answer. That question is step two, and skipping it is the most common way a fast answer becomes a wrong one. Do this before the next unit · Have somebody send you a real term question with no context — just a word and a language pair. Work all six steps, and hold yourself to forty-eight hours.Write down what you asked at step two and what the answer changed. Then present the solution properly: the term, the definition, the context, and the source. An answer without a source is not a solution; it is an opinion delivered promptly.

chunks.title: Terminological analysis
chunks.text: Terminological analysis · التحليل المصطلحي · Where a term begins and ends — and which words around it are actually part of it. lede · Analysis is the centre of subject-field research: identifying the terms of the field and analysing the contexts they appear in. The hard part is not finding candidates. It is deciding how much of the phrase is the term. split · The two parts of a complex term · Determinatum · المُحدَّد · The base word being qualified — advertising in subliminal advertising, editing in film editing. Determinant · المُحدِّد · The element qualifying it — desktop in desktop publishing. Only determinants that fundamentally modify the base are part of the term. card · Essential and inessential, and why the same word can be either. Charitable institution is a term: charitable changes what kind of institution this is. Charitable man is not: charitable merely describes a man.Same determinant, opposite verdicts. Intricate in intricate technology product only says the product is complex. Initial in initial verification technique only says it comes first in a series. Neither changes the concept, so neither belongs to the term. list · Five things to weigh when identifying a unit · The relationship between determinant and determinatum. Degree of lexicalization — how fixed the combination has become. Classification of concepts — where it sits in the field's structure. Collocation — the company it habitually keeps. Typographic indications — italics, capitals, quotation marks, bold: a field flagging its own terms · card · The practical test

chunks.title: Terminological analysis (cont.)
chunks.text: Ask whether removing the determinant leaves you with a different concept or the same concept less precisely described.Different concept: the determinant is essential and the term is the whole phrase. Same concept: the determinant is a passing description, the term is the base word alone, and taking the phrase into a glossary would put a sentence fragment there for ever. Same adjective, two verdicts · A term · charitable institution · Not a term · charitable man — charitable describes the man; remove it and you still have the same concept, a man · Why the first is one · مؤسسة خيرية — remove charitable and you have institution, a different concept with a different legal standing. This is the distinction that decides what goes on the record. Put charitable man in a termbase and you have recorded a description; the next terminologist will have to take it out, and will wonder what else in the file is not a term. Do this before the next unit · Take a specialised page and mark every noun phrase of two or more words. For each, delete the first element and write what remains.Sort them into two piles: different concept and same concept, vaguer. Only the first pile is terminology. Expect the second pile to be larger than you assumed — that over-collection is the standard beginner's fault, and this exercise is the cure.

chunks.title: Comparative terminology
chunks.text: Comparative terminology · المصطلحية المقارنة · Two terms, two languages, and the question of whether they are really equivalent. lede · Every method so far applies to one language or several. In bilingual and multilingual work there is one further step: compare the source and target terms and decide whether they are equivalent — which they frequently are not, in ways a dictionary will not tell you. card · Full equivalence · Two terms from different languages are fully equivalent when they have the same meaning and are used in the same way in a given subject field.They can be fully equivalent while representing the concept from a different point of view. English black out names the darkness; Arabic انقطاع الكهرباء names the interruption of supply. Different angle on the same concept, same use — fully equivalent. list · Partial equivalence, and its two causes · Language communities form and name concepts out of their own experience, so a source term often covers only part of what its supposed equivalent covers: Discrepancies in meaning. One term is generic and the other specific. Or one has shifted or acquired a new sense while the other has not moved. Discrepancies in usage. Even where two terms cover exactly the same concept, they may differ in register, in geographic area, in age, or in frequency of use. card · What partial equivalence costs you

chunks.title: Comparative terminology (cont.)
chunks.text: When two terms are only partly equivalent, the possibility of using one in exactly the same meaning and situation as the other is limited — and the limit is rarely visible in the sentence you are working on.Which is why the record notes it. A term marked partial, with the discrepancy named, warns the next user. A term filed as an equivalent with no qualification asserts something stronger than the research supports. Different point of view, still fully equivalent · English · black out · What the words say · a going-dark — the term is built on the effect · Arabic · انقطاع الكهرباء — a cutting-off of electricity: the term is built on the cause. Two languages describing one concept from opposite ends, and equivalent all the same, because equivalence is tested on meaning and use in the field — not on whether the two terms are built the same way. Do this before the next unit · Take eight English-Arabic term pairs from a glossary you trust. Judge each: full or partial equivalence.For every partial one, name the cause — generic against specific, a shift in one language, or a difference of register, region, age or frequency. Expect at least three of the eight to be partial and filed as though they were not. That is the normal state of most glossaries.

chunks.title: Terminological records
chunks.text: Terminological records · البطاقة المصطلحية · Where the research lives so that it can be changed. lede · Terminologists work with living language, and that is precisely the problem with vocabularies, glossaries and specialised dictionaries: once published, what they contain is fixed and hard to modify. A record is easy to file, change, update or replace, which is why the record — not the publication — is where terminological data is kept. card · What a record is · An electronic document holding readily accessible information on a term specific to a subject field, on the concept it represents, and on the source in which it was found.Three things, and the third is not optional. A record without its source is an assertion; with it, it is evidence somebody else can check. split · Two formats · Sequential · متتابع · Each field appears in turn, in a predetermined order. Used by some computerized management systems. Condensed · مختصر · The whole record visible at a glance. The better format on paper, where records have to be consulted, filed and stored by hand. list · The eleven fields of a monolingual record · Entry — the term itself · Definition · Source · Date of publication · Volume, issue and page number · Grammatical labels · Usage and semantic labels · Context · Fields — and subfields · Authors and dates · card · Read that list again

chunks.title: Terminological records (cont.)
chunks.text: Four of the eleven fields — source, date, volume/issue/page, authors and dates — exist for one purpose: so that any entry can be traced back and re-checked years later by somebody who was not there.That is the whole difference between a termbase and a list of words somebody was once confident about. The same term, recorded two ways · A list entry · informed consent — موافقة مستنيرة · What it does not say · Which field. Which definition. Who said so, where, and when. Whether the equivalence is full or partial. A record · Entry, definition, the context it was found in, the source with its date and page, the field and subfield, and who entered it when. The first can be produced in a minute and has to be re-researched by whoever inherits it. The second takes an hour and never has to be done again — which is the entire economics of terminology work. Do this before the next unit · Build one complete monolingual record, all eleven fields, for a single term in a field you know.Then hand it to somebody else and ask them to verify the entry from your record alone. If they cannot reach your source and confirm your definition without asking you a question, a field is doing no work — find out which one.

chunks.title: Definitions
chunks.text: Definitions · التعريف المصطلحي · Four rules that are easy to state and are broken constantly. lede · A terminological definition exists to give a clear understanding of a term in a given subject field, and it needs only the essential characteristics of that term as used there. That is narrower than a lexicographic or encyclopedic definition, which lists every meaning across every area of application. list · The four rules · Not obscure. Explaining the unknown with more unknown language fails the purpose. What is obscure to the layman but plain to the specialist is justifiably technical — the test is the intended reader, not simplicity for its own sake. Neither too broad nor too narrow. It must not take in things the term does not apply to, nor leave out things it does. By the old rule of logic it should be able to replace the term in any statement without altering the meaning. Not circular. It may not use the term or any grammatical variant of it. One who studies or specializes in herpetology defines herpetologist circularly, and tells a reader who did not already know precisely nothing. Not negative where it can be affirmative. Say what a term means, not what it does not. Defining chair as not a bed and not a couch explains nothing. card · The exception to the fourth rule

chunks.title: Definitions (cont.)
chunks.text: Some terms are essentially negative in meaning and require a negative definition. Undifferentiated means having no special structure or function. Achromatic means having no colour.A negative definition of a negative term works, because its point of reference is an implied alternative — there is a differentiated state, there is colour. That is not the case for chair. split · Two methods · Genus and difference · الجنس والفصل · Name the larger class the concept belongs to, then the characteristic separating it from everything else in that class. Man as a rational animal: the genus is animal, the difference is rationality. The oldest and best-known method, used in both lexicography and terminology. Partition · التعريف بالتجزئة · Specify a whole by its parts. Used in addition to genus and difference when the object consists of several parts. One definition, four rules applied · The term · letter of credit · A definition that fails · “A credit given by letter.” — circular, obscure, and too broad all at once · Genus and difference · خطاب اعتماد — a bank undertaking (genus) to pay a seller on presentation of specified documents (difference) Test it against rule two: put the definition in place of the term in any sentence and see whether the meaning survives. It does — which is the check that separates a definition from a description. Do this before the next unit

chunks.title: Definitions (cont.)
chunks.text: Write terminological definitions for five terms in one field, by genus and difference.Then audit each against all four rules, in order, and write which rule it broke on the first attempt. Almost everyone breaks the second — too broad — and catching your own is faster once you have named the pattern.

chunks.title: Term formation and standardisation
chunks.text: Term formation and standardisation · توليد المصطلح وتوحيده · Where new terms come from — and it is almost never from nowhere. lede · Term formation is the creation of new designations in special languages. Neologisms that spring from an inventor's mind with no prior history are rare. Terms are made by adding new meaning to existing words, by changing the morphology or grammatical class of what is already there, and by borrowing. card · It varies by field, and the variation is not random. In the biological sciences, where strict rules of nomenclature apply, classical derivation is favoured.In the earth sciences there is a lot of borrowing, because geologists, mineralogists and meteorologists tend to take a substance's term from the language of the place it commonly occurs.In computer science there is almost none, because the field developed almost entirely in English-speaking countries. Knowing which pattern a field follows tells you what its next term will probably look like. list · Three characteristics of modern English term formation. Productive. English has enriched its vocabulary by coining for centuries, in the general lexicon and in special languages alike — and the explosion in telecommunications, computer science, genetics and space exploration has made the need unprecedented.

chunks.title: Term formation and standardisation (cont.)
chunks.text: A preference for composition and metaphor. Compounds and derived forms have been the chief source of new words for a thousand years and are first in numerical importance among new terms. They offer precision and transparency — a user can often read the meaning off the parts. Metaphor and analogy are economical and use suggestion to communicate. A tradition of borrowing. Historically from Latin, Greek, French and German — the languages strongly represented in law, medicine, science and technology — and still from anywhere it makes contact with. card · Where the terminologist comes in · Semantic change — altering the meaning of an established word through analogy, metonymy and the like — is one of the two main ways new terms are formed.The terminologist's contribution is to help ensure new coinages follow the time-honoured patterns of that change. A term formed the way the field's terms have always been formed is guessable, memorable and likely to be adopted. One formed against the pattern has to be learned twice and is often quietly replaced. card · And the rule from unit one still holds · Coining is the last resort, warranted only when every available source has been researched and the evidence shows no term exists for the concept.Standardisation is the other end of the same work: settling which term carries the concept, and recording that decision where the next person will find it. The four work methods close where they started. Transparency, and what it buys · A compound · laughmeter · Why it works

chunks.title: Term formation and standardisation (cont.)
chunks.text: A user who has never met the term can read the concept off its parts — a device that measures laughter · The Arabic problem · مقياس الضحك — transparent in the same way, because the compound was rebuilt rather than transliterated. Had it been borrowed as لافميتر the Arabic reader would have to be told what it means. Composition kept the transparency; borrowing would have spent it. That is the choice term formation is, every time. The last one · Find five terms coined in English in the last twenty years. For each, identify the process: semantic change, composition, derivation, metaphor, or borrowing.Then propose an Arabic term for each, and say which process you used and why. Finally, check whether an Arabic term already exists. Where one does, you have just demonstrated unit one's rule to yourself: identify before you create.

chunks.title: What translation is
chunks.text: What translation is · ما الترجمة؟ Three things decide your strategy before you translate a word. lede · Translation is the interpretation of a source text's meaning and the production of an equivalent meaning in another language. Peter Newmark (1981) puts it as the attempt to replace a written message or statement in one language by the same message or statement in another — so the focus is the transfer of the meaning the author intended. list · Nida's three factors · Eugene Nida (1964) adds that three things besides the meaning itself determine how the process runs: The nature of the message — which is to say the text type. The purpose of the author, and by proxy of the translator. The type of audience. card · Text type decides the strategy · Translation is a text-based activity, and the type of the source text sets the approach before you make a single choice.Religious and legal texts pull translators towards the literal, because the form is part of what is binding. Spoken passages from films, conferences and official meetings pull them towards the communicative, because the effect on the hearer is what has to survive. card · And the audience decides the register · A story for children is translated in simple, polite language. A medical text for experts or researchers is translated in the highly technical register its readers expect and can read.Same skill, opposite surface. Getting this wrong is not a vocabulary failure — it is having failed to ask who is going to read the thing. split · And the distinction to keep straight · Translator · مترجم تحريري

chunks.title: What translation is (cont.)
chunks.text: Written texts. Time to stop, research, revise. Interpreter · مترجم شفوي · Spoken passages, in real time. Both require deep cultural and linguistic understanding, expert knowledge of the subject matter, and the ability to communicate clearly and appropriately. One event, two readerships, two right translations · Arabic (a Kuwaiti news item) استقبل سمو أمير البلاد رئيس مجلس الوزراء صباح اليوم بقصر بيان. For a Kuwaiti readership · Titles, palace and protocol all kept — because in that setting the form is part of the information · For a foreign wire service · The Amir of Kuwait received the Prime Minister at Bayan Palace this morning. Nothing was mistranslated in either. The second drops honorifics an English reader does not parse and would read as flattery — a decision made on audience, which is Nida's third factor doing real work. Unit nine returns to exactly this. Do this before the next unit · Take one Kuwaiti news item and translate it twice: once for KUNA's English service, once for a British paper.List every difference. Then say, for each, which of Nida's three factors caused it. If a difference answers to none of the three, you made it for no reason, and it should come out.

chunks.title: Literal translation
chunks.text: Literal translation · الترجمة الحرفية · It works more often than people admit — and fails in a way you can predict. lede · Literal — also called direct or formal — translation takes existing content in one language and renders it word for word, or sentence by sentence, into the other. It is the simplest type, it is the approach most automated systems use, and it is not automatically wrong. list · When it works · When there is no difference between the two languages in manner of expression and in cultural meaning or association. These four cross intact, because the image exists on both sides: To give the green light — يعطي الضوء الأخضر · To fish in troubled waters — اصطاد في الماء العكر · From a different angle — من زاوية مختلفة · Calm before the storm — الهدوء قبل العاصفة · card · When it fails: structure · Between languages of distant sources like Arabic and English the structures do not line up, and the translator has to modify structure and content to meet the reader's expectations.شمس الدنيا becomes It's sunny: the English has a dummy subject it where the Arabic has الدنيا, and an adjective sunny where the Arabic has the noun شمس. Going the other way, on foot becomes على الأقدام — the English singular has to become an Arabic plural. list · When it fails: idiom and proverb · This is the larger failure, and the one with cultural content. Arabic proverbs rendered word for word into English: أنت أرنب — You are rabbit · اللي فات مات — What passed died · يوم لك ويوم عليك — A day for you, a day against you. زاد الطين بلة — It increased the clay moistness · list

chunks.title: Literal translation (cont.)
chunks.text: And it fails in the other direction too · English idioms rendered word for word into Arabic produce sentences that parse and say nothing: One can't get blood from a stone — الواحد لا يستطيع أن يحصل على الدم من الحجر · Like father, like son — مثل الأب، مثل الابن · Keep it under your hat — اتركها تحت قبعتك · card · Which is why the next unit exists · Each of those eight is a real saying with a real meaning, and not one of those meanings is in the translation. When the two cultures do not share the image, the literal route is closed and you need a method that carries the effect instead. One proverb, literally · Arabic · زاد الطين بلة · Word for word · It increased the clay moistness — every word correct, and no English reader can recover the meaning · The meaning · It made matters worse. / Add salt to injury. The literal version is not a bad translation of the words. It is a good translation of the words and a failed translation of the proverb — which is the distinction this course is about. Do this before the next unit · Collect six Kuwaiti expressions you use daily. Translate each one literally into English, on purpose.Then sort them: which literal versions would an English reader actually understand, and which are nonsense? The ones that survive share an image with English. Write down what that image is — that is the thing literal translation is carrying.

chunks.title: Communicative translation
chunks.text: Communicative translation · الترجمة التواصلية · Translate the effect, not the wording — and know what you are giving up. lede · Communicative translation attempts to produce on its readers an effect as close as possible to that obtained on the readers of the original (Newmark, 1981). It has a target-language bias: it is free and idiomatic, it tries to make the reading easier for a reader who does not anticipate difficulties, and it emphasises the force of the message rather than its literal form. list · The same sayings, communicatively · Every pair in the previous unit has an answer. The translator's job is to find the target language's own saying, not to describe the source one: Let bygones be bygones — اللي فات مات · You win some, you lose some — يوم لك ويوم عليك · Add salt to injury — زاد الطين بلة · One can't get blood from a stone — إنك لا تجني من الشوك العنب. Like father, like son — هذا الشبل من ذاك الأسد. Man proposes and God disposes — أنت تريد، وأنا أريد، والله يفعل ما يريد · It is not my cup of tea — هذه ليست لعبتي · A Jack of all trades is a master of none — سبع صنايع والبخت ضايع. Keep your nose out of other people's business — يا داخل بين البصلة وقشرتها ما بطولك إلا ريحتها · card · It also fixes the wording nobody notices · The standard English for شرطة مكافحة الشغب is riot police — not anti-riot police, not riot combat police, both of which are what the Arabic structure would give you.Most communicative translation is not dramatic. It is knowing what the target language actually says. card · The social formula has no words in it

chunks.title: Communicative translation (cont.)
chunks.text: نعيماً is said to someone who has just had a haircut or a bath. Translated word for word it is a blessing; translated communicatively it is nice haircut.That is the whole move. The Arabic performs a social act and the English names the occasion, because English has no formula for the moment and Arabic has nothing else. card · And the formula that changes meaning every time. إن شاء الله has no single English equivalent, because its translation depends on what it means in the situation.It can be I hope, I promise, or I am not sure. It can be a way of refusing a promise. It can express dislike or antipathy without saying so. A translator who always renders it God willing has translated the words and missed the act every time but one. The same two words, two different acts · A question and its answer · — بتخلص الشغل بكرة؟‎ — إن شاء الله. Always the same rendering · God willing — which tells an English reader nothing about whether the work will be done · What each one is doing · As a promise: Yes, it'll be ready tomorrow. · As a soft refusal: We'll see. · As genuine uncertainty: I hope so. A Kuwaiti hearer reads which of these is meant from tone, situation and who is speaking. The English reader has none of that, so the translator has to choose — and choosing is not taking a liberty here, it is the only way to be accurate. Do this before the next unit

chunks.title: Communicative translation (cont.)
chunks.text: Two parts.One. Listen for إن شاء الله five times in one day and write down, each time, which act it was performing and the English you would use. You should end with five different renderings.Two. Take the nine pairs above and test them. For each, ask: does the Arabic saying do the same job as the English one, or only sound like it? Proverb pairs circulate widely and some of them do not survive the question. Finding the one that does not is worth more to you than memorising the other eight.

chunks.title: Machine translation
chunks.text: Machine translation · الترجمة الآلية · Mechanical substitution, and exactly where it breaks. lede · Machine translation is a sub-field of computational linguistics investigating the use of software to translate text or speech from one language to another. At a basic level it performs mechanical substitution of words in one language for words in another — and that alone rarely produces a good translation, because what is needed is recognition of whole phrases and their closest counterparts in the target language. card · Arabic into English: two phrases missed at once. A woman describes a problem she took to her mother-in-law. She says she نشرت غسيلها أمام الناس, and that وافق شنٌّ طبقة.The machine gives I spread my laundry in front of people and he agreed to launch a class. The first is a correct rendering of a unit it did not see. The second is not even that — it has read a proverb about two well-matched people as a sentence about launching something. A translator gives I let the cat out of the bag and every Jack has his Jill. card · English into Arabic: a name read as a country. BBC sport news indicated that Jordan's trainers will be sold for a record $560,000.The machine returns الحذاء الرياضي الأردني — the Jordanian trainer. It has taken Jordan for the country. Nothing in the sentence is mistranslated word by word; the whole thing is about the wrong subject. card · Where it is genuinely useful

chunks.title: Machine translation (cont.)
chunks.text: As a draft, and for getting the gist of a document you would otherwise not read at all.What it cannot do is know the subject or read the culture. Which means someone has to be able to tell when the output is wrong — and that takes more knowledge than producing the translation yourself, not less. card · A Gulf case it will always fail · Machine systems are trained overwhelmingly on Modern Standard Arabic and on Levantine and Egyptian usage. Kuwaiti and Gulf vocabulary is thinly represented, and culture-specific items barely at all.Feed one القرقيعان or الديرة and you will get a transliteration or a guess — الديرة flattened to the country when it means one's own town. Neither tells a foreign reader what happened. One sentence, by machine and by hand · English (BBC sport) Jordan's trainers will be sold for a record $560,000. Machine · سيتم بيع الحذاء الرياضي الأردني بمبلغ قياسي قدره ٥٦٠ ألف دولار — the Jordanian trainer, a shoe belonging to a country · Human (communicative) أشارت تقارير رياضية في قناة البي بي سي الإخبارية إلى بيع حذاء أسطورة كرة السلة الأمريكية مايكل جوردن برقم قياسي بلغ ٥٦٠٬٠٠٠ دولار أمريكي. Two things the human did. It resolved Jordan to Michael Jordan — which required knowing who he is, not knowing English. And it added أسطورة كرة السلة الأمريكية, because an Arabic reader may not recognise the name unglossed. That second move is explicitation, and unit six is about it. Do this before the next unit

chunks.title: Machine translation (cont.)
chunks.text: Put five Kuwaiti sentences through a machine translator — ones with local vocabulary and at least one proper name, not standard news prose.Mark every error and label it: wrong word, missed phrase, or missing culture. You will find the third is most of them, and it is the one no amount of better software has yet fixed.

chunks.title: Cohesion and coherence
chunks.text: Cohesion and coherence · السبك والحبك · Arabic joins its sentences aloud. English joins them silently. lede · A stylistic difference that runs through every text in this language pair: English prefers coherence — implicit connectedness — while Arabic prefers cohesion — connectedness made explicit with conjunctions and coordinators. card · What that means at the desk · Translating into English, you do not have to use conjunctions as frequently as Arabic does. Keep them all and the English reads like a chain of clauses with no shape.Translating into Arabic, you may need them more frequently than the English has them. Leave them out and the Arabic reads as a series of disconnected statements — grammatical, and somehow not joined up. card · English splitting where Arabic joins · All requests for leave without pay must be in writing. They must be submitted to the human resources office.Two English sentences, no connector, and the relation is left for the reader to see. The Arabic joins them: تُحرَّر كل الطلبات الخاصة بالإجازة بدون أجر كتابةً، كما يجب تقديمها إلى مكتب الموارد البشرية — and would read oddly without the كما. card · And the reverse · An Arabic paragraph built on و after و, with وحيث and ولهذا marking each turn, becomes in English four sentences with the connectors removed and the logic carried by the sequence itself.Nothing is lost. The connection has moved from the words to the arrangement, which is where English keeps it. One event, two ways of joining it up · Arabic

chunks.title: Cohesion and coherence (cont.)
chunks.text: لقد تعرّض معلّم الرياضيات لحادث هذا الصباح، وحيث نُقل على إثره إلى المستشفى، ولهذا لن يقوم بإعطاء محاضرات لهذا اليوم، وحيث سنعود للبيت باكراً اليوم. Every connector kept · The maths teacher had an accident this morning, and he was sent to hospital, and he is not going to give us lectures today, and we will go home early. — childish in English, and the original is not · English coherence · The Math teacher had an accident this morning. He has been sent to hospital. He is not going to give us lectures for today. We will go home early today. Four sentences, four full stops, and every و gone. The cause, the consequence and the sequence are all still there — carried by the order of the sentences instead of by words. That is what implicit connectedness means in practice. Do this before the next unit · Take an Arabic paragraph and count its coordinators. Translate it into English and count them again.The second number should be much lower. Then read your English aloud: if it still sounds like a list, you moved the words and kept the Arabic joinery. Then do it in reverse — take an English paragraph of short sentences and see how many connectors the Arabic wants back.

chunks.title: Explicitation
chunks.text: Explicitation · التصريح والشرح الثقافي · Saying out loud what the source left for readers who already knew. lede · Where source and target readers do not share a cultural presupposition, the translator uses explicitation — also called cultural explanation, substitution, functional equivalence or paraphrase. It is the explanation of the source-text terms and realities: making what is implicit in the source explicit in the target, to keep the target text appropriate and accessible. card · The simplest form: say what the thing is · The Beatles becomes الفرقة الموسيقية البريطانية ذا بيتلز. A Farewell to Arms becomes الرواية الأمريكية المشهورة وداعاً للسلاح.Four words added in each case, and the ambiguity is gone. The Arabic reader now knows that one is a band and the other is a novel — which the English reader knew without being told. card · In literature: the footnote · In Kanafani's Men in the Sun a passage turns on the name Hatim. Kilpatrick's translation keeps the name and adds a note: Hatim, of the bedouin tribe of Tayy, is proverbial among the Arabs for his limitless generosity and hospitality.Without it the sentence still parses and the point vanishes. The reader has no idea why this name settles anything. card · In fiction: the gloss inside the sentence

chunks.title: Explicitation (cont.)
chunks.text: A Mahfouz narrator fears that anyone overhearing his wife complain would take him for ريا أو سكينة.The English reads: would have thought I was a cold-blooded killer like those dreadful women in Alexandria in Egypt: Rayya and Sakina. Everything after killer is the translator's. It is inside the sentence because a novel's reader will not stop for a footnote. list · In news: the headline that has to be unpacked. A local headline assumes the reader's whole context. A foreign one has none of it: الأردنيون في مواجهة مع الحكومة لإلغاء وادي عربة → Jordanians urge their government to scrap Wadi Araba's peace treaty with Israel — the reader is told what Wadi Araba is. دجاج عمرو خالد يثير الجدل وعلماء الأزهر يطالبونه بالتوبة والاعتذار → The Egyptian Muslim activist and television preacher, Amr Khaled, is in hot water over a chicken advertisement. The scholars of the famous Egyptian Islamic university Al-Azhar are urging him to apologize and repent. — the person and the institution both named. صباح الجزائري تنتقد باب الحارة وتتبرأ منه → The famous Syrian actress and star of the Syrian Ramadan TV series Bab Al-Harah, Sabah Al-Jazairi, criticized and disowned the TV series. — where the machine gave only the bare names, which name nobody. card · The cost, and the limit

chunks.title: Explicitation (cont.)
chunks.text: Explicitations are traces of the translator's attempt to interpret the original and make it easier to process and more cohesive for the target reader (Blum-Kulka, 2000). They ease comprehensibility and readability — and they make the translation longer, flatter and more explanatory than the original ever was.Explain a joke and it is no longer a joke. The judgement is how much the reader needs in order to get what the source reader got — and then stopping. A Kuwaiti reference that means nothing abroad · Arabic · اجتمعوا في الديوانية ليلة القرقيعان. Kept as it stands · They gathered in the diwaniyya on Gergean night — two loan words, and a reader who now knows neither what the room is nor what the night is · With explicitation · They gathered at the diwaniyya, the household's regular evening reception room, on the night of Gergean — the mid-Ramadan celebration when children go from house to house collecting sweets. Twice the length, and the only version that works. Note what was not done: neither term was replaced with a Western near-equivalent. Halloween would be shorter, familiar, and wrong about the occasion, the month and the meaning. Do this before the next unit · Find a Kuwaiti news item containing at least three references a foreign reader would not have — a place, an institution, an occasion.Translate it twice: once with footnotes, once with everything glossed in the text. Compare the lengths and decide which you would publish and for whom. Then mark the one reference you would leave unexplained, and say why the reader can live without it.

chunks.title: Collocations and idioms
chunks.text: Collocations and idioms · المتلازمات والتعابير · Both languages are clear, both are correct, and only one of them is what people say. lede · A collocation is two or more words that often go together. Collocations and idioms are culturally bound — they do not apply across languages. When words collocate they may give a meaning that is different or unnatural in the target language, which is why literal translation produces unnatural pairings and communicative translation is needed. split · Natural and unnatural English · Natural · المألوف · the fast train · fast food · a quick shower · a quick meal · Unnatural · غير المألوف · the quick train · quick food · a fast shower · a fast meal · card · Nothing in the meanings explains it · Fast and quick are near-synonyms, and each takes its own company. You catch a bus; you cannot hold one.Arabic does the same. Break the law rendered literally is يكسر القانون — grammatical, and not Arabic. The natural collocation is يخالف القانون. There is no rule to derive; the obligation is to know what the target language says, which is why the target language should be the one you know best. card · Idioms mean what their words do not · He is a black sheep rendered literally is إنه خاروف أسود, which makes no sense in Arabic. Communicatively it is إنه سيّئ الأخلاق.An idiom should be translated communicatively whenever the literal meaning does not make sense on the other side. list · English into Arabic · to break the ice — يمهّد الطريق · he looks blue — يبدو حزيناً · he is in the clouds — هو شارد الذهن · strong tea — شاي ثقيل

chunks.title: Collocations and idioms (cont.)
chunks.text: to carry coals to Newcastle — يبيع مياه في حارة السقّايين · to kick the bucket — لقي حتفه / مات · when pigs fly — لما ينوّر الصوان · to sweat like a pig — يتصبّب عرقاً · list · Arabic into English · ابتسامة مصطنعة — a forced smile · دم ولحم — flesh and blood · ليل ونهار — day and night · واضح زي الشمس — clear as crystal · مدخّن شره — a heavy smoker · دليل دامغ — a smoking gun · ما بسوى بصلة — not worth a damn · ابن حلال — a good sort · ابن كار — made for the job · ابن سوق — a born businessman. يا خبر أسود — Bloody hell! · يختي عليها — How cute! · يا خيبتك — What a dead loss you are! card · Notice the last row · Those three are not hard because the meaning is obscure. They are hard because the difficulty is tone: how rude, how affectionate, how mocking, and whether an English reader would take the speaker for a friend or an enemy.A dictionary will not settle it. Only knowing both registers will. card · Replacing an idiom with a different one entirely. In Men in the Sun, Kilpatrick renders ليكسر الفخار بعضه with a verse from the Bible — Let the dead bury their dead — because it carries the same meaning for an English reader.That is a real choice with a real cost: the target reader now hears a scriptural register the Arabic did not have. Sometimes that is the best available trade. It should be a decision, not an accident. card · A whole text of them at once

chunks.title: Collocations and idioms (cont.)
chunks.text: An English news paragraph on the George Floyd case runs a political hot potato, a stitch in time saves nine and live and learn in three consecutive sentences.The machine gives غرزة في الوقت المناسب تنقذ تسعة — a sentence about sewing. The communicative version replaces it with the Arabic proverb that does the job: درهم وقاية خير من قنطار علاج. Same argument, different image, and an Arabic reader who does not stumble. A Gulf collocation with no English partner · Arabic · الحمد لله على السلامة · Word for word · Praise be to God for the safety — pious, odd, and not what is being done · What the act is · Said to someone back from travel or out of hospital: Welcome back · Glad you're back safely · Thank God you're all right. English has no fixed formula for this moment, so there is no counterpart to find — only a choice about which part to keep: the welcome, the relief, or the thanks. Whichever you pick, something in the Arabic is not going with it. This is the same problem as نعيماً in unit three. Do this before the next unit · List ten Kuwaiti social formulae — for a new purchase, a haircut, a safe return, a death, an exam result, a new baby.For each, ask whether English has a fixed phrase for that moment. Where it does, use it. Where it does not, write what you would say instead and what the Arabic loses. Expect more than half to have no English formula at all — that gap is the subject of this whole course.

chunks.title: Cultural associations
chunks.text: Cultural associations · الإيحاءات الثقافية · The word is right. What it makes the reader feel is wrong. lede · Language and culture are part and parcel of each other and cannot be separated. Language marks cultural identity — language is culture — so translating a language implies translating a culture. And culture is a fuzzy set of attitudes, behavioural conventions, assumptions and values shared by a set of people, which means connotation does not travel with denotation. card · The same animal, opposite meanings · ذيب — the wolf — has a positive association in Arab culture and a negative one in English. A good communicative translation is brave or strong, not wolf.The owl runs the other way. As wise as an owl becomes ذكي or حكيم, never حكيم كالبومة, because the owl carries a negative association in Arabic that does not exist in English. Both times: every word correct, and the sentence meaning the opposite of what it meant. list · Where this bites hardest · Loaded history. Crusade campaigns is neutral or admiring in English usage. Rendered as حملات صليبية it imports a charge the English never had, so translators use حملات غربية instead. Behaviour ordinary in one culture and not the other. Let's grab a beer after work becomes لنخرج بعد العمل — the alcohol removed, or substituted with coffee or juice. The act survives; the detail that does not belong is dropped.

chunks.title: Cultural associations (cont.)
chunks.text: Political vocabulary. Kilpatrick renders Kanafani's المجاهدين as the Freedom Fighters, and مجاهدو الطيرة as the commandos in Al-Tira — precisely to avoid conveying to an English audience the negative feelings the obvious English word would import. Identity terms. A word naming a people, a faith or an origin can be neutral on one side and a charge on the other, in either direction. This is the case that most needs naming rather than carrying across: the translator's job is to render what was meant, not to deliver a charge the reader will feel and the author never sent. card · What you are actually deciding · Whether to protect the reader's response or the source's wording. Both are defensible; only one can be had.What is not defensible is not noticing — carrying a word across and leaving the reader to receive a charge the author never sent. A compliment that arrives as an accusation · Arabic (Gulf) فلان جِمَل · Literally · He is a camel — in English an insult, or at best a joke · What it says in the Gulf · He has enormous endurance — he carries what others cannot. The camel is the Gulf's emblem of patience and endurance, and the comparison is praise. English animal vocabulary carries no such association, so the image has to be dropped and the quality named — exactly the move the course makes with ذيب, and the reverse of the one it makes with the owl. Do this before the next unit

chunks.title: Cultural associations (cont.)
chunks.text: Take five animals and five colours. For each, write what it connotes in Kuwait and what it connotes in English.Mark every pair that disagrees. Then find one real sentence containing one of them and translate it — and say in a line whether you kept the image or the effect, and why that was the right trade in that text.

chunks.title: Politeness and address
chunks.text: Politeness and address · المجاملة وألقاب المخاطبة · What is polite in one language is strange, cold or rude in the other. lede · Communicative translation may involve altering discourse markers, address terms or titles, because translation involves a shift in the audience. What is polite in Arabic may be impolite in English and the reverse, so the translator makes the modifications the target culture's politeness standards require. card · English into Arabic: what comes out · Vulgar and taboo expressions are routinely deleted, because Arabic culture values politeness far more than faithfulness and accuracy.A line from Wuthering Heights — he cursed and defied: execrated God and man, and gave himself up to reckless dissipation — comes into Arabic as صبّ سخطه على الحياة والناس. You may think that is wrong. It is what the target culture's norms produce, and knowing it is the difference between choosing and drifting. list · Arabic into English: what comes out · Arabic politeness expressions and address terms that are not familiar in English are dropped, to keep the target text appropriate for its audience: قال أبو قيس: الأخ أسعد يحكي الحق → Abu Qais remarked: “Assad's quite right.” — الأخ gone. ما رأي عم الحاج رضا أن يصعد إلى سيارتي؟ → “How would Haj Rida like to get into my lorry?” — عم gone, الحاج kept because it identifies him.

chunks.title: Politeness and address (cont.)
chunks.text: بحث جلالة الملك عبد الله الثاني حفظه الله ورعاه مع أخيه فخامة الرئيس المصري… → King Abdullah of Jordan discussed with the Egyptian President El-Sisi… — four honorifics and the word brother all gone, and the sentence has lost nothing an English reader needed. card · A Gulf case English cannot do at all · Teknonymy — addressing someone as أبو أحمد or أم أحمد, father or mother of their eldest son.It is warm, respectful and slightly formal all at once, and it is the ordinary way adults address each other. English has no equivalent register. Abu Ahmad means nothing to the reader; Mr Al-Otaibi is correct and colder; the first name is accurate and loses the respect. There is no right answer, only a choice and a reason. Court protocol for a foreign wire · Arabic (a Kuwaiti news item) استقبل حضرة صاحب السمو أمير البلاد الشيخ نواف الأحمد الجابر الصباح حفظه الله ورعاه بقصر السيف العامر صباح اليوم سمو الشيخ صباح خالد الحمد الصباح حفظه الله ورعاه. Every honorific carried over · His Highness the Possessor of Highness the Amir of the Country Sheikh… may God preserve and protect him… received His Highness Sheikh… — accurate, and unreadable · As the BBC published it · The Amir Nawaf of Kuwait received this morning the Prime Minister Sabah Al-Sabah at the Kuwaiti ruling palace.

chunks.title: Politeness and address (cont.)
chunks.text: Count what went: حضرة صاحب السمو, both instances of حفظه الله ورعاه, most of each name, and the epithet on the palace. What stayed is the office, the name and the fact. A Kuwaiti outlet publishing in English may keep His Highness deliberately — that is an editorial decision about who the paper speaks for, not a translation error. Do this before the next unit · Take one Amiri Diwan statement in Arabic and translate it for three readerships: KUNA English, a British paper, and a Kuwaiti English-language paper.The three will differ mainly in how much honorific survives. Write one line for each explaining who the reader is and what that reader needs — which is the whole of this unit.

chunks.title: Ideology in translation
chunks.text: Ideology in translation · الأيديولوجيا في الترجمة · Six places where beliefs, not language, decide what the translation says. lede · Translating between English and Arabic involves not only linguistic and cultural considerations but ideological ones. Ideology in translation is the influence of beliefs, values, politics and worldview on how a text is interpreted and represented in another language — and it shapes how translators handle power, religion, gender, colonialism and identity, whether or not anyone intends it. list · Six kinds · Religious. Jesus is the son of God renders literally as يسوع هو ابن الله, which contradicts Islamic doctrine, where Jesus is a prophet and not divine. A translation for an Islamic context typically reframes or footnotes it: يسوع، الذي يُعتقد في المسيحية أنه ابن الله. Gender. A woman can lead a nation — يمكن للمرأة أن تقود أمة — may be ideologically sensitive in conservative contexts, and be rephrased cautiously or avoided in certain media. Colonial and postcolonial. The British brought civilization to the East — جلب البريطانيون الحضارة إلى الشرق — implies cultural inferiority to an Arab readership. A translator may challenge it: ادّعى البريطانيون أنهم جلبوا الحضارة إلى الشرق — claimed, which is a real intervention in the text. Political. Freedom of speech is a universal right is neutral in English and sensitive where speech is regulated. It may be framed more cautiously: حرية التعبير مكفولة في حدود القانون.

chunks.title: Ideology in translation (cont.)
chunks.text: Media framing. One event, two outlets: قُتل ثلاثة فلسطينيين في اشتباكات مع القوات الإسرائيلية against قامت قوات الاحتلال الإسرائيلي بقتل ثلاثة متظاهرين فلسطينيين. Same report. The framing alone changes the tone and the implication. Secular against religious. Darwin's theory of evolution challenges the creationist view may be softened and framed with caution: نظرية داروين في التطور تُعد مثار جدل بالنسبة للرؤية الدينية للخلق. card · Why this is on a translation syllabus · Because every choice above is made with grammar: active or passive, who is named as agent, which verb, what gets a qualifier, what gets a reporting frame like claimed or faced accusations.That is your equipment. Ideology is not a topic beside translation technique; it is what technique does when the subject is contested. One event, and where the ideology sits · English news · Israeli forces killed three Palestinian protesters. One outlet · قُتل ثلاثة فلسطينيين في اشتباكات مع القوات الإسرائيلية — no agent, and clashes makes it mutual · The other · قامت قوات الاحتلال الإسرائيلي بقتل ثلاثة متظاهرين فلسطينيين. Neither version contains a false word. The difference is voice, naming and the choice of noun for the parties — three ordinary grammatical choices doing the entire political work of the sentence. This is why a translator cannot become neutral by translating carefully; the careful choices are the political ones. Do this before the next unit

chunks.title: Ideology in translation (cont.)
chunks.text: Find one story reported by two outlets with opposing positions, in English and in Arabic.Compare them on four points only: active or passive, who is named as agent, the verb chosen for the action, and what each calls the parties. Write the four differences down. You have just done ideological analysis with nothing but grammar.

chunks.title: Self-censorship
chunks.text: Self-censorship · الرقابة الذاتية · The changes nobody asked for — and the hardest thing to see in your own work. lede · Ideological self-censorship is when translators deliberately alter, omit or soften content to align with the politics, religion or culture of the target audience — often without being explicitly instructed to do so. It is internalised censorship: the translator anticipates what might be considered inappropriate or controversial and adapts pre-emptively. list · Four documented patterns · Theology. God is just a concept created by man becomes لله مفاهيم متعددة تختلف من شخص لآخر — there are multiple concepts of God that vary from person to person. The claim has been replaced by a survey of opinion, to avoid blasphemy or offence. Gender. A woman doesn't need a man to be complete becomes المرأة كيان مستقل يمكنه الاعتماد على ذاته في بعض الأمور — in certain matters. The qualifier is doing all the work, and the empowerment is toned down. Politics. The regime was corrupt and brutally suppressed opposition becomes واجه النظام اتهامات تتعلق بالفساد وتعامله مع المعارضة — statement turned into allegation, often out of real fear of surveillance, professional repercussions or legal trouble. Social norms. She poured a glass of wine and lit a cigarette becomes سكبت لنفسها شراباً وجلست بهدوء. Two culturally disapproved acts removed from a sentence that was characterising someone. card · Notice what these have in common

chunks.title: Self-censorship (cont.)
chunks.text: Every one is fluent, plausible and defensible in isolation. None reads as censorship. That is exactly what makes it hard to catch in your own work — you do not experience it as changing the text, you experience it as finding the natural phrasing.And the fourth example shows the cost most clearly: the wine and the cigarette were characterisation. Remove them and a specific woman becomes a generic one. card · This is not an instruction to translate provocatively. Real constraints exist. Publishers have policies, countries have laws, and some adaptations are the condition of the book appearing at all.The professional standard is not never soften. It is know that you did, be able to say which constraint you were answering, and tell whoever commissioned the work. A softening you can name is an editorial decision. A softening you cannot see is a loss of control over your own translation. card · Where this course ends · Every unit here has been one version of a single question: what did you change, and can you say why?Literal against communicative, explicitation, the wolf and the owl, the honorifics, the passive voice, the wine. None of them has a rule that decides it. All of them have an answer you should be able to give out loud — and that answer is what a commentary is, and what the rest of the minor will ask you for. A softening you could defend, and the line to put in the file · English source · She poured a glass of wine and lit a cigarette. Self-censored · سكبت لنفسها شراباً وجلست بهدوء — fluent, publishable, and a different woman · The honest options

chunks.title: Self-censorship (cont.)
chunks.text: Translate it as written, or soften it and record the change: “Alcohol and smoking neutralised for the target market; characterisation affected.” The second option is not a worse translation than the first. It is the same translation with the decision made visible — which is the only thing that separates a professional adaptation from an invisible one. The last one · Take a page you have already translated and read it against the source hunting only for softenings — a qualifier added, an accusation turned into a report, a detail quietly gone.For each, write one line: what you changed, and which constraint you were answering. If you cannot name a constraint, you did not adapt it — you flinched, and the text is now saying something you never decided to say.

Scripture · c. 400 · Why Michelangelo's Moses has horns · Translating the Hebrew Bible into Latin, Jerome met qaran in Exodus 34, where Moses comes down from Sinai. The root can mean to shine or horn. The Vulgate reads cornuta, horned — and for a thousand years European art gave Moses horns, Michelangelo's statue in Rome included. קָרַן · qaran (shone / sent out rays) cornuta · horned · One word with two senses, and the translator picked one. Whether Jerome misread or meant it figuratively is still argued; what is not argued is that the choice outlived him by a millennium. Form against meaning, at its most visible. Horns of Moses · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horns_of_Moses · Diplomacy · 1956 · “We will bury you” Khrushchev told Western ambassadors in Moscow Мы вас похороним. Rendered word for word, We will bury you ran on front pages as a threat. In context it was a Marxist commonplace: communism will outlive capitalism and be there at its funeral. Мы вас похороним · We will bury you · meant: we will outlast you. Every word was correct. The meaning was not. This is the course's central distinction — between what a sentence says and what it is used to say — with a Cold War attached. We will bury you · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_will_bury_you · Language Log · https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=61527 · Myth · 1963 · Kennedy was not a jelly doughnut · Kennedy's Ich bin ein Berliner is often said to mean I am a doughnut, because a Berliner is also a pastry. Germans in the crowd understood him perfectly: the article ein is correct for a figurative claim of belonging.

chunks.text: Included as a warning. Half the famous “translation blunders” online are invented. Before you quote one, find where it was reported — which is why every case on this page links to its source. Health · 2022 · Monkeypox becomes mpox · On 28 November 2022 the World Health Organization made mpox the preferred term, phasing out monkeypox over a year. The concept did not change; the term did, because the old one was feeding stigma and keeping people from testing. A term is a decision made by someone with authority, recorded with a date. Your termbase entry for this concept now needs both forms, which one is current, and since when. WHO news release · https://www.who.int/news/item/28-11-2022-who-recommends-new-name-for-monkeypox-disease · Science · 2006 · Pluto loses a definition · Nothing about Pluto changed in 2006. The International Astronomical Union wrote, for the first time, a definition of planet — and Pluto no longer met it. A new term, dwarf planet, was created for what was left over. Terminology starts from the concept. Change the definition and the term's coverage changes with it. Every language's term for planet had to follow. IAU definition of planet · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAU_definition_of_planet · Engineering · 1999 · Mars Climate Orbiter · One team's software reported thrust in pound-force seconds; NASA's navigation software expected newton-seconds. Nobody converted. The $125 million spacecraft entered Mars's atmosphere too low and was lost. Two teams, one word, two concepts underneath it — and no shared record saying which one. This is exactly what a termbase and an agreed standard exist to prevent.
