chunks.title: احتفلت الجمعية الثقافية مساءَ أمس بتكريم نخبةٍ من المترجمين الشباب، وذلك في أمسيةٍ حضرها لفيفٌ من الأدباء والأكاديميين. وأكّد رئيس الجمعية في كلمته أنّ الترجمة جسرٌ يصل الشعوب بعضها ببعض، مشيراً إلى أنّ العناية بالمترجمين الشباب واجبٌ لا ترف. واختُتمت الأمسية بقراءاتٍ شعريةٍ مترجمة، وسط أجواءٍ سادها الودّ والتقدير.
chunks.text: Cultural news · احتفلت الجمعية الثقافية مساءَ أمس بتكريم نخبةٍ من المترجمين الشباب، وذلك في أمسيةٍ حضرها لفيفٌ من الأدباء والأكاديميين. وأكّد رئيس الجمعية في كلمته أنّ الترجمة جسرٌ يصل الشعوب بعضها ببعض، مشيراً إلى أنّ العناية بالمترجمين الشباب واجبٌ لا ترف. واختُتمت الأمسية بقراءاتٍ شعريةٍ مترجمة، وسط أجواءٍ سادها الودّ والتقدير. Practice text written for the handbook. A possible opening: Last night, the Cultural Society honoured a group of outstanding young translators at an event attended by writers and academics. Split the long Arabic sentence, keep the image of translation as a bridge, and render الودّ والتقدير as a warm, appreciative atmosphere.

chunks.title: computer → كمبيوتر
chunks.text: computer → كمبيوتر · The foreign word enters the language as it is. Formal Arabic also has حاسوب. Section 4.2 · Answer: Borrowing · الاقتراض (the word crossed over whole)

chunks.title: skyscraper → ناطحة سحاب
chunks.text: skyscraper → ناطحة سحاب · The parts were translated and reassembled — a calque. Section 4.2 · Answer: Calque · النسخ (each part translated: sky + scraper)

chunks.title: the White House → البيت الأبيض
chunks.text: the White House → البيت الأبيض · Each part translated literally; the result is the established name. Section 4.2 · Answer: Calque · النسخ (translated part by part, and now established)

chunks.title: after his return → بعد أن عاد
chunks.text: after his return → بعد أن عاد · The noun return becomes the verb عاد: same idea, different part of speech. Section 4.2 · Answer: Transposition · الإبدال (a noun became a verb)

chunks.title: It is not difficult. → إنّه سهل.
chunks.text: It is not difficult. → إنّه سهل. Saying the same thing from the other side — modulation. Section 4.2 · Answer: Modulation · التطويع (negative turned positive: a new viewpoint)

chunks.title: You can’t miss it. → ستجده بسهولة.
chunks.text: You can’t miss it. → ستجده بسهولة. The literal version sounds foreign, so the viewpoint changes: “you will find it easily”. Section 4.2 · Answer: Modulation · التطويع (the same fact from another angle)

chunks.title: Once upon a time → كان يا ما كان
chunks.text: Once upon a time → كان يا ما كان · Both are set story openers doing the same job — equivalence. Section 4.2 · Answer: Equivalence · التكافؤ (one fixed formula replaces another)

chunks.title: a drop in the ocean → غيضٌ من فيض
chunks.text: a drop in the ocean → غيضٌ من فيض · An idiom with the same meaning but a different image (Husni & Newman, 2015, p. 33). Section 4.2 · Answer: Equivalence · التكافؤ (a different fixed expression, same function)

chunks.title: They are like Romeo and Juliet. → هما كقيس وليلى.
chunks.text: They are like Romeo and Juliet. → هما كقيس وليلى. A famous pair of lovers from one culture replaced by one from the other — adaptation. Section 4.2 · Answer: Adaptation · التكييف (the cultural reference was replaced)

chunks.title: الجبر → algebra
chunks.text: الجبر → algebra · Borrowing runs both ways; English is full of Arabic loans. Section 4.2 · Answer: Borrowing · الاقتراض (the Arabic word crossed into English)

chunks.title: للّه دَرُّه!
chunks.text: للّه دَرُّه! An inexperienced translator may render للّه درّه “by a mock-exoticism like ‘his milk is due to God/Allah’, rather than as ‘how wonderful so-and-so is!’” — Husni & Newman (2015), p. 1. Recognise the fixed expression first; then translate what it does. Start Here · Answer: How wonderful he is! (the meaning: an exclamation of praise)

chunks.title: فقدَ اللاعبُ أعصابَه بعد الهدف الثاني.
chunks.text: فقدَ اللاعبُ أعصابَه بعد الهدف الثاني. A classic false friend: فقد أعصابه means to become angry, while English to lose one’s nerve means to lose one’s courage. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 29. Section 3.2 · Answer: The player lost his temper after the second goal. (the Arabic meaning)

chunks.title: فعلتُ ذلك من أجل عينيك.
chunks.text: فعلتُ ذلك من أجل عينيك. English for your eyes only marks a confidential document; Arabic من أجل عينيك means “for your sake”. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 29. Section 3.2 · Answer: I did it for your sake. (the Arabic meaning)

chunks.title: دخل القاعة ساحباً ذيلَه.
chunks.text: دخل القاعة ساحباً ذيلَه. سحب ذيله looks like the English with one’s tail between one’s legs, but the Arabic means “to strut” — the opposite of shame. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 31. Section 3.2 · Answer: He strutted into the hall. (the Arabic meaning)

chunks.title: عضَّ أناملَه حين سمع الخبر.
chunks.text: عضَّ أناملَه حين سمع الخبر. In Arabic you bite your fingertips (عضّ أنامله) in anger; an English speaker bites their nails out of anxiety, as in “a nail-biting wait”. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 31. Section 3.2 · Answer: He was seething with anger when he heard the news. (the Arabic meaning)

chunks.title: أثلجَ الخبرُ صدري.
chunks.text: أثلجَ الخبرُ صدري. What is heart-warming in English “cools the breast” in Arabic, أثلج الصدر, a language rooted in desert heat. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 28. Section 6.1 · Answer: The news warmed my heart. (the English image for the same feeling)

chunks.title: يعيش عيشةً باردة.
chunks.text: يعيش عيشةً باردة. Coolness means comfort in Arabic, so the easy life is a “cold life”, عيش بارد. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 28. Section 3.2 · Answer: He lives an easy, comfortable life. (the Arabic meaning)

chunks.title: لكلِّ جوادٍ كبوة.
chunks.text: لكلِّ جوادٍ كبوة. “Every steed can stumble” is said to excuse a mistake: don’t be too harsh, nobody’s perfect. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 37. Section 3.2 · Answer: Nobody’s perfect. (the same advice)

chunks.title: ماذا تقولين يا أمّي؟ — said by an annoyed thirteen-year-old
chunks.text: ماذا تقولين يا أمّي؟ — said by an annoyed thirteen-year-old · Which English line fits the speaker? Arabic novels often give dialogue in formal Arabic; the English must still sound like the character. Husni and Newman suggest What’re you saying, Mum?, or for an annoyed boy What’re you on about, Mum? (Husni & Newman (2015), p. 77). Section 5.2 · Answer: What’re you on about, Mum? (the speaker’s voice)

chunks.title: فاتَها القطار.
chunks.text: فاتَها القطار. said of a woman who did not marry · فاته القطار is the Arabic counterpart of that ship has sailed, but it collocates mostly with marriage. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 31–32. Section 3.2 · Answer: She missed her chance to marry. (the sense this idiom usually carries)

chunks.title: شدَّ حزامَه استعداداً للرحلة.
chunks.text: شدَّ حزامَه استعداداً للرحلة. شدّ حزامه can mean to tighten one’s belt (live frugally), but it also means “to prepare oneself” — and here the context (استعداداً) decides. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 31. Section 3.2 · Answer: He got himself ready for the journey. (the sense the context gives)

chunks.title: جاء بخُفّي حُنين.
chunks.text: جاء بخُفّي حُنين. Hunayn’s shoes stand for coming back with nothing after a failed attempt. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 29. Section 3.2 · Answer: He came back empty-handed. (the meaning)

chunks.title: كالمستجير من الرمضاء بالنار.
chunks.text: كالمستجير من الرمضاء بالنار. Both say the escape was worse than the danger. The book lists the Standard Arabic form and dialect versions, such as the Levantine and Gulf من تحت الدلف لتحت المزراب. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 32. Section 3.2 · Answer: Out of the frying pan into the fire. (same meaning: escaping into worse trouble)

chunks.title: عصفورٌ في اليد خيرٌ من عشرةٍ على الشجرة.
chunks.text: عصفورٌ في اليد خيرٌ من عشرةٍ على الشجرة. An equivalent proverb with similar form and meaning — only the numbers differ (ten on the tree, two in the bush). Husni & Newman (2015), p. 38. Section 3.2 · Answer: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. (same meaning)

chunks.title: إذا كثُرَ الربابنةُ غرقت السفينة.
chunks.text: إذا كثُرَ الربابنةُ غرقت السفينة. “If there are too many captains, the ship will sink” — a proverb with the same meaning in a different image. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 39. Section 3.2 · Answer: Too many cooks spoil the broth. (same meaning)

chunks.title: غابت السباعُ ولعبت الضباع.
chunks.text: غابت السباعُ ولعبت الضباع. “When the lions were absent, the hyenas played.” Same situation, different animals. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 39. Section 3.2 · Answer: When the cat’s away, the mice will play. (same meaning)

chunks.title: مَن حفرَ حفرةً لأخيه وقعَ فيها.
chunks.text: مَن حفرَ حفرةً لأخيه وقعَ فيها. The book gives the English idiom as an equivalent that conveys the result of the Arabic proverb. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 39. Section 3.2 · Answer: He was hoist with his own petard. (same meaning: caught by one’s own trap)

chunks.title: بيضةُ اليوم خيرٌ من دجاجةِ الغد.
chunks.text: بيضةُ اليوم خيرٌ من دجاجةِ الغد. “An egg today is better than a chicken tomorrow”: take the sure thing now. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 39. Section 3.2 · Answer: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. (same meaning)

chunks.title: Patience is a virtue.
chunks.text: Patience is a virtue. Religious language is more common in Arabic proverbs, so an English non-religious proverb often comes back with a religious flavour; this one is often preferred to the secular الصبر مرّ وثمره حلو. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 38. Section 3.2 · Answer: العجلةُ من الشيطان والتأنّي من الرحمن (same meaning, as Arabic usually says it)

chunks.title: إذا كان الكلامُ من فضّةٍ فالسكوتُ من ذهب.
chunks.text: إذا كان الكلامُ من فضّةٍ فالسكوتُ من ذهب. An equivalent with the same form and meaning — the usual case with these “newer” proverbs. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 38. Section 3.2 · Answer: Speech is silver, silence is golden. (same meaning)

chunks.title: الكلابُ تنبح والقافلةُ تسير.
chunks.text: الكلابُ تنبح والقافلةُ تسير. When English has no proverb, the book borrows the Arabic one with a clear rendering: carry on despite the critics. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 39. Section 3.2 · Answer: The dogs bark, but the caravan moves on. (borrowed whole — and understood)

chunks.title: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
chunks.text: When in Rome, do as the Romans do. English often shortens it to “When in Rome …”; the book advises completing it in the translation. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 39. Section 3.2 · Answer: إذا كنتَ في روما فافعل ما يفعله الرومان (the proverb, completed in Arabic)

chunks.title: القردُ في عينِ أمِّه غزال.
chunks.text: القردُ في عينِ أمِّه غزال. The Arabic is tender: love sees beauty. The book renders it by borrowing, with the image kept. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 40. Section 3.2 · Answer: In its mother’s eyes, the monkey is a gazelle. (the tender meaning, kept)

chunks.title: رجع بخُفّي حُنين.
chunks.text: رجع بخُفّي حُنين. The folk tale of Hunayn’s shoes: returning with nothing. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 29. Section 3.2 · Answer: He came back empty-handed. (same meaning)

chunks.title: بالعافية — said to someone who is eating
chunks.text: بالعافية — said to someone who is eating · "with health" The situation chooses the equivalent. Over food it is a table courtesy; to someone recovering from illness the same words wish them health. Answer: Enjoy your meal. (what English says at the table)

chunks.title: اللّه يعطيك العافية — said to someone working
chunks.text: اللّه يعطيك العافية — said to someone working · "may God give you health" Said to someone working, it thanks and encourages. Function, not words, crosses over. Answer: Thanks for your hard work. (the same function)

chunks.title: سلامتك — said to someone who is ill
chunks.text: سلامتك — said to someone who is ill · "your safety" It looks like a farewell and works as a get-well wish. Answer: Get well soon. (the same function)

chunks.title: عن إذنك — to pass someone or leave
chunks.text: عن إذنك — to pass someone or leave · "by your leave" Everyday politeness lands as everyday politeness. Answer: Excuse me. (the same function)

chunks.title: نَعيماً — said to someone freshly showered or barbered
chunks.text: نَعيماً — said to someone freshly showered or barbered · "blissfully" English has no slot for it at all. Knowing when to say nothing is part of the craft. Answer: Nothing: English has no equivalent here. (omission is the honest answer)

chunks.title: كلّ عام وأنتم بخير — said on a feast day
chunks.text: كلّ عام وأنتم بخير — said on a feast day · "every year and you are well" A festive greeting needs a festive greeting. Answer: Happy holidays! / Have a happy Eid! (a festive greeting)

chunks.title: It’s raining cats and dogs.
chunks.text: It’s raining cats and dogs. Arabic has its own downpour image, “as if from the mouths of waterskins”. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 34–35. Section 3.2 · Answer: إنّ الدنيا تمطر كأفواه القِرَب (same meaning: a downpour)

chunks.title: an iron fist in a velvet glove
chunks.text: an iron fist in a velvet glove · The best case: a target-language idiom with similar form and meaning. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 33. Section 3.2 · Answer: قبضةٌ حديديةٌ في قفّازٍ مخملي (same image, same meaning)

chunks.title: a drop in the ocean
chunks.text: a drop in the ocean · An idiom with similar meaning but a different form. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 33. Section 3.2 · Answer: غيضٌ من فيض (same meaning, different image)

chunks.title: to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds
chunks.text: to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds. Same meaning, completely different image. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 33. Section 3.2 · Answer: لعبَ على الحبلين (same meaning: playing both sides)

chunks.title: to back the wrong horse
chunks.text: to back the wrong horse · A paraphrase that keeps some of the source culture. Notice how many expressions share the horse and mean something else. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 33. Section 3.2 · Answer: راهنَ على الجواد الخاسر (same meaning, image kept)

chunks.title: to have green fingers
chunks.text: to have green fingers · Borrowing works for some culture-bound idioms. Watch the other “hand” idioms: يد بيضاء means a favour or benefit (Husni & Newman (2015), p. 46). Husni & Newman (2015), p. 33. Section 3.2 · Answer: يدُه خضراء (borrowed whole — good with plants)

chunks.title: as patient as an owl — for Arab readers
chunks.text: as patient as an owl — for Arab readers · In the West the owl stands for wisdom; in Arab culture it is “the night crow”, a harbinger of bad luck. Drop it, or use an Arabic animal with the same meaning. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 19. Section 2.1 · Answer: أصبرُ من الجمل (same quality, an image Arab readers trust)

chunks.title: as patient as Job
chunks.text: as patient as Job · A target-language simile with similar meaning. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 36. Section 3.3 · Answer: صبرُ أيّوب (same meaning)

chunks.title: as strong as a horse
chunks.text: as strong as a horse · Translating as strong as a horse as قوي مثل فرس “would provoke ridicule from most Arabic speakers”; Arabic says قوي كالأسد. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 35–36. Section 3.3 · Answer: قويٌّ كالأسد (the Arabic simile for strength)

chunks.title: heart-warming news
chunks.text: heart-warming news · English warms the heart; Arabic cools the breast. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 28. Section 6.1 · Answer: خبرٌ يُثلِج الصدر (same feeling: coolness is comfort)

chunks.title: heavy rain
chunks.text: heavy rain · English heavy has about thirty Arabic partners depending on the noun: مطر غزير, ضباب كثيف, وجبة دسمة … Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 16–17. Section 3.1 · Answer: مطرٌ غزير (the Arabic partner)

chunks.title: heavy fog
chunks.text: heavy fog · Same English adjective, a different Arabic partner. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 16. Section 3.1 · Answer: ضبابٌ كثيف (the Arabic partner)

chunks.title: a heavy smoker
chunks.text: a heavy smoker · Husni & Newman (2015), p. 16. Section 3.1 · Answer: مدخّنٌ مُفرِط (the Arabic partner)

chunks.title: heavy losses
chunks.text: heavy losses · Husni & Newman (2015), p. 17. Section 3.1 · Answer: خسائرُ هائلة (the Arabic partner)

chunks.title: a warm reception
chunks.text: a warm reception · Looking only at dictionary meaning gives استقبال ساخن; native speakers say استقبال حارّ. And a tepid reception, استقبال فاتر, is the opposite. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 1, 16. Section 3.1 · Answer: استقبالٌ حارّ (the Arabic partner)

chunks.title: imminent danger
chunks.text: imminent danger · Native speakers “plump for” خطر مُحدِق, literally “encircling danger”. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 15–16. Section 3.1 · Answer: خطرٌ مُحدِق (the Arabic partner)

chunks.title: ارتكبَ جريمة
chunks.text: ارتكبَ جريمة · A restricted collocation: perpetrate and ارتكب both join only with crime and other wrongdoing. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 3. Section 3.1 · Answer: to commit a crime (the English partner)

chunks.title: ضربَ خيمة
chunks.text: ضربَ خيمة · One Arabic verb, many English partners: ضرب ضريبة impose a tax, ضرب رقماً قياسياً break a record, ضرب مثلاً give an example. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 18. Section 3.1 · Answer: to pitch a tent (the English partner)

chunks.title: ضربَ رقماً قياسياً
chunks.text: ضربَ رقماً قياسياً · Husni & Newman (2015), p. 18. Section 3.1 · Answer: to break a record (the English partner)

chunks.title: أدّى يميناً
chunks.text: أدّى يميناً · أدّى also needs a new English verb each time: do one’s duty, provide a service, bear witness. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 17–18. Section 3.1 · Answer: to swear an oath (the English partner)

chunks.title: pay attention
chunks.text: pay attention · The basic sense of pay is to give money; its partners change it. Learn words with their partners. Section 3.1 · Answer: يَنتبِه (the Arabic verb)

chunks.title: strong tea
chunks.text: strong tea · English calls tea strong; Arabic calls it heavy — the very adjective it refused for rain. Section 3.1 · Answer: شايٌ ثقيل (the Arabic partner)

chunks.title: سَنَذْهَبُ إِلَى هُناكَ بَعْدَ ساعَتَيْنِ
chunks.text: سَنَذْهَبُ إِلَى هُناكَ بَعْدَ ساعَتَيْنِ · بعد with a stretch of time is English in, not after. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “After/afterwards”. A to Z · Answer: We will go there in two hours’ time. (the book’s rendering)

chunks.title: عِشْتُ هُنا مُنْذُ ثَلاثَةِ أَعْوامٍ
chunks.text: عِشْتُ هُنا مُنْذُ ثَلاثَةِ أَعْوامٍ · منذ is since for a starting point and for for a period, and both need the present perfect. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “During/for/in/since”. A to Z · Answer: I have lived here for three years. (present perfect + for a period)

chunks.title: وَجَّهَ لي خَمْسَ نَصائِحَ قَبْلَ مُغادَرَتي
chunks.text: وَجَّهَ لي خَمْسَ نَصائِحَ قَبْلَ مُغادَرَتي · Advice is uncountable, so a number needs pieces of. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Advise/advice”. A to Z · Answer: He gave me five pieces of advice before I left. (the book’s rendering)

chunks.title: قالَتْ إِنَّهُ كانَ ذاهِباً لِلْبَيْتِ
chunks.text: قالَتْ إِنَّهُ كانَ ذاهِباً لِلْبَيْتِ · Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Say/tell”. A to Z · Answer: She said that he was going home. (only say takes a that-clause directly)

chunks.title: زَحَفَ الجَيْشُ إِلَى جَنُوبِ شَرْقِ البِلادِ
chunks.text: زَحَفَ الجَيْشُ إِلَى جَنُوبِ شَرْقِ البِلادِ. English always puts north or south before east or west. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Northeast/southeast/…”. A to Z · Answer: The troops moved towards the southeast of the country. (north/south always comes first)

chunks.title: Dr Sarah Johnson
chunks.text: Dr Sarah Johnson · Arabic says الدكتورة سارة, with the title before the first name. How does English refer to her? Arabic uses a title with the first name; English keeps it for the last name. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Terms of address”. A to Z · Answer: Dr Johnson agreed on this matter. (English puts the title before the surname)

chunks.title: هذِهِ المُهِمَّةُ أَصْعَبُ مِنْ أَنْ نَقُومَ بِها
chunks.text: هذِهِ المُهِمَّةُ أَصْعَبُ مِنْ أَنْ نَقُومَ بِها. The elative + من + أن is the usual Arabic for too … to. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Too”. A to Z · Answer: This is too difficult a task for us to do. (too + adjective + a + noun)

chunks.title: نَسِيتُ الحَقِيبَةَ في الفُنْدُقِ الَّذِي نُقِيمُ فِيهِ
chunks.text: نَسِيتُ الحَقِيبَةَ في الفُنْدُقِ الَّذِي نُقِيمُ فِيهِ. Arabic needs a resumptive pronoun (عائد); English does not, and adding one is a typical error. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Relative pronouns”. A to Z · Answer: I forgot the suitcase in the hotel (that) we are staying at. (the book’s rendering)

chunks.title: لَمْ يَعُدْ شَلَلُ الأَطْفالِ مَرَضاً قاتِلاً
chunks.text: لَمْ يَعُدْ شَلَلُ الأَطْفالِ مَرَضاً قاتِلاً. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Anymore/no more/no longer/any longer”. A to Z · Answer: Polio is no longer a deadly disease. (لم يعد, ‘has stopped being’)

chunks.title: “The number of cars on the road has increased dramatically.”
chunks.text: “The number of cars on the road has increased dramatically.” Husni & Newman (2013), entries “Amount/number” and “Number/figure/digit/numeral”. A to Z · Answer: ازْدادَ عَدَدُ السَّيّاراتِ كَثِيراً (عدد for countables)

chunks.title: “Can you see that tall building over there?”
chunks.text: “Can you see that tall building over there?” Husni & Newman (2013), entry “High/tall”. A to Z · Answer: هَلْ تُشاهِدُ ذلِكَ المَبْنَى العالِيَ؟ (the book’s rendering)

chunks.title: “The court recess runs every year from the first of July until the end of September.”
chunks.text: “The court recess runs every year from the first of July until the end of September.” Courts and parliaments have a recess; Arabic uses عطلة. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Holiday/holidays/vacation/leave”. A to Z · Answer: تَبْدَأُ العُطْلَةُ القَضائِيَّةُ كُلَّ عامٍ مِنْ أَوَّلِ يُولْيُو (the book’s rendering)

chunks.title: “Helium is non-flammable.”
chunks.text: “Helium is non-flammable.” Technical English uses only flammable, because inflammable is misread as ‘not flammable’. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Flammable, inflammable”. A to Z · Answer: غازُ الهِيلْيُوم غَيْرُ قابِلٍ لِلِاشْتِعالِ (non-flammable)

chunks.title: “He drinks too much.”
chunks.text: “He drinks too much.” Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Too”. A to Z · Answer: يُفْرِطُ في الشَّرابِ (أفرط في, ‘to be excessive in’)

chunks.title: Naguib Mahfouz · Nagib Machfus · Nadjib Mahfoez
chunks.text: Naguib Mahfouz · Nagib Machfus · Nadjib Mahfoez. Spelling a name by the sounds of each target language: what does the A to Z call this? Both are forms of romanization; the scholarly transliteration of the same name is Najīb Maḥfūẓ. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Transliteration and transcription”. A to Z · Answer: Transcription (sounds rendered by the nearest target letters)

chunks.title: Arabic honorifics and terms of address
chunks.text: Arabic honorifics and terms of address · Translating Arabic into English, what generally happens to them? Into Arabic, markers of respect must be added, so the target is an amplified version of the original. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Terms of address”. A to Z · Answer: They are toned down or left out (Arabic → English)

chunks.title: صلّى الله عليه وسلّم → ‘Peace Be Upon Him’ (PBUH)
chunks.text: صلّى الله عليه وسلّم → ‘Peace Be Upon Him’ (PBUH) Where does the A to Z say this rendering belongs? It remains a highly ‘foreignizing’ device that makes a general text unnecessarily exotic. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Terms of address”. A to Z · Answer: In texts for a Muslim readership (not in general media texts)

chunks.title: The A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation
chunks.text: The A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation · What is the book’s focus, in its own words? The authors add that this practical aim is still rooted in theory. Husni & Newman (2013), Introduction. A to Z · Answer: Common errors, in both directions, at the level of words and structures (the microstructural elements)

chunks.title: مَجْلِس الأُمَّة
chunks.text: مَجْلِس الأُمَّة · Kuwait: what is the official English name? Each Arab legislature has its own official English name. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 110–111. Legal Translation · Answer: National Assembly (Kuwait’s official translation)

chunks.title: مَحْكَمة التَّمْيِيز
chunks.text: مَحْكَمة التَّمْيِيز · Kuwait: what is the official English name? A French calque from the Civil Law tradition, used in Kuwait, Jordan and the UAE. Husni & Newman (2015), Table 3.2. Legal Translation · Answer: Court of Cassation (Kuwait’s official translation)

chunks.title: null and void
chunks.text: null and void · How does Arabic render this doublet? Arabic usually renders English legal doublets with a single word. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 124–125. Legal Translation · Answer: باطِل (one word for the pair)

chunks.title: in compliance with
chunks.text: in compliance with · What is the customary Arabic? None of the nine dictionary verbs for comply fits this phrase. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 123. Legal Translation · Answer: عَمَلاً بِـ (the customary rendering)

chunks.title: “Each State Party shall adopt such measures as may be necessary.”
chunks.text: “Each State Party shall adopt such measures as may be necessary.” How did the UN Arabic text render shall? Legal shall is never a future; Arabic often renders it with the imperfect. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 138–140. Legal Translation · Answer: تَتَّخِذُ كُلُّ دَوْلةٍ طَرَفٍ التَّدابِيرَ اللّازِمة (a plain imperfect)

chunks.title: “The Distributor does agree that he is responsible for the cost of reassembly.”
chunks.text: “The Distributor does agree that he is responsible for the cost of reassembly.” What happens to the declarative do? The performative do works like hereby and is not translated. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 141. Legal Translation · Answer: يُوافِقُ المُوَزِّعُ عَلَى أَنْ يَكُونَ مَسْؤُولاً (do is never rendered)

chunks.title: consideration
chunks.text: consideration · In a contract, what does this mean? A legal homonym: same form, unrelated technical meaning. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 128. Legal Translation · Answer: مَبْلَغ (the legal meaning: an amount of money)

chunks.title: motion
chunks.text: motion · In court, what does this mean? Husni & Newman (2015), p. 129. Legal Translation · Answer: طَلَب (the legal meaning: an official request)

chunks.title: “[The Council] decides to remain seized of the matter.”
chunks.text: “[The Council] decides to remain seized of the matter.” What does seized mean here? One of three legal senses of seize. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 125–126. Legal Translation · Answer: يُقَرِّرُ أَنْ يُبْقِيَ المَسْأَلةَ قَيْدَ نَظَرِهِ الفِعْلِيّ (it keeps the matter under its consideration)

chunks.title: وزارة الخارجية
chunks.text: وزارة الخارجية · For the United Kingdom, which recognized translation must be used? Recognized translations depend on the country, not on the words. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 132. Legal Translation · Answer: Foreign Office (the UK’s own name)

chunks.title: فَصْل
chunks.text: فَصْل · In a Moroccan law, what does it correspond to? Husni & Newman (2015), Table 3.3. Legal Translation · Answer: Article (in Morocco, فصل is the article)

chunks.title: attorney (British usage)
chunks.text: attorney (British usage) What is the right Arabic? In the UK attorney is short for attorney-in-fact; power of attorney is سند التوكيل. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 109. Legal Translation · Answer: وَكِيل (someone acting for another, as in power of attorney)

chunks.title: lawful (in a secular law)
chunks.text: lawful (in a secular law) Which Arabic word fits? Only قانوني and شرعي are used in the secular sense. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 121. Legal Translation · Answer: قانُونِيّ (secular)

chunks.title: mens rea
chunks.text: mens rea · What is the Arabic? Latin terms in English law come from the Roman occupation, the Church and Norman law. Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 123–124. Legal Translation · Answer: نِيّة جُرْمِيّة (criminal intent)

chunks.title: عِدّة
chunks.text: عِدّة · Which strategy does the book give for this term? Islamic terms are rendered by an equivalent, a paraphrase or a borrowing, depending on readership. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 126. Legal Translation · Answer: Paraphrase: ‘legally prescribed waiting period before marrying’ (an exegetic translation)

chunks.title: Not word for word, but sense for sense.
chunks.text: Not word for word, but sense for sense. Whose principle is this? St Jerome followed Cicero in this. Bassnett (2014), pp. 54–56. Bassnett · Answer: Cicero and Horace (non verbum de verbo, sed sensum exprimere de sensu)

chunks.title: Metaphrase, paraphrase and imitation.
chunks.text: Metaphrase, paraphrase and imitation. Whose three types are these? Dryden chose paraphrase, the middle way. Bassnett (2014), p. 69. Bassnett · Answer: Dryden (Preface to Ovid’s Epistles, 1680)

chunks.title: Intralingual, interlingual, intersemiotic.
chunks.text: Intralingual, interlingual, intersemiotic. Whose three types of translation? Bassnett (2014), p. 25. Bassnett · Answer: Jakobson (rewording, translation proper, transmutation)

chunks.title: “Give one another a hearty handshake all round” for “greet one another with a holy kiss”.
chunks.text: “Give one another a hearty handshake all round” for “greet one another with a holy kiss”. Which kind of equivalence does Bassnett use this to criticize? J. B. Phillips’s rendering of Romans 16:16. Bassnett (2014), p. 36. Bassnett · Answer: Dynamic equivalence (Nida’s equivalent effect)

chunks.title: What exists in common between all existing translations of a single work.
chunks.text: What exists in common between all existing translations of a single work. Whose term is this, and what is it? Bassnett (2014), pp. 36–37. Bassnett · Answer: Popovič’s invariant core (the stable semantic elements)

chunks.title: A Finnish or Japanese ‘bathroom’ is not an English one.
chunks.text: A Finnish or Japanese ‘bathroom’ is not an English one. Which category did Catford use this for? Bassnett argues that ‘home’ and ‘democracy’ are just as culture-bound. Bassnett (2014), pp. 40–42. Bassnett · Answer: Cultural untranslatability (no matching situational feature)

chunks.title: The translator should be visible; foreignization over domestication.
chunks.text: The translator should be visible; foreignization over domestication. Whose argument? Venuti builds on Schleiermacher’s 1813 distinction. Bassnett (2014), pp. 46–47. Bassnett · Answer: Lawrence Venuti (The Translator’s Invisibility, 1995)

chunks.title: Translate so the text functions in the situation in which it is used, for the people who use it.
chunks.text: Translate so the text functions in the situation in which it is used, for the people who use it. Which theory? Skopos is Greek for ‘purpose’. Bassnett (2014), pp. 83–84. Bassnett · Answer: Skopos theory (Reiss & Vermeer, 1984)

chunks.title: Established literatures translate less; young or unsettled ones translate more.
chunks.text: Established literatures translate less; young or unsettled ones translate more. Whose idea? Bassnett (2014), p. 85. Bassnett · Answer: Itamar Even-Zohar (polysystem theory, 1978)

chunks.title: Better a live sparrow than a stuffed eagle.
chunks.text: Better a live sparrow than a stuffed eagle. Who said it? Bassnett (2014), p. 78. Bassnett · Answer: Edward FitzGerald (translator of the Rubáiyát)

chunks.title: The first systematic study of translation in English, 1791.
chunks.text: The first systematic study of translation in English, 1791. Whose was it? Bassnett (2014), p. 72. Bassnett · Answer: Alexander Fraser Tytler (Essay on the Principles of Translation)

chunks.title: Executed in 1546 after a ‘mistranslation’ of Plato; wrote five principles of translation.
chunks.text: Executed in 1546 after a ‘mistranslation’ of Plato; wrote five principles of translation. Who was he? Bassnett (2014), pp. 63–64. Bassnett · Answer: Étienne Dolet (La manière de bien traduire, 1540)

chunks.title: Phonemic, literal, metrical, poetry into prose, rhymed, blank verse, interpretation.
chunks.text: Phonemic, literal, metrical, poetry into prose, rhymed, blank verse, interpretation. Whose list of strategies? Bassnett (2014), p. 93. Bassnett · Answer: Lefevere (seven strategies, from Catullus 64)

chunks.title: “Block out” the work; render idiom by idiom; beware faux amis; never embellish.
chunks.text: “Block out” the work; render idiom by idiom; beware faux amis; never embellish. Whose rules? Bassnett (2014), pp. 125–126. Bassnett · Answer: Hilaire Belloc (six rules for prose, 1931)

chunks.title: anuvad
chunks.text: anuvad · What does the Sanskrit word for translation mean? Bassnett (2014), p. 146. Bassnett · Answer: ‘saying after’ (a temporal image (Harish Trivedi))

chunks.title: Recognition, comprehension, reproduction.
chunks.text: Recognition, comprehension, reproduction. What are these three, in Husni and Newman? Husni & Newman (2015), p. 15. Concepts · Answer: The three levels of the problem of translating collocations (obstacles the translator must negotiate)

chunks.title: to perpetrate a crime · اِرْتَكَبَ جريمةً
chunks.text: to perpetrate a crime · اِرْتَكَبَ جريمةً · What kind of collocation is this? The verb has a limited collocational range. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 3. Concepts · Answer: Restricted collocation (the verb joins only words related to ‘crime’)

chunks.title: to go · to motion
chunks.text: to go · to motion · Which has the wider collocational range, and why? Likewise shoulder has more meanings than the medical clavicula. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 2. Concepts · Answer: To go: the more generic the word, the wider its range (range depends on specificity)

chunks.title: to pass up on + opportunity
chunks.text: to pass up on + opportunity · Which type of collocation do the authors call this? Arabic examples include اعتكف في with جامع or مسجد. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 15. Concepts · Answer: Lexicogrammatical collocation (a lexical item with a grammatical combination)

chunks.title: A fixed expression whose meaning is not the sum of the meanings of its words.
chunks.text: A fixed expression whose meaning is not the sum of the meanings of its words. What is it? Husni & Newman (2015), p. 26. Concepts · Answer: An idiom (non-literal, metaphorical meaning)

chunks.title: فقدَ أعصابَه · to lose one’s nerve
chunks.text: فقدَ أعصابَه · to lose one’s nerve · Why are these false friends? Meaning is not always transferred with form. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 29. Concepts · Answer: Reinterpretation: the Arabic means ‘to lose one’s temper’ (the form was borrowed, the meaning changed)

chunks.title: cover story → موضوع الغلاف
chunks.text: cover story → موضوع الغلاف · Which process made this a false friend? In English, a cover story is either the main story on a cover or a made-up story; the Arabic calque has only one of these senses. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 29. Concepts · Answer: Partial borrowing (of two English senses, Arabic took one)

chunks.title: Two varieties of a language side by side in one community, each with a definite role.
chunks.text: Two varieties of a language side by side in one community, each with a definite role. What is this, and who defined it in 1959? In Arabic, the ‘high’ variety is fuṣḥā and the ‘low’ varieties are the dialects. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 59. Concepts · Answer: Diglossia, Charles Ferguson (a ‘high’ and a ‘low’ variety)

chunks.title: diglossia
chunks.text: diglossia · Who introduced the term, and for which language? The word literally means ‘bilingual’ in Greek. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 58. Concepts · Answer: Ioannis Psicharis, for Greek (demotiki and katharevousa, 1886–9)

chunks.src: Heritage fuṣḥā, contemporary fuṣḥā and three levels of colloquial (1973).
chunks.title: Heritage fuṣḥā, contemporary fuṣḥā and three levels of colloquial (1973).
chunks.text: Heritage fuṣḥā, contemporary fuṣḥā and three levels of colloquial (1973). Whose model of Egyptian Arabic is this? Husni & Newman (2015), p. 60. Concepts · Answer: El-Said Badawi (the first Arab scholar to examine diglossia in detail)

chunks.title: A translation memory returns a segment that differs only slightly from the new one.
chunks.text: A translation memory returns a segment that differs only slightly from the new one. What is this called? Translation memory tools work best for translators who stay in one field. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 166. Concepts · Answer: A fuzzy match (differences are minimal)

chunks.title: Compounding
chunks.text: Compounding · Which language uses it far more? The difference lies in lexical structure and word formation. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 40. Concepts · Answer: English (compounding is extremely active)

chunks.title: The doctor examined the case.
chunks.text: The doctor examined the case. doctor settles which case this is. Section 2.3 · Answer: فحص الطبيبُ الحالة. (context decides)

chunks.title: شربنا من عينِ ماءٍ باردة.
chunks.text: شربنا من عينِ ماءٍ باردة. عين is an eye, a spring and a spy; ماء beside it decides. Section 2.3 · Answer: We drank from a cold water spring. (context decides)

chunks.title: He sat on the bank and watched the water.
chunks.text: He sat on the bank and watched the water. Two unrelated meanings under one spelling (homonymy); water settles it. Section 2.3 · Answer: جلس على ضفّة النهر وراقب الماء. (context decides)

chunks.title: The company fired three employees.
chunks.text: The company fired three employees. fire means “shoot” with a gun, “dismiss” with an employee, “bake” with ceramic and “cauterise” with a wound. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 3. Section 2.3 · Answer: فصلت الشركة ثلاثة موظفين. (context decides)

chunks.title: The plane took off at noon.
chunks.text: The plane took off at noon. take off needs a different Arabic verb each time: خلع، أقلع، قلّد، نجح، بتر، خفّض. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 10. Section 2.3 · Answer: أقلعت الطائرة ظهراً. (context decides)

chunks.title: She took off her coat.
chunks.text: She took off her coat. Same phrasal verb, a different object, a different Arabic verb. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 10. Section 2.3 · Answer: خلعت معطفها. (context decides)

chunks.title: Little John found his toybox. The box was in the pen.
chunks.text: Little John found his toybox. The box was in the pen. Bar-Hillel’s famous example of why a machine struggles: only knowledge of the world tells you which pen. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 170. Section 8.4 · Answer: كان الصندوق في حظيرة اللعب (سياج الطفل). (context decides: a playpen)

chunks.title: تطهير الجرح
chunks.text: تطهير الجرح · Related senses (polysemy) are dangerous because the wrong reading almost makes sense. Section 2.3 · Answer: cleaning the wound (context decides)

chunks.title: احتجاز الرهائن
chunks.text: احتجاز الرهائن · The same noun holds back water (احتجاز المياه) and holds people; the object decides. Section 2.3 · Answer: holding hostages (context decides)

chunks.title: قام المدير بتوقيع العقد.
chunks.text: قام المدير بتوقيع العقد. قام بـ before a verb that can simply be used is the commonest padding in translated Arabic. Section 9.1 · Answer: وقّع المديرُ العقد. (the verb does its own work)

chunks.title: تمّ اختراق الهدنة من جانب الحكومة.
chunks.text: تمّ اختراق الهدنة من جانب الحكومة. A passive with the doer named (من قبل، من طرف، من جانب) is common in media Arabic but “not considered normative usage” and is “frowned upon by careful users of Arabic” — Husni & Newman (2013), entry “The passive”. Section 9.1 · Answer: اخترقت الحكومةُ الهدنة. (an actor, doing something)

chunks.title: مَن المسؤول: الشرطة أم المتظاهرون؟!
chunks.text: مَن المسؤول: الشرطة أم المتظاهرون؟! Which English punctuation would a reviser keep? Arabic writers may stack marks to show intensity; “in translation, these must be reduced”. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Punctuation”. Section 5.1 · Answer: Who is responsible, the police or the demonstrators? (English punctuation)

chunks.title: Each State Party shall adopt such measures as may be necessary.
chunks.text: Each State Party shall adopt such measures as may be necessary. In legal English shall expresses obligation, not the future, and Arabic legal texts often render it with the present tense (المضارع). Husni & Newman (2015), pp. 138–140. Section 7.2 · Answer: تتخذ كل دولة طرف التدابير اللازمة. (the present tense: an obligation)

chunks.title: The employee shall be deemed to have been appointed under probation for three months.
chunks.text: The employee shall be deemed to have been appointed under probation for three months. Legal shall with the third person expresses obligation. Husni & Newman (2013), entry “Will/shall”. Section 7.2 · Answer: يُعتبَر الموظف معيَّناً تحت الاختبار لمدة ثلاثة شهور. (the binding rule)

chunks.title: الحكومة أعلنت عن إجراءات جديدة.
chunks.text: الحكومة أعلنت عن إجراءات جديدة. Starting news prose with the subject is the shape of the English showing through. Section 9.1 · Answer: أعلنت الحكومة عن إجراءات جديدة. (the verbal sentence Arabic news prefers)

chunks.title: مطار القاهرة
chunks.text: مطار القاهرة · The single biggest mistake with إضافة is to render every one with English of; English prefers a compound or ’s-genitive: Cairo airport, Salwa’s mother. Husni & Newman (2015), p. 50. Section 3.4 · Answer: Cairo airport (an English compound)

chunks.title: He is a brave and daring officer.
chunks.text: He is a brave and daring officer. This English came from شجاع مِغوار. Which version would a reviser keep? Arabic pairs near-synonyms for emphasis; English usually turns the pair into one expression (omission, Section 4.3). Husni and Newman list the same move for binomials such as بلا قيد أو شرط → unconditionally (2015, p. 22). Section 3.4 · Answer: He is a very brave officer. (one strong phrase for the Arabic pair)

chunks.title: The life is beautiful in this city.
chunks.text: The life is beautiful in this city. الحياة carries its article; English life in the general sense takes none. Section 9.1 · Answer: Life is beautiful in this city. (English drops the article)

chunks.title: He married from her last year.
chunks.text: He married from her last year. تزوّج من has a preposition; English marry does not. Section 9.1 · Answer: He married her last year. (no preposition in English)

chunks.text: خ · Which sign is this letter? The handshape for خاء in the @ksl_dictionary alphabet. KSL · Answer: خاء (خاء)

chunks.title: sign → دال
chunks.text: sign → دال · ksl/dal.webp · Which letter is this sign? This is the handshape for دال in the @ksl_dictionary alphabet. KSL · Answer: د (دال)

chunks.title: د
chunks.text: د · Which sign is this letter? The handshape for دال in the @ksl_dictionary alphabet. KSL · Answer: دال (دال)

chunks.title: sign → ذال
chunks.text: sign → ذال · ksl/dhal.webp · Which letter is this sign? This is the handshape for ذال in the @ksl_dictionary alphabet. KSL · Answer: ذ (ذال)

chunks.title: ذ
chunks.text: ذ · Which sign is this letter? The handshape for ذال in the @ksl_dictionary alphabet. KSL · Answer: ذال (ذال)

chunks.title: sign → راء
chunks.text: sign → راء · ksl/ra.webp · Which letter is this sign? This is the handshape for راء in the @ksl_dictionary alphabet. KSL · Answer: ر (راء)

chunks.text: ر · Which sign is this letter? The handshape for راء in the @ksl_dictionary alphabet. KSL · Answer: راء (راء)

chunks.title: sign → زاي

chunks.title: Kuwaiti Sign Language
chunks.text: Kuwaiti Sign Language · What is it? “Not Arabic performed with the hands. Not gestures agreed on for convenience. Not the same language as the sign language of Egypt, or Jordan, or America.” KSL · Answer: The language of Kuwait's Deaf community, a language of its own (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: One sign language for the whole world?
chunks.text: One sign language for the whole world? Is there one? Two countries sharing a spoken language can have sign languages that are not mutually intelligible at all. KSL · Answer: No. Sign languages arise in communities, over generations (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: The Ministry of Education's KSL dictionary
chunks.text: The Ministry of Education's KSL dictionary · How many signs does it hold? The Ministry gives its reason too: sign vocabulary is shaped by the culture and the place it grows in. KSL · Answer: More than 2,000, collected from Kuwaiti Deaf signers (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: KSL or ArSL?
chunks.text: KSL or ArSL? What did Kuwaiti Deaf signers, interpreters and teachers answer (Almubayei, 2024)? So material labelled Arabic sign language is very often ArSL, a different language. Never put an ArSL sign on a Kuwaiti page. KSL · Answer: KSL, or KSL and ArSL together, not ArSL alone (Almubayei (2024))

chunks.title: A deaf client arrives
chunks.text: A deaf client arrives · What do you do first? An interpreter booked for the wrong language is worse than none, because everyone in the room believes communication is happening. KSL · Answer: Ask which language they use, and use the one you are told (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: Deaf, with a capital D
chunks.text: Deaf, with a capital D · What does it describe? Small d deaf is a fact about hearing; capital D Deaf is about belonging. A deaf person may not be Deaf. KSL · Answer: Belonging: someone who uses a sign language and identifies with its community (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: الصمّ والبُكم
chunks.text: الصمّ والبُكم · Should you use this term? It is still in wide circulation, but it is not what people call themselves. KSL · Answer: No. Use الصمّ (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: In the room with an interpreter
chunks.text: In the room with an interpreter · Who do you speak to? Speak to the person, and look at the person. KSL · Answer: The person, not the interpreter (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: Getting a signer's attention
chunks.text: Getting a signer's attention · Which is right? Do not hold someone's hands while they are signing: you are interrupting a sentence. KSL · Answer: A wave, a tap on the shoulder, or the lights (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: Fingerspelling
chunks.text: Fingerspelling · What does it produce? Fingerspelling gives letters as handshapes; a lexical sign is one sign for one word, and belongs to KSL. KSL · Answer: Arabic, in the air (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: When to fingerspell
chunks.text: When to fingerspell · Which is one of the cases the lessons give? Spell for names, words with no established sign, technical or foreign terms the first time, and emphasis. KSL · Answer: A name of a person, a place or an institution (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: The face
chunks.text: The face · What does it do in a sign? Brows, mouth, head and posture are not expression added to a sign; they are often the grammar. KSL · Answer: Often carries the grammar of the sentence (the KSL lessons)

chunks.title: The four levels
chunks.text: THE WHOLE TEXT · Method طَريقة · One decision, taken before you start, that governs everything after: what kind of translation is this going to be? Literal or free, foreign-sounding or domesticated. It follows from the brief — who asked for it, for which reader, to do what job. SOUNDS LIKE · “This manual will be communicative: the reader must be able to work the machine without noticing the translation.” THIS WORD, THIS PHRASE · Procedure إجراء الترجمة · A technique for translating a word, phrase or sentence. There are seven of them, named by Vinay and Darbelnet, and they are the subject of the guide next door. Procedures 1–3 are direct; 4–7 are oblique. SOUNDS LIKE · “I turned the noun phrase into a verb: transposition.” (Section 4.2) THIS PROBLEM · Strategy استراتيجية الترجمة · A planned solution to a translation problem. Where a procedure names the move, a strategy answers the harder question: this expression has no equivalent, so what will I do about it? Choose a strategy for each problem, not one strategy for the whole text. SOUNDS LIKE · “There is no English for العِدّة, so I will explain it: explanatory translation.” (Section 4.3) THE TWO TEXTS, COMPARED · Shift تَحَوُّل · Not a choice but an observation: a difference between source and target that shows up when you lay them side by side. A shift is the evidence; the procedure is the act that produced it. SOUNDS LIKE · “The source has a passive, the target an active.” WHY IT MATTERS IN PRACTICE

chunks.title: The four levels (cont.)
chunks.text: A reviewer who writes "too literal" is talking about method. One who writes "wrong term" is talking about a procedure. If you cannot tell which you are being asked to change, you will fix the wrong thing. This is also the backbone of a commentary (Section 9.3): name the problem, state the decision, give the reason, name the procedure or strategy, and cite the source.

chunks.title: The strategies
chunks.text: A strategy is a planned solution to a problem; a procedure names the move you made. One per problem, not one per text. Functional translation الترجمة الوظيفية · Use a target-language expression that does the same job, whatever its shape. The first thing to reach for with an idiom. FOR INSTANCE · spill the beans → يُفشي السرّ · mark my words → تذكّر كلامي · Cultural substitution الإبدال الثقافي · Replace a cultural reference with one the target reader already knows. FOR INSTANCE · They are like Romeo and Juliet. → هما كقيس وليلى · Addition الإضافة · Add what the new reader needs but the old one did not. Common from English into Arabic, because Arabic is a language of elaboration (لغة إسهاب). FOR INSTANCE · the Fed → مجلس الاحتياطي الفيدرالي الأمريكي · Omission الحذف · Leave out what the target language does not need. Common from Arabic into English, where repeated synonyms sound laboured. Also used for politeness. FOR INSTANCE · شجاعٌ ومِغوار → very brave · Explanatory translation الترجمة الشرحية · Explain an expression that has no equivalent. The last option, not the first — used for cultural and technical words. FOR INSTANCE · الزكاة, الصدقة, العِدّة · Compensation التعويض · Something is lost here, so make an equal effect somewhere else. FOR INSTANCE · A pun that dies in line two is replaced by a different pun in line four, so the page keeps its wit. Domestication التوطين · Make the translation feel local to the target reader. FOR INSTANCE · The brief decides between this and its opposite. Neither is right in general. Foreignisation التغريب

chunks.title: The strategies (cont.)
chunks.text: Keep the foreign flavour of the source, so the reader knows they are reading a translation. FOR INSTANCE · Venuti argued for this; a tourist brochure usually argues against it. A more general word التعميم · When the target language has no exact word, go one step up. FOR INSTANCE · prawns and shrimps → روبيان · A more neutral word التحييد · When the source word carries a feeling that would land wrongly in the target text. FOR INSTANCE · A word that is merely blunt in one language can read as an insult in the other. Paraphrase إعادة الصياغة · Say the meaning in other words when no single word will carry it. FOR INSTANCE · jet lag → إرهاق السفر · Loan word plus explanation الاقتراض مع الشرح · Keep the word and gloss it once, so the reader gains the term and its meaning together. FOR INSTANCE · waqf (a charitable endowment in Islam)

chunks.title: How to work
chunks.text: Habits, not terms. None of these has an Arabic name to learn or a place in a commentary — they are simply the working practices that change a translation most. Read the whole text before translating any of it. Genre, purpose and audience decide sentence-level choices. Settling them at sentence one means revising from sentence two. Work from the brief, not from the sentence · Who asked for this, for which reader, to do what? A brief you never asked for is a brief you invented. Search parallel texts, not dictionaries · For a contract or a leaflet, find three real ones written natively in the target language. A dictionary gives a word; a parallel text gives the convention. Name the problem before solving it · Lexical, cultural, register, pragmatic? Each has different solutions, and misdiagnosing it wastes the search. Leave a marker and move on · A hard segment solved under pressure is usually solved badly. Flag it, keep moving, return with the whole text in your head. Verify an official equivalent; never infer one. Institutions, laws, drugs and treaties have fixed forms. Inventing a plausible one is the error hardest to see and most damaging to find. Revise twice, with different questions · First against the source: was anything lost or added? Then against the target alone: does this read as something written in this language? Ask the client, and say why · An ambiguity, a factual error, a term with no settled equivalent: these are the client's decisions. Raising them is professional practice, not weakness.

chunks.title: The three readings
chunks.text: READING 1 · With the original · Is anything missing, added or changed? This reading is about fidelity, and it is the only one where you may look at both texts at once. READING 2 · Without the original · Does it sound natural? If a sentence sounds translated, rewrite it. Cover the source; you cannot hear your own English or Arabic while the other language is in front of you. READING 3 · The details · Numbers, names, spelling, punctuation, titles and captions. The errors that embarrass a translator most are almost never errors of meaning. THE ORDER IS NOT OPTIONAL · Fidelity, then fluency, then detail. Read for naturalness with the source still in front of you and you will not hear the translation — the original keeps telling you what the sentence means, so you cannot tell whether your own sentence says it.

chunks.title: English into Arabic
chunks.text: Translating into Arabic. Most of these are not errors of meaning — the sentence is understood and still sounds translated. COMMON ERROR — STARTING EVERY SENTENCE WITH THE SUBJECT · NOT THIS · الحكومة أعلنت… THIS · أعلنت الحكومة… Grammatical, and it still sounds translated. Arabic news prose normally opens with the verb. COMMON ERROR — OVERUSING قام بـ · NOT THIS · قام الوزير بزيارة الكويت · THIS · زار الوزير الكويت · The light verb is carrying nothing. Arabic already has the verb you need. COMMON ERROR — COPYING THE ENGLISH PASSIVE · NOT THIS · تمّ افتتاح المعرض من قِبَل الوزير · THIS · افتتح الوزير المعرض · English reaches for the passive far more readily than Arabic. If the doer is named, name them. COMMON ERROR — NUMBERS THREE TO TEN · NOT THIS · ثلاث طلاب · THIS · ثلاثة طلاب · With 3 to 10 the number takes the opposite gender to the counted noun. COMMON ERROR — HAMZA AND TAA MARBUTA · NOT THIS · انشاء · مدرسه · الى · THIS · إنشاء · مدرسة · إلى · Orthography, not style — and the first thing a reader notices. COMMON ERROR — WORD-FOR-WORD COLLOCATIONS · NOT THIS · كسر القانون · THIS · خالف القانون · English breaks a law; Arabic does not break it. Learn the partner, not the word. COMMON ERROR — ENGLISH PUNCTUATION · NOT THIS · نعم, سأحضر. هل ستحضر أنت? THIS · نعم، سأحضر. هل ستحضر أنت؟ Arabic has its own comma and its own question mark. Using the English ones is a spelling error.

chunks.title: Arabic into English
chunks.text: Translating into English. Arabic habits that English does not share, and the article and copula that Arabic does not have. COMMON ERROR — LONG SENTENCES JOINED WITH “AND” …and… and… and… Split them with full stops. Arabic coordinates where English subordinates or stops. One Arabic sentence is often three English ones. COMMON ERROR — REPEATED SYNONYMS · brave and daring · very brave · Arabic doubles for emphasis; English reads the double as two separate claims. Omission is the fix. COMMON ERROR — AN EXTRA “THE” The life is beautiful. Life is beautiful. No article before a general idea in English, however firmly الـ sits there in the Arabic. COMMON ERROR — A MISSING “IS” He in the office. He is in the office. The Arabic nominal sentence has no copula. English always needs one. COMMON ERROR — ARABIC PREPOSITIONS · He married from her. He married her. تزوّج من has a preposition and marry does not. Prepositions have to be learned verb by verb. COMMON ERROR — MISSING CAPITALS IN A TITLE BEFORE A NAME · minister of health Ahmad Ali · Minister of Health Ahmad Ali · A title immediately before a name is capitalised in English. Arabic marks none of this.

chunks.title: Simultaneous
chunks.text: THE DISTINCTION WORTH KEEPING · In everyday speech الترجمة الفورية is used for interpreting in general, and an interpreter is مترجم فوري. That usage is real and you will hear it daily. But in a commentary, an exam or a contract, الفورية names one mode and الشفهية names the field — and a client who asks for الفورية and is given التتابعية has been given something that takes twice as long. MODE 1 · Simultaneous · الترجمة الفورية · Rendered while the speaker is still speaking. What it is · The interpreter works in a soundproof booth, hears the speaker through headphones and speaks into a microphone at the same time. The audience hears the rendering a few seconds behind the original, and the two voices run together throughout. Where it is used · What it demands · Where it goes wrong · WHAT THE COMPASS PRACTISES · The Booth runs against a clock, so what it trains is الترجمة الفورية. The other modes are taught here and not yet practised here — consecutive needs a note system and a pause, sight translation needs a document in front of you, and neither fits a sixty-second drill. Naming them is the first half of learning them.

chunks.title: Consecutive
chunks.text: MODE 2 · Consecutive · الترجمة التتابعية · التتبعية · التعاقبية · Rendered after the speaker pauses, from notes and memory. The interpreter sits near the speaker, listens through a passage — which may run several minutes — taking notes of the main ideas, and delivers the whole of it once the speaker stops.

chunks.title: Sight translation
chunks.text: MODE 3 · Sight translation · الترجمة المنظورة · الترجمة بالنظر · A written text, read out in the other language, on the spot. The interpreter is handed a document and speaks it in the other language immediately, without a written draft. Written input, spoken output — which is why it sits inside interpreting rather than translation.

chunks.title: Whispered
chunks.text: MODE 4 · Whispered · الترجمة الهمسية · Simultaneous, whispered to one or two listeners, with no equipment. The interpreter sits or stands beside the listener and renders simultaneously in a low voice. Technically the same mode as الفورية, stripped of the booth, the headphones and the microphone.

chunks.title: Relay
chunks.text: MODE 5 · Relay · الترجمة المرحلية · الترجمة عن طريق التتابع · Through a third language, when no interpreter has both. A speech in Arabic is rendered into English by one interpreter, and the other booths work from that English rather than from the Arabic. The English booth becomes the pivot, and everyone downstream is listening to a translation of a translation.

chunks.title: Remote
chunks.text: MODE 6 · Remote · الترجمة الفورية عن بُعد · The same modes, with the interpreter not in the room. Simultaneous or consecutive delivered over a platform, by video or by telephone. A working arrangement rather than a mode of its own, and it changes the work enough to be taught separately.

chunks.title: Liaison, escort and bilateral interpreting
chunks.text: NOT SETTLED · Liaison, escort and bilateral interpreting · ترجمة المرافقة · الترجمة الثنائية · WHAT IT IS · Short two-way exchanges between a small number of people, rendered in both directions by one interpreter who is part of the conversation rather than behind glass: a business visit, a hospital reception, a factory tour, an official accompanying a delegation. In practice it is consecutive in very short turns. NEEDS EDITORIAL VERIFICATION · The English names are settled; the Arabic is not. ترجمة المرافقة, الترجمة الثنائية and الترجمة الحوارية are all in use for overlapping senses, and no single form has become standard. Treat it as needing editorial verification before you put it in a commentary — cite the source you take it from, or give the English with your Arabic in brackets.

chunks.title: CollocationsEnglish → Arabic
chunks.text: COLLOCATIONS · ENGLISH → ARABIC · COLLOCATIONS · ARABIC → ENGLISH · DISCOURSE MARKERS · BOTH DIRECTIONS · CONTEXT-DEPENDENT EXPRESSIONS · ARABIC → ENGLISH · SPEECH ACTS · ENGLISH → ARABIC · ENGLISH → ARABIC · Collocations التَّلازُم اللَّفظيّ · A collocation is a pairing the language has already made for you. Agreement takes a different Arabic verb depending on which verb stands beside it in English, and choosing the wrong one is not a grammar mistake — it is the mistake that marks a text as translated. reach an agreement · → · يتوصل إلى اتفاق · Arriving at it after negotiation. توصّل إلى carries the sense of getting there. sign an agreement · → · يوقّع اتفاقية · The physical act, and note the shift to اتفاقية — the formal instrument rather than the understanding. enter into an agreement · → · يدخل في اتفاق · Becoming party to it. Legal and commercial register. bilateral agreement · → · اتفاق ثنائي · Two parties. ثنائي is the standard diplomatic adjective. preliminary agreement · → · اتفاق مبدئي · Agreed in principle, not yet final. binding agreement · → · اتفاق ملزم · ملزم is the legal term of art for what obliges the parties. WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS · The English verb does not decide the Arabic verb. The stage of the agreement does: arriving at it, signing it, or entering into it are three different moments, and Arabic names them separately. A CHAMBER · FREE TO WANDER · NOTHING HERE IS SCORED

chunks.title: CollocationsArabic → English
chunks.text: The same problem, running the other way. Arabic اتخذ covers a range that English splits between make, take and adopt, and no rule predicts which. The object chooses the verb. اتخذ قرارًا · make a decision · The default. Take a decision is heard in British and institutional English; make is safer. اتخذ إجراءات · take measures · Also take action, take steps. Here English does use take. اتخذ موقفًا · take a position · adopt a position · Adopt is the more formal and more diplomatic of the two. اتخذ خطوات · take steps · Fixed pairing; make steps is not English. اتخذ سياسة · adopt a policy · Only adopt. Neither make nor take collocates with policy here. Rendering every اتخذ as take produces English that is grammatical and wrong: take a decision exists in British usage but make a decision is the unmarked choice, and take a policy is not English at all.

chunks.title: Discourse markersBoth directions
chunks.text: Discourse markers أدَوات الرَّبط · Connectors are the joints of an argument. They are rarely one-to-one, they differ sharply in register, and Arabic prose joins clauses far more often than English does — so a marker-for-marker rendering produces English that sounds relentlessly linked. however · ومع ذلك · غير أنّ · Concession. غير أنّ is the more formal. therefore · لذلك · ومن ثَمّ · Consequence. ومن ثَمّ belongs to academic and legal prose. moreover · علاوة على ذلك · Adding weight to the same line of argument. nevertheless · مع ذلك · ومع هذا · Stronger concession than however; the obstacle is conceded and passed. in contrast · في المقابل · Sets two things side by side rather than conceding. on the other hand · من ناحية أخرى · Expects a on the one hand somewhere before it; Arabic is less strict about the pair. as a result · ونتيجة لذلك · Result, stated plainly. in addition · بالإضافة إلى ذلك · Neutral addition; lighter than moreover. accordingly · وبناءً عليه · Formal, and common in legal and administrative Arabic. Two habits worth unlearning. First, ومع ذلك and مع ذلك are not interchangeable with every however: English often signals contrast by position and punctuation alone. Second, Arabic will happily open a sentence with و where English simply starts a new sentence — the right rendering is often nothing at all.

chunks.title: Context-dependent expressionsArabic → English
chunks.text: Context-dependent expressions تَعابير رَهينة السِّياق. Some expressions have no translation at all until you know who is saying them, to whom, and when. Storing one equivalence for them is the error — it teaches a phrase that will be wrong most of the times it is used. بالعافية — said to someone eating · Enjoy your meal · Bon appétit · Literal gloss: with health. The function is a table courtesy, and English uses a borrowed French phrase for it as often as an English one. بالعافية — said to someone who has just bathed · — often nothing at all · English has no formula for this moment. The honest rendering may be silence, or a neutral pleasantry, depending on the text. Forcing enjoy your meal here is nonsense. بالعافية — said to someone working hard · Keep it up · More power to you · Now it is encouragement. Same three syllables, a different speech act. الله يعطيك العافية · Thank you for your effort · Well done · Thanks for your trouble. A thanks-and-blessing said to someone who has done work for you. The English depends on the relationship: a colleague, a shopkeeper and a superior take three different renderings. بالعافية is the clearest case. It is a well-wishing formula built on health, and what it means in English is decided entirely by the moment.

chunks.title: Speech actsEnglish → Arabic
chunks.text: Speech acts الأفعال الكَلاميّة · Ask what the sentence is doing, not what it says. A request, an apology, a refusal and an offer each have their own formulas in each language, and politeness does not map degree for degree. Could you possibly send me the report? هل يمكنك إرسال التقرير؟ Neutral and direct. Appropriate between colleagues; it loses the English hedging, which is usually the right call. Could you possibly send me the report? هل بالإمكان إرسال التقرير؟ More impersonal — the agent disappears. Useful in institutional writing where naming the person would be too pointed. Could you possibly send me the report? هل تتكرم بإرسال التقرير؟ Markedly deferential: تتكرم casts the act as a kindness being granted. Right for a superior; obsequious between equals. I'm afraid that won't be possible. للأسف، هذا غير ممكن · A refusal. English softens with I'm afraid; Arabic with للأسف. The softener is not decoration — removing it changes the act from a refusal into a rebuff. English marks politeness largely by grammatical distance — could you possibly, I was wondering if. Arabic marks it more by lexical choice and by blessing formulas. A literal rendering of English hedging often lands as odd rather than polite.

chunks.title: “I don't want to go.”
chunks.text: EVERYDAY MSA · “I don't want to go.” لا أُريد أن أذهب. Neutral. Broadcast Arabic, subtitles, plain prose. KUWAITI · EVERYDAY MSA · FORMAL · CLASSICAL · WHY THIS CHAMBER HAS NO SCORE · All four Arabic lines mean the same thing, and none is more correct than the others. What changes is who is speaking, to whom, and where — and the English has to move with it. Pick the wrong level and the translation is accurate and still wrong. A CHAMBER · FREE TO WANDER · NOTHING HERE IS SCORED

chunks.title: ت ر ج م
chunks.text: TO TRANSLATE, TO INTERPRET · تَرجَمة · translation · tarjama · مُتَرجِم · translator · mutarjim · تُرجُمان · the court interpreter of the Ottoman and earlier chanceries. English dragoman is this word, borrowed centuries ago through Italian and French — a fossil of contact, not a translation you may use today. Modern تُرجُمان renders as interpreter · turjumān · تَرجَمَ · he translated · tarjama · مُتَرجَم · translated — of a text · mutarjam · WHAT IS ACTUALLY GOING ON · Both languages borrow and both languages derive. English borrows (algebra, safari) and derives (nation, national, nationalise, nationality); Arabic borrows (بنك, ديمقراطيّة, تِلفاز) and derives. The difference is the mechanism. English derivation stacks affixes onto the front and back of a stem, so the stem stays visibly intact. Arabic derivation threads a consonantal root through a pattern (وَزْن), so the root is interleaved with the pattern rather than sitting at one end of it: ك-ت-ب in the pattern مَفعول gives مَكتوب, and in مَفعَلة gives مَكتَبة.

chunks.title: ت ر ج م (cont.)
chunks.text: Two consequences a translator meets constantly. First, the pattern carries meaning of its own — فاعِل gives the one who does it, مَفعول the one it is done to, مَفعَل the place — so a reader can often infer a word never met before. Second, a root's family is a network of related but not predictable senses: derivation gives you the likely reading, context gives you the actual one. مَكتوب is written, and it is also a letter, and it is also what is fated — three different English words, and only the sentence around it decides which. That is where the translating happens: not in the root, but in the choice the root leaves open. A CHAMBER · FREE TO WANDER · NOTHING HERE IS SCORED
