chunks.title: The present
chunks.text: The present · الحاضر · The English simple present (states, general truths, stative verbs, habits) is usually the Arabic imperfect, or a nominal sentence for ‘to be’. The present progressive (happening now, or temporary; never with stative verbs) is the imperfect, an active participle with intransitive verbs, or قامَ بِـ + verbal noun. Both presents can refer to the near future: سَـ / سَوْفَ + imperfect. The imperfect is negated with لا; a participle with لَيْسَ. ‘Have’ for possession or illness is not progressive: ‘I have a headache’ (عِنْدِي صُداعٌ), not *‘I am having a headache’. “The sun sets in the west.” تَأْفُلُ الشَّمْسُ في المَغْرِبِ · “I am coming/on my way.” أَنا قادِمٌ · “The opposition are organizing unprecedented demonstrations against the government.” تَقُومُ المُعارَضَةُ بِاحْتِجاجاتٍ غَيْرِ مَسْبُوقَةٍ ضِدَّ الحُكُومَةِ · “I am not travelling today.” لَسْتُ مُسافِراً اليَوْمَ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Presently/at present
chunks.text: Presently/at present · عمّا قريب / في الوقت الحاضر · ‘Presently’ means in a short while: عَنْ / بَعْدَ قَلِيلٍ, عَمّا / عَنْ / مِنْ قَرِيبٍ with the imperfect, with or without سَـ / سَوْفَ. ‘At present’ means now: في الوَقْتِ الحاضِرِ, الآنَ. “We will have a solution presently.” سَيَكُونُ لَدَيْنا حَلٌّ عَمّا قَرِيبٍ · “She is leaving at present.” تُغادِرُ الآنَ · presently-at-present

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Price/prize
chunks.text: Price/prize · ثمن / سعر / جائزة · A ‘price’ is what you pay (سِعْر, pl. أَسْعار; ثَمَن, pl. أَثْمان); a ‘prize’ is what you win (جائِزَة, pl. جَوائِز). ‘Price’ goes with ‘pay’ (دَفَعَ) and, in Arabic, with ‘cost’ (كَلَّفَ); ‘prize’ with ‘award’ (مَنَحَ), ‘win’ (أَحْرَزَ, حازَ, فازَ) and ‘receive’ (تَسَلَّمَ). On the stock exchange, سِعْر is preferred to ثَمَن. “He won/received the Nobel Prize for chemistry.” أَحْرَزَ / تَسَلَّمَ / حازَ عَلَى / فازَ بِجائِزَةِ نُوبِل في الكِيمِياءِ · “No matter how much it cost.” مَهْما كَلَّفَ الثَّمَنُ · “Share prices have continued to rise at the stock exchange.” اسْتَمَرَّتْ أَسْعارُ الأَسْهُمِ في الارْتِفاعِ في البُورْصَةِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Principal/principle
chunks.text: Principal/principle · مدير / رئيسي / مبدأ · ‘Principal’ as a noun is the head of a school or college (مُدِير); as an adjective it means chief (رَئِيسِيّ). ‘Principle’ is only a noun, a basis for beliefs or actions (مَبْدَأ, pl. مَبادِئ). “The principal opposition parties decided on a plan to put forward two joint nominees.” أَقَرَّتِ الأَحْزابُ الرَّئِيسِيَّةُ في المُعارَضَةِ خُطَّةً لِتَقْدِيمِ مُرَشَّحَيْنِ مُشْتَرَكَيْنِ. “There was an agreement on the principle of withdrawal.” كانَ هُناكَ اتِّفاقٌ حَوْلَ مَبْدَإِ الانْسِحابِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Punctuation
chunks.text: Punctuation · علامات الترقيم · English punctuation is tightly ruled; Arabic punctuation is a 20th-century borrowing from Western (mostly English) practice and is used very inconsistently, so the translator has to normalize it. Quotation marks (عَلاماتُ اقْتِباس): Arabic also uses them for emphasis, foreign company names and dialect words, where English uses italics or nothing; forms range from «…» to “…”. Round brackets (قَوْسانِ): still used for Qur’anic quotation (hence بَيْنَ القَوْسَيْنِ, ‘in inverted commas’), and in formal Arabic for foreign names, borrowings, titles, foreign abbreviations and asides. In English: omit for names, titles and abbreviations; italics for borrowings; keep for asides. Exclamation and question marks: Arabic piles them up for intensity (!؟); English uses one. Suspension points (…): English uses them only in literature, for a pause or unfinished thought, never for ‘etc.’; Arabic uses them freely at the end of lists or for emphasis, so they are usually dropped or replaced by a comma. According to the CEO of Exxon Mobil the price of oil will have to be between 60 and 70 dollars per barrel. قالَ رَئِيسُ شَرِكَةِ «إِكْسُون مُوبِيل»: يَجِبُ أَنْ يَتَراوَحَ سِعْرُ بَرْمِيلِ النَّفْطِ بَيْنَ 60 وَ70 دُولاراً. “We spoke with the actress during the shooting of the soap Nur Maryam.” تَحَدَّثْنا مَعَ الفَنّانَةِ في كَوالِيسِ مُسَلْسَلِ (نُور مَرْيَم) “Who is responsible, the police or the demonstrators?” مَنِ المَسْؤُولُ: الشُّرْطَةُ أَمِ المُتَظاهِرُونَ؟!

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Relative pronouns
chunks.text: Relative pronouns · الأسماء الموصولة · English chooses who/whom/which/that/whose/where by person, place or thing, by grammatical role, and by preposition, and separates defining clauses (no commas, pronoun can drop) from non-defining ones (with commas). Arabic ignores human versus non-human; what matters is whether the antecedent is definite. Only definite antecedents take a relative pronoun. Forms: الَّذِي, الَّتِي; dual اللَّذانِ / اللَّذَيْنِ, اللَّتانِ / اللَّتَيْنِ; plural الَّذِينَ, اللّاتِي / اللَّواتِي. Arabic needs a resumptive pronoun (عائِد) when the antecedent is the object of a verb or preposition; this is why Arabic speakers write *‘the house that I lived in it’. Place: ‘where’ (حَيْثُ, with a fixed ending). Indefinite antecedent: no pronoun: رَجُلٌ كانَ هُناكَ ‘a man who was there’. Non-specific: whichever (أَيّ), whatsoever (أَيّ, ما, ماذا, مَهْما), whoever (مَنْ). “The man whose dog I saw.” الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي رَأَيْتُ كَلْبَهُ · “The two girls who are in the hotel.” البِنْتانِ اللَّتانِ في الفُنْدُقِ · “I forgot the suitcase in the hotel (that) we are staying at.” نَسِيتُ الحَقِيبَةَ في الفُنْدُقِ الَّذِي نُقِيمُ فِيهِ · “A man that we saw there.” رَجُلٌ رَأَيْناهُ هُناكَ · “Whoever said that is a liar.” مَنْ قالَ هذا فَهُوَ كَذّابٌ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Rise/raise
chunks.text: Rise/raise · ارتفع / رفع · To ‘rise’ is to go up (ارْتَفَعَ); to ‘raise’ is to make something go up (رَفَعَ). A pay increase is a ‘rise’ (British) or a ‘raise’ (American). “The prices rose last week.” ارْتَفَعَتِ الأَسْعارُ الأُسْبُوعَ الماضِي · “The government raised prices last week.” رَفَعَتِ الحُكُومَةُ الأَسْعارَ الأُسْبُوعَ الماضِي

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Say/tell
chunks.text: Say/tell · قال / أخبر · ‘Say’ takes no personal object; ‘tell’ usually does. Arabic: قالَ (+ إِنَّ) for say; حَكَى, تَحَدَّثَ, حَدَّثَ, أَخْبَرَ for tell. Only ‘say’ can be followed directly by a ‘that’-clause. “He only said a few words to me.” لَمْ يَتَحَدَّثْ مَعِي إِلّا قَلِيلاً · “He was telling me what (had) happened to his family during the war.” كانَ يُخْبِرُنِي بِما حَصَلَ لِعائِلَتِهِ خِلالَ الحَرْبِ. “She said (NOT *told) that he was going home.” قالَتْ إِنَّهُ كانَ ذاهِباً لِلْبَيْتِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Self
chunks.text: Self · نفس / ذات · English adds ‘-self’ to a pronoun; Arabic uses نَفْس (pl. أَنْفُس) with a suffix. As the first term of an iḍāfa, نَفْس means ‘same’. ذات renders ‘self’ in compounds: الثِّقَةُ بِالذّاتِ ‘self-confidence’, احْتِرامُ الذّاتِ ‘self-respect’, الحُكْمُ الذّاتِيُّ ‘self-determination’. ‘In itself’: في (حَدِّ) ذاتِهِ. “I can’t imagine myself in a world without paper, pens and books.” لا أَتَصَوَّرُ نَفْسِي في عالَمٍ مِنْ دُونِ أَوْراقٍ وَأَقْلامٍ وَكُتُبٍ · “They, themselves, elected themselves.” انْتَخَبُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ · “This crisis, in itself, is harmful to the national interest.” هذِهِ الأَزْمَةُ في حَدِّ ذاتِها إِضْرارٌ بِالمَصالِحِ الوَطَنِيَّةِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Sensible/sensitive
chunks.text: Sensible/sensitive · حصيف / حسّاس · ‘Sensible’ is about good judgement (حَصِيف, حَكِيم); ‘sensitive’ is about feeling (حَسّاس). “His father was a sensible man who realized the importance of education.” كانَ أَبُوهُ رَجُلاً حَصِيفاً يَعْرِفُ أَهَمِّيَّةَ التَّعْلِيمِ. “Jojoba oil is excellent for people with sensitive skins.” زَيْتُ الجُوجُوبا رائِعٌ خُصُوصاً لِلْأَشْخاصِ الَّذِينَ يُعانُونَ مِنْ جِلْدٍ حَسّاسٍ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Shade/shadow
chunks.text: Shade/shadow · ظلّ / شبح · ‘Shade’ is a place out of the sun; a ‘shadow’ is the shape something casts. Arabic uses ظِلّ (pl. أَظْلال, ظِلال, ظُلُول) for both; a moving shadow of a person or animal can be شَبَح (pl. أَشْباح); figuratively, ظَلام also works. تَحْتَ / في ظِلِّ: ‘under the auspices of’, but في ظِلِّ can also mean ‘in (the) light of’. تَقَلَّصَ ظِلُّهُ ‘his authority dwindled’; وِزارَةُ الظِّلِّ ‘shadow cabinet’. “I noticed a shadow moving outside the bedroom.” لاحَظْتُ شَبَحاً مُتَحَرِّكاً خارِجَ غُرْفَةِ النَّوْمِ. “Diplomacy should take place in the light of day, not in the shadows.” تَجْدُرُ مُمارَسَةُ الدِّبْلُوماسِيَّةِ في النُّورِ وَلَيْسَ في الظَّلامِ. “The project was completed under the auspices of the UN.” تَمَّ المَشْرُوعُ تَحْتَ ظِلِّ الأُمَمِ المُتَّحِدَةِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Some/any
chunks.text: Some/any · بعض / أيّ · ‘Some’ is for affirmative sentences, ‘any’ for questions and negatives. Arabic uses بَعْض (in an iḍāfa or with a suffix) and أَيّ. ‘Some’ and ‘some of’ are both بَعْض, without مِنْ. ‘Some’ and ‘any’ are often not translated at all, especially with ‘there was/were’. ‘Any’ meaning ‘whatever’: أَيّ … كانَ in the perfect (بِأَيَّةِ صِفَةٍ كانَتْ ‘in any capacity’). ‘In any case’ (anyway): عَلَى / في كُلِّ حالٍ. ‘some (of the) ministers’ · بَعْضُ الوُزَراءِ (NOT *بَعْضٌ مِنَ الوُزَراءِ) “I’ll bring you some coffee in a minute.” سَوْفَ أُحْضِرُ لَكَ فِنْجاناً مِنَ القَهْوَةِ خِلالَ دَقِيقَةٍ · “There weren’t any tourists in the church.” لَمْ يَكُنْ هُناكَ أَيُّ سائِحٍ في الكَنِيسَةِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Sometime/sometimes
chunks.text: Sometime/sometimes · سابقاً / أحياناً · ‘Sometimes’ means now and then (أَحْياناً); ‘sometime’ means at one time, formerly (سابِقاً). ‘Sometimes … sometimes’ is تارَةً … تارَةً, تارَةً … طَوْراً, or تارَةً … (تارَةً) أُخْرَى. “He was a sometime professor at Harvard.” كانَ أُسْتاذاً في جامِعَةِ هارْفارْد سابِقاً · “Sometimes/at times she chides me, other times she turns to me for help.” تَلُومُنِي تارَةً وَتارَةً تَتَوَسَّلُنِي

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Still
chunks.text: Still · ما زال / حتى الآن / مع ذلك · ‘Still’ changes meaning with context. ‘As before, now or in future’: ما زالَ / لا يَزالُ + adjective, accusative noun or imperfect. ‘Until now’: حَتَّى / إِلَى الآنَ. ‘Yet, however’: مَعَ أَنَّ, مَعَ ذلِكَ. “It was still difficult.” ما زالَ صَعْباً · “She still loves me.” لا تَزالُ تُحِبُّنِي · “I still don’t know his name.” لا أَعْرِفُ اسْمَهُ حَتَّى الآنَ · “The newspaper apologized about the mistakes in the article, but he still sued them.” اعْتَذَرَتِ الجَرِيدَةُ لَهُ عَنِ الأَخْطاءِ في المَقالَةِ وَمَعَ ذلِكَ رَفَعَ عَلَيْها دَعْوَى

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Subjunctive
chunks.text: Subjunctive · المضارع المنصوب · The English subjunctive is the bare infinitive for all persons (or, in formal British English, should + infinitive) after verbs and phrases of demand, advice or necessity (advise, ask, demand, insist, propose, recommend, request, suggest, urge; it is best, crucial, essential, imperative, important, vital that). The Arabic subjunctive shares the name but little else. Arabic uses it after purpose particles (لِـ, كَيْ, لِكَيْ, حَتَّى: ‘in order to, so that’), after لَنْ (negative future), and after أَنْ with verbs of desire, intention and need. “It is imperative that you be there.” عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَكُونَ هُناكَ · “They demanded (that) the government release the leader of the party.” طالَبُوا الحُكُومَةَ بِإِطْلاقِ سَراحِ زَعِيمِ الحِزْبِ. “So that the international community takes its responsibilities.” لِكَيْ يَتَحَمَّلَ المُجْتَمَعُ الدَّوْلِيُّ مَسْؤُولِيّاتِهِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Suffixes
chunks.text: Suffixes · اللواحق · Arabic has no English-style derivational suffixes, so there is never a one-to-one match. The usual solutions are an iḍāfa (‘presidency’, مُدَّةُ الرِّئاسَةِ) or a noun phrase (‘infallible’, مُنَزَّهٌ عَنِ الخَطَإِ; ‘drinkable’, قابِلٌ لِلشُّرْبِ).

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Terms of address
chunks.text: Terms of address · صيغ المخاطبة والألقاب · Address is culture-bound. Arabic has more honorifics and uses them more widely, and first names on first meeting can seem disrespectful. Translate according to context, the relationship between the people and what the speaker intends: tone honorifics down or drop them into English, add them into Arabic. حَضْرَتُكَ is sometimes ‘sir’ but usually just ‘you’. Titles such as حاجّ or أُسْتاذ appear even when the person is no pilgrim or teacher. Arabic puts a title before the first name, English before the surname: الدُّكْتُورَةُ سارَة is ‘Dr Johnson’, not ‘Dr Sarah’. Formulas for the dead (المَرْحُومُ before the name, رَحِمَهُ اللهُ after) are translated once and then dropped; رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ after the Companions is omitted. صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ (‘PBUH’) suits texts for a Muslim readership, not general media. English · Arabic · His Majesty (the) Sultan · (حَضْرَةُ) صاحِبِ الجَلالَةِ السُّلْطانُ · His Majesty (the) King · (حَضْرَةُ) صاحِبِ الجَلالَةِ المَلِكُ · His/Her Royal Highness · (حَضْرَةُ) صاحِبِ / صاحِبَةِ السُّمُوِّ المَلَكِيِّ · His Excellency the President · فَخامَةُ الرَّئِيسِ · His Excellency the Prime Minister · صاحِبُ السَّعادَةِ رَئِيسُ الوُزَراءِ · His Highness Shaykh …, the Minister for … سُمُوُّ الشَّيْخِ … وَزِيرُ … His Excellency the Minister for … (حَضْرَةُ) مَعالِي وَزِيرِ … His Excellency the Ambassador · سَعادَةُ السَّفِيرِ · His Grace the Duke · سُمُوُّ الدُّوق · His Eminence … (Cardinal) نِيافَةُ (الحَبْرِ) … (كَرْدِينال) Shaykh … (Islamic scholars) فَضِيلَةُ الشَّيْخِ …

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Terms of address (cont.)
chunks.text: Shaykh … (high-ranking scholars, e.g. al-Azhar) صاحِبُ الفَضِيلَةِ الشَّيْخُ … His Eminence the Mufti · سَماحَةُ المُفْتِي · His Royal Highness / His Excellency / His Majesty / Your Excellency. سُمُوُّهُ / مَعالِيهِ / جَلالَتُهُ / سَعادَتُكُمْ. “Dr Johnson agreed on this matter.” (NOT *‘Dr Sarah…’) وافَقَتِ الدُّكْتُورَةُ سارَة عَلَى هذا الأَمْرِ. “Excuse me sir, where is the entrance(, please)?” يا أُسْتاذُ، أَيْنَ المَدْخَلُ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ؟

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: There is/are …
chunks.text: There is/are … هناك / كان هناك / سيكون هناك · Arabic has no present copula, so ‘there is/are’ depends on tense, sentence type and whether a place is named. Present: affirmative هُناكَ / هُنالِكَ; questions with هَلْ / أَ; negative لَيْسَ; negative question أَلَيْسَ. Add هُناكَ when no place is given. Past: كانَ (subject nominative, predicate accusative); questions هَلْ / أَ كانَ; negative لَمْ يَكُنْ (there has not been) or ما كانَ (there wasn’t); أَلَمْ يَكُنْ for negative questions. Future: سَيَكُونُ; negative لَنْ يَكُونَ; أَسَيَكُونُ, أَلَنْ يَكُونَ. If the place is ‘there’, Arabic puts هُناكَ at the end, while English repeats ‘there’. كانَ هُناكَ دَلْوٌ ‘There was a bucket’ differs from كانَ دَلْواً ‘It was a bucket’. English often adds ‘any’ in negatives and questions, and uses ‘no’ rather than ‘not’. “There is a school in the centre of town.” هُناكَ / هُنالِكَ مَدْرَسَةٌ في وَسَطِ المَدِينَةِ · “Is there no coffee?” أَلَيْسَتْ هُناكَ / هُنالِكَ قَهْوَةٌ؟ “There were no/have not been any newspapers in the waiting room.” لَمْ تَكُنْ هُناكَ جَرائِدُ في غُرْفَةِ الانْتِظارِ · “There will not be (any) money in the bank.” لَنْ تَكُونَ هُناكَ أَمْوالٌ في المَصْرِفِ · “Is there no coffee there?” أَلَيْسَتْ قَهْوَةٌ هُناكَ؟

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Time
chunks.text: Time · زمن / وقت / مرّة / عصر · ‘Time’ has several Arabic equivalents depending on the sense. Abstract: زَمَن (pl. أَزْمان), or تَوْقِيت (‘summer time’, ‘GMT’). A point or period: وَقْت (pl. أَوْقات); an appointed time: تَوْقِيت, مِيقات (pl. مَواقِيت). An English plural may be an Arabic singular and vice versa. Era, age, epoch: عَصْر (pl. عُصُور, أَعْصُر, أَعْصار), دَهْر (pl. دُهُور; also a very long time), زَمَن, زَمان, وَقْت. زَمَن is also grammatical ‘tense’. One occurrence: مَرَّة. Expressions: كَمِ السّاعَةُ؟ ‘What’s the time?’; عَلَى مَرِّ الزَّمانِ ‘in the course of time’; حانَ وَقْتُ الذَّهابِ ‘it’s time to go’; قَضَيْنا وَقْتاً مُمْتِعاً ‘we had a good time’; المَرَّةُ القادِمَةُ ‘next time’; مَرَّةً بَعْدَ مَرَّةٍ ‘time and again’. As a verb: ‘to time a race’ (دَوَّنَ / سَجَّلَ وَقْتَ), ‘He timed the attack perfectly.’. “Time was one of the things that occupied people’s minds.” إِنَّ الزَّمَنَ مِنَ الأَشْياءِ الَّتي شَغَلَتْ فِكْرَ الإِنْسانِ. “The post office opening times during Ramadan are from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m.” مَواقِيتُ / أَوْقاتُ عَمَلِ مَكاتِبِ البَرِيدِ في شَهْرِ رَمَضانَ مِنَ الثّامِنَةِ صَباحاً إِلَى الخامِسَةِ مَساءً. “He has lived in exile for a long time/for ages.” أَقامَ في بِلادِ الغُرْبَةِ دَهْراً · “This time, I’ll forgive him.” سَأَغْفِرُ لَهُ هذِهِ المَرَّةَ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Too
chunks.text: Too · جداً / أكثر من اللازم / أفرط في · No single Arabic word matches ‘too’. The usual solutions are the elative meaning ‘more than necessary’ (أَكْثَرُ مِنَ اللّازِمِ, أَكْثَرُ مِمّا يَنْبَغِي, أَكْثَرُ مِمّا يَجِبُ), the verb أَفْرَطَ في + noun, or the adverb جِدّاً. ‘Too + adjective + for/to + infinitive’ becomes an elative + مِنْ + أَنْ: ‘too young to vote’, أَصْغَرُ سِنّاً مِنْ أَنْ يُدْلِيَ بِصَوْتِهِ. English needs ‘too difficult a task’, not *‘too difficult task’. Arabic speakers often misuse ‘too’ as a plain intensifier (*‘He loves her too much’ meaning ‘very much’). Idioms: ‘It’s not too bad’ (هُوَ بَيْنَ بَيْنَ); ‘It’s too good to be true’ (أَغْرَبُ مِنْ أَنْ يُصَدَّقَ). “He drinks too much.” يُفْرِطُ في الشَّرابِ · “She talked too much.” تَكَلَّمَتْ أَكْثَرَ مِمّا يَنْبَغِي · “The circumstances were too sensitive to be mentioned.” كانَتِ الظُّرُوفُ أَكْثَرَ حَساسِيَّةً مِنْ أَنْ نَسْتَطِيعَ الكَلامَ عَنْها · “This is too difficult a task for us to do.” هذِهِ المُهِمَّةُ أَصْعَبُ مِنْ أَنْ نَقُومَ بِها

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Transliteration and transcription
chunks.text: Transliteration and transcription · النقحرة والكتابة الصوتية · There is no single agreed system for writing Arabic in Latin letters (romanization). Transliteration is strictly letter for letter; transcription renders sounds. Scholarly forms (Najīb Maḥfūẓ) and everyday ones (Naguib Mahfouz, Nagib Machfus, Nadjib Mahfoez) can look like different people. Choose by audience and be consistent. Unicode guidance says a system should be standard, complete, predictable, pronounceable and reversible; no common Arabic system manages all five. Narrow (scholarly): ء ’, ث th, ج j, ح ḥ, خ kh, ذ dh, ش sh, ص ṣ, ض ḍ, ط ṭ, ظ ẓ, ع ‘, غ gh, ق q; long vowels ā ī ū; diphthongs ay, aw. ة is -a, but -at in the first term of an iḍāfa (mudarrisa, mudarrisat al-kulliyya); nisba -ī / -iyya; tanwīn usually dropped (except set words like jiddan); doubled consonants written twice (dubb); no assimilation (al-shams); hyphen after the article (al-qamar); Western numerals; bi ’l-qalam after a vowel; capitalize Al- at the start of a sentence. Use naturalized forms: imam, not imām, just as ‘taco’ or ‘bikini’ are now English. Colloquial: transcribe the actual sound (Egyptian nagm for najm; Palestinian al-’uds), with e, o, ē, ō if needed. Broad (for general readers), in order: (1) a recognized form if there is one, (2) the form closest to the Arabic (Ahmad, not Ahmed), (3) fewer letters (Hasan, not Hassan), (4) consistency.

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Transliteration and transcription (cont.)
chunks.text: Proper names: do not translate them (Ibrahim stays Ibrahim, not Abraham), but use an established English form if one exists (سارة → Sarah); for names originally English or French, restore the original (ميشال → Michel), while ميخائيل stays Mikha’il. Historic Spanish place names keep their Arabic forms: طُلَيْطِلَة Toledo, قُرْطُبَة Cordoba, الحَمْراء Alhambra. English into Arabic: forms vary (غواتيمالا / جواتيمالا; شارل / تشارلز); short vowels are lengthened (دانيال), consonant clusters are allowed (شنغهاي), emphatics are frequent (قُنْصُل). Put the foreign name in brackets the first time, and in technical texts give the Latin-script form as well. English · Arabic · Anne · آن · Charles · تشارلز · Daniel · دانيال · David · دايفد · Edward · إدوارد · Elisabeth · إليزابيث · Francis · فرانسيس · George · جورج · Graham · غراهام / جراهام · Henry · هنري · James · جيمس · John · جون · Mary · ماري · Michael · مايكل · Paul · بول · Peter · بطرس · Sarah · سارا · Susan · سوسن / سوزان · Thomas · توماس · William · وليم · Michelangelo · ميكيلانجيلو · Napoleon Bonaparte · نابليون بونابرت · Picasso · بيكاسو · Common Arabic names, broad forms · عبد الرحمن ’Abd ar-Rahman · عبد الله ’Abdullah · عادل ’Adil, Adel · حسن Hasan · حسين Husayn, Hussein · محمد Muhammad · مصطفى Mustafa · يوسف Yusuf, Youssef · زينب Zaynab, Zeinab. “Professor Andy Smith wrote an article on internal medicine.” كَتَبَ البُرُوفِسُور (أَنْدِي سْمِيث) مَقالَةً حَوْلَ الأَمْراضِ الباطِنِيَّةِ · transliteration-and-transcription

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Until/till/by
chunks.text: Until/till/by · حتى / إلى / قبل · ‘Until’ (informally ‘till’) is for an ongoing state; ‘by’ is for something done at or before a point. Arabic: حَتَّى (+ genitive) or إِلَى for until, قَبْلَ for by. حَتَّى also means ‘up to (and including)’, close to بِما في ذلِكَ ‘including’; ‘in order to’ with the subjunctive; and ‘even’. “We’ll stay here until the evening.” سَنَبْقَى هُنا حَتَّى المَساءِ · “I hope you will be able to do it by Friday.” آمُلُ أَنْ تَعْمَلَهُ قَبْلَ يَوْمِ الجُمْعَةِ. “The investigators searched the building from the basement up to (including) the roof.” فَتَّشَ المُحَقِّقُونَ المَبْنَى مِنَ السِّرْدابِ حَتَّى السَّقْفِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Wa and fa
chunks.text: Wa and fa · الواو والفاء · Both can mean ‘and’ but are not interchangeable. Only فَـ introduces the result of a condition; only وَ introduces a circumstantial clause (حال); وَ is the one used between nouns (English uses commas and one ‘and’ before the last item). فَـ links cause and effect or a sequence (also ثُمَّ, وَبَعْدَ ذلِكَ, وَبَعْدَهُ): ‘and so’, ‘thus’, ‘as a result’, ‘therefore’. فَـ can be contrastive: ‘yet’, ‘however’. “I saw Salwa, Leila and Sally.” رَأَيْتُ سَلْوَى وَلَيْلَى وَسالِي (NOT فَلَيْلَى) “He failed the exam and (so he) had to leave the university.” فَشِلَ في الامْتِحانِ فَيَجِبُ أَنْ يَتْرُكَ الجامِعَةَ. “Her accomplice confessed, yet she insists on denying her involvement.” رُغْمَ اعْتِرافِ شَرِيكِها فَهِيَ تَنْفِي تَوَرُّطَها بِإِلْحاحٍ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: When/if
chunks.text: When/if · إذا / لمّا / حين · Both appear in conditionals, but ‘when’ implies certainty. Arabic: إِذا (or لَوْ) for ‘if’; لَمّا or حِينَ for ‘when’. “If he gets here [not certain], I shall tell him what happened.” إِذا جاءَ فَأَحْكِي لَهُ ما حَصَلَ · “When he becomes managing director [certain], he will make a few changes.” لَمّا يُصْبِحُ مُدِيراً تَتَغَيَّرُ بَعْضُ الأَشْياءِ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Whether (it be) … or
chunks.text: Whether (it be) … or · سواء كان … أو · Meaning ‘irrespective of’, it is rendered by لَوْ كانَ … أَوْ / أَمْ, إِنْ كانَ … أَوْ / أَمْ, سَواءٌ كانَ … أَوْ / أَمْ, and sometimes a simple coordinator. “There is no such thing as unimportant art, whether it be locally or internationally.” لا يُوجَدُ فَنٌّ بِلا أَهَمِّيَّةٍ سَواءٌ كانَ مَحَلِّيّاً أَوْ عالَمِيّاً. “He will do it, whether he wants/likes to or not (willy-nilly).” سَيَعْمَلُ غَصْباً أَمْ طَوْعاً / مِنْ غَيْرِ غَصْبٍ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: While/whereas
chunks.text: While/whereas · في حين / بينما · Both mark contrast and are often interchangeable, but only ‘while’ also expresses simultaneity. Arabic: في حِينِ (أَنَّ), عَلَى / في حِينِ أَنَّ, بَيْنَما (also simultaneous), حَيْثُ. “Foreign forces liberated the South, whereas/while the North was freed by domestic resistants.” تَوَلَّتِ القُوّاتُ الأَجْنَبِيَّةُ تَحْرِيرَ الجَنُوبِ عَلَى حِينِ أَنَّ الشَّمالَ تَحَرَّرَ عَلَى يَدِ مُقاوِمِي الدّاخِلِ. “He was reading while she was cooking dinner.” كانَ يَقْرَأُ بَيْنَما كانَتْ تُعِدُّ العَشاءَ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Will/shall
chunks.text: Will/shall · سـ / سوف · Traditionally ‘shall’ was for the first person and ‘will’ for the others; formal usage no longer keeps this, and both contract to ’ll. In legal English, ‘shall’ expresses obligation with the second and third persons. “We shall/’ll be here.” سَنَكُونُ هُنا · “The employee shall be deemed to have been appointed under probation for three months.” يُعْتَبَرُ المُوَظَّفُ مُعَيَّناً تَحْتَ الاخْتِبارِ لِمُدَّةِ ثَلاثَةِ شُهُورٍ

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Wish
chunks.text: Wish · تمنّى / ودّ / لو · ‘Wish’ takes many constructions: + to + infinitive, + clause, + that, + pronoun, + for. With a past or present reference, the hypothetical past (subjunctive) marks something unreal; with a future reference, a possibility. Arabic can render it as hypothetical ‘if only …’ (لَوْ, ‘would that’) or as ‘like’ or ‘want’. Verbs: رَغِبَ في (+ أَنْ before a verb), تَمَنَّى, اشْتاقَ, رَجا, ارْتَجَى; they also cover ‘hope’, ‘look forward to’, ‘want’. Watch the prepositions Arabic needs and English does not. “I wish you were here.” أَتَمَنَّى لَوْ كُنْتَ هُناكَ · “I wish we knew how much they were making on the deal.” أَوَدُّ لَوْ عَرَفْنا كَمْ سَيَكْسِبُونَ مِنْ هذِهِ الصَّفْقَةِ · “If only I knew/had known about his fraud …” لَوْ كُنْتُ قَدْ عَرَفْتُ / أَعْرِفُ عَنِ احْتِيالِهِ. “Israel wishes to obtain US assistance to implement its project.” تَرْغَبُ إِسْرائِيلُ في الحُصُولِ عَلَى مُساعَدَةِ الوِلاياتِ المُتَّحِدَةِ مِنْ أَجْلِ تَطْبِيقِ خُطَطِها

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2013). A to Z of Arabic–English–Arabic Translation. Saqi.
chunks.title: Appendix I: Tenses
chunks.text: Appendix I: Tenses · ملحق: الأزمنة · An overview of English tenses and their usual Arabic forms. Tense · English form · Arabic form · Example · Present simple · PRESENT · imperfect · He has dinner at eight · يَتَعَشَّى في السّاعَةِ الثّامِنَةِ مَساءً · Present progressive · to be + -ing · imperfect; active participle (intransitive) He is drinking coffee · يَشْرَبُ قَهْوَةً; He is coming · هُوَ قادِمٌ · Past simple · PAST · perfect · He went to the office · ذَهَبَ إِلَى المَكْتَبِ · Past progressive · was + -ing · كانَ + imperfect; كانَ + active participle; كانَ + سَـ / سَوْفَ. He was driving / used to drive the car · كانَ يَقُودُ السَّيّارَةَ; I was going to say something · كُنْتُ سَأَقُولُ شَيْئاً · Present perfect · have + past participle · قَدْ + perfect · He has bought a house · قَدِ اشْتَرَى بَيْتاً · Past perfect · had + past participle · كانَ + قَدْ + perfect · He had told her · كانَ قَدْ أَبْلَغَها · Future simple · will + infinitive · سَـ / سَوْفَ + imperfect · He will leave the country · سَيُغادِرُ البِلادَ · Future perfect · will have + past participle · يَكُونُ + قَدْ + perfect · He will have finished the job · يَكُونُ قَدِ انْتَهَى العَمَلَ · Future progressive · will be + -ing · سَـ / سَوْفَ + imperfect; يَكُونُ + participle · He will be travelling · يَكُونُ مُسافِراً

chunks.title: Appendix II: Modality
chunks.text: Appendix II: Modality · ملحق: الجهة · An overview of English modals of obligation, possibility and ability, with Arabic forms. Type · English · Arabic form · Example · Obligation · must / have to / should · يَجِبُ أَنْ; يَجِبُ عَلَى + pron + أَنْ · You must tell him what he needs to know · يَجِبُ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَقُولَ لَهُ ما يَحْتاجُ إِلَى المَعْرِفَةِ · Obligation · had to · كانَ عَلَى + pron · They had to fire him · كانَ عَلَيْهِمْ يَفْصِلُوهُ · Obligation · should have / ought to have · كانَ مِنَ الواجِبِ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ · He should have behaved more politely · كانَ مِنَ الواجِبِ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَتَصَرَّفَ بِأَدَبٍ أَكْثَرَ · Obligation · must have · لا بُدَّ أَنَّ … كانَ · He must have been here · لا بُدَّ أَنَّهُ كانَ هُنا · Possibility · may / might · قَدْ + imperfect · He may be the only one to applaud · قَدْ يَكُونُ الوَحِيدَ الَّذِي يُصَفِّقُ · Possibility · may have / might have · رُبَّما + perfect; رُبَّما كانَ + قَدْ · He might have behaved differently · رُبَّما كانَ قَدْ تَصَرَّفَ بِشَكْلٍ مُخْتَلِفٍ · Ability · can · أَمْكَنَ أَنْ; يَسْتَطِيعُ + verbal noun / أَنْ. You can pick up the books tomorrow · يُمْكِنُكَ أَنْ تَأْخُذَ الكُتُبَ غَداً · Ability · could · (قَدْ) تَمَكَّنَ مِنْ + verbal noun / أَنْ · They could solve their problems · قَدْ تَمَكَّنُوا مِنْ حَلِّ مُشْكِلاتِهِمْ · Ability · could have · كانَ مِنَ المُمْكِنِ أَنْ · We could have helped you · كانَ مِنَ المُمْكِنِ أَنْ نُساعِدَكَ · Ability · will be able to · سَـ / سَوْفَ يَكُونُ قادِراً عَلَى; سَيَسْتَطِيعُ; سَيَقْدِرُ عَلَى

chunks.title: Appendix II: Modality (cont.)
chunks.text: He will be able to drive you to the airport · سَيَسْتَطِيعُ تَوْصِيلَكَ لِلْمَطارِ · appendix-ii-modality

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2015). Arabic–English–Arabic Translation: Issues and Strategies, ch. 3 “Legal translation”, pp. 94–164. Routledge., pp. 94–98
chunks.title: What legal language is
chunks.text: What legal language is · ما اللغة القانونية؟ 94–98 · Legalese is known for passive verbs, impersonality, nominalizations, long idea-packed sentences, difficult words, double negatives and poor layout, and readers outside the profession often cannot follow it. Yet legal language reaches everyone: a toaster warranty, the terms on a plane ticket or any official form brings words like ‘liability’ and ‘compliance’ into daily life. Three things set it apart. It has to speak to experts and lay readers at once. In law, language is both the tool and the thing studied, so words are the law’s ‘chemical elements’. And it changes very slowly: a statute may read like one written two hundred years ago, sometimes because it must in order to be valid. That need to comply explains much of its formulaic style. Prescriptive (regulatory) texts impose obligations with sanctions: constitutions, treaties, laws, contracts. Descriptive texts are still legal instruments but not normative: declarative (witness statements, affidavits), directive (a lawyer’s brief), exhortatory (petitions), expressive (closing arguments), commissive (marriage vows, wills). Metalegal texts talk about the law (textbooks, articles on jurisprudence) and are not legal instruments themselves. By producer: legislative, judicial, scholarly and private texts (wills, agreements).

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2015). Arabic–English–Arabic Translation: Issues and Strategies, ch. 3 “Legal translation”, pp. 94–164. Routledge., pp. 94–98
chunks.title: What legal language is (cont.)
chunks.text: Real documents mix categories: a witness statement is both expressive and exhortatory. So it is better to speak of ‘languages of the law’ than one legal register. The audience also varies, from one person to a state, and spoken legal language is less formal and less binding (verba volant).

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2015). Arabic–English–Arabic Translation: Issues and Strategies, ch. 3 “Legal translation”, pp. 94–164. Routledge., pp. 98–108
chunks.title: Translating between legal systems
chunks.text: Translating between legal systems · ترجمة الأنظمة القانونية · 98–108 · Unlike chemistry, which is the same everywhere, law is tied to a system and a culture, so the legal translator has to know how the law works in both communities. You need not be a lawyer, but you must understand the legal effect a sentence is meant to have and how to get that effect in the other language. The aim is to say what the legislator meant ‘and in the way they customarily say it’. The two main families are Common Law (judge-made, case law; England, the USA, Canada, Ireland, Australia) and Civil Law (codified statutes; continental Europe, rooted in Roman law). Systems mix: Louisiana and Quebec have Civil Law roots; Algeria, Morocco, Syria and Tunisia have French-style Civil Law alongside Islamic law; Oman’s system draws on English Common Law. Islamic law (شَرِيعة), sourced in the Qur’an and Sunnah and extended by إِجْماع (consensus) and قِياس (analogy), applies in Arab states beside a secular code, or alone, as in Saudi Arabia. Arabic legal drafting can be literary and elevated (the preambles of several Arab constitutions), while English drafting aims to be concise and precise. Common Law judgments are long, because they cite precedent; Civil Law statutes state principles broadly, while Common Law statutes define everything. The faithfulness argument (the letter of the law, precision, penalties for deviation) is weaker than it looks: translation always interprets, and some ambiguity is deliberate and must be kept.

chunks.src: Husni, R. & Newman, D. L. (2015). Arabic–English–Arabic Translation: Issues and Strategies, ch. 3 “Legal translation”, pp. 94–164. Routledge., pp. 98–108
chunks.title: Translating between legal systems (cont.)
chunks.text: Contracts often contain business, finance or engineering terms: the legal translator must know the subject matter too. System-bound terms cluster around the profession (solicitor, القاضي), the courts (High Court, مَحْكَمة شَرْعِيّة) and areas of law (equity, اجْتِهاد). chunks.title: Differences inside one system
chunks.text: Differences inside one system · الاختلاف داخل النظام الواحد · 108–111 · The same system can name things differently. Lawyer, attorney, solicitor, barrister, advocate and counsel can all be مُحامٍ in Arabic, but they are not synonyms. In the UK an ‘attorney’ acts for someone else (وَكِيل; power of attorney, سَنَد التَّوْكِيل); the solicitor/barrister split does not exist in the USA; Scotland says advocate. In the Maghreb, a عَدْل (pl. عُدُول) is a judge’s assistant who does a notary’s work (كاتِب عَدْل). Identical names do not mean identical courts: New Zealand’s High Court corresponds to the US or UK Supreme Court, and ‘District Court’ means different things in Ireland, the USA and Scotland. Think in terms of equivalence, not word-for-word. Dictionary paraphrases such as ‘local courts with special competence limited to the area over which they have jurisdiction’ are not usable translations. Arab court names show their Civil Law origins in French calques (Court of Cassation, Court of First Instance), which British and American English use only for continental courts. chunks.title: Layout and presentation
chunks.text: Layout and presentation · الشكل والإخراج · 111–119 · Operative documents (wills, birth certificates) follow fixed layouts; statutes are rigid too. A UK Act runs: short title, long title, enacting formula, then Parts, Chapters, cross-headings and numbered sections. Australia uses Chapter–Part–Division–Section; in US Acts, ‘Section’ and ‘Title’ correspond to the UK ‘Part’ and ‘Chapter’. Today’s practice is to make the translation mirror the source layout as closely as possible, especially for forms and certificates, including bold, italics and underlining. In Arabic–English work the trend is to flip everything into mirror image for the new script direction. Put signatures, stamps and photos in square brackets: [STAMP: …], [signature]. Arabic marks emphasis with font changes (it has no capitals) and uses bold heavily; English frowns on mixed fonts and keeps bold for headings and vital information, using capitals and bold to show hierarchy. chunks.title: Lexis and terminology
chunks.text: Lexis and terminology · المصطلح القانوني · 120–123 · Ideally one legal concept has one term, but polysemy is everywhere. ‘Law’ alone covers a rule, the body of law, the police (‘The law was on the heels of the fugitive’, كانَتِ الشُّرْطةُ تَتَعَقَّبُ الهارِبَ), a branch of study and a law of nature (النَّوامِيس الطَّبِيعِيّة). Arabic dictionaries list many words for ‘law’, and several belong only to Islamic law, so they must never be used for secular law. For ‘lawful’, only قانُونِيّ and شَرْعِيّ are secular; حَلال is religious. Arabic · Meaning · قانُون (pl. قَوانِين) law (generic) شَرْع / شَرِيعة · Islamic law · الحُقُوق · Law as a subject of study (capital L: ‘He studied Law’) نامُوس (pl. نَوامِيس) natural law · مَرْسُوم (pl. مَراسِيم) decree, act, edict, regulation · تَشْرِيع · legislation · دُسْتُور · constitution; regulations, statutes · ضابِط (pl. ضَوابِط) general moral rule · قَرار covers resolution (Security Council resolution, قَرار مَجْلِسِ الأَمْن), award (arbitral award, قَرار التَّحْكِيم), adjudication, decision, order, indictment and ruling. لائِحة covers indictment (لائِحة اتِّهام), regulation (Council Regulations), bill (true bill) and rule (administrative rule). قاعِدة covers rule (substantive rule, قاعِدة مَوْضُوعِيّة; peremptory rule, قاعِدة آمِرة), database, base, norm, jus (jus soli, قاعِدة حَقِّ الأَرْض) and lex (lex specialis, قاعِدة التَّخْصِيص). مَرْسُوم covers decree (royal decree, مَرْسُوم مَلَكِيّ) and ruling (Ruling on the General Amnesty, مَرْسُوم العَفْوِ العامّ).

chunks.title: Features of English legal language
chunks.text: Features of English legal language · سمات الإنجليزية القانونية · 123–126 · Archaisms: aforesaid, heretofore, witnesseth. Latin (Roman occupation, the Church, Norman law): mens rea (نِيّة جُرْمِيّة), sub iudice (أَمامَ القاضي), viva voce (شَفَوِيّاً). Norman French, the language of the courts until 1362: naturalized forms (crime, جَرِيمة; verdict, قَرار) and unchanged ones (sans frais, دُونَ نَفَقة; tort, جَرِيرة شَخْصِيّة). Polysemy: ‘seize’ means to impound (حَجَزَ), to arrest (قَبَضَ عَلَى), or for the Security Council ‘to remain seized of the matter’ (يُقَرِّرُ أَنْ يُبْقِيَ المَسْأَلةَ قَيْدَ نَظَرِهِ الفِعْلِيّ). Binomial pairs and doublets are fixed legal idioms. Arabic usually renders the whole pair with one word, though occasionally a pair is kept (خالِص ومُطْلَق ‘free and clear’). In the other direction, decide whether بَيْن is plain ‘between’ or formulaic ‘by and between’; most translators follow the target genre’s expectations. chunks.title: Features of Arabic legal language
chunks.text: Features of Arabic legal language · سمات العربية القانونية · 126–128 · Islamic legal terms have no ready English equivalents, and the strategy depends on readership and text type: a marriage contract between Muslims keeps more borrowed terms than a trade contract. Usage also varies by region: religious endowments are وَقْف (pl. أَوْقاف) in the East and حَبْس (pl. حُبُوس) in North Africa. بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ has competing translations (‘In the Name of God/Allah, the Compassionate, the Merciful’; ‘the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate’; ‘the Most Beneficent, the Most Merciful’). It used to be left out of legal translations; today it is increasingly kept, and it should never be dropped from certificates and forms. Titles: legal translation is more literal than general translation, so titles and formulas are usually kept, with English equivalents and blessings in square brackets. Translating into Arabic, add the expected titles and formulas so the text is accepted. chunks.title: Shared features: jargon, homonyms, repetition, collocation
chunks.text: Shared features: jargon, homonyms, repetition, collocation · سمات مشتركة · 128–131 · Both languages have core jargon: courts, professions, ‘pursuant to’, ‘liability’ (مَسْؤُولِيّة), ‘to remand’ (أَعادَ الدَّعْوَى). The twenty most frequent words in a Leeds Arabic legal corpus are all technical: المادة، القانون، المحكمة، المتهم، القضاء، الدعوى، حقوق، قرار، الدستور، الجنائية، القضائية، النيابة، الحكم، الجرائم، التحقيق، الأمن، الشرطة، التعذيب، يجوز، السلطة. Even ‘Graduation Certificate’ varies by country: إِفادة التَّخَرُّج (Libya), وَثِيقة التَّخَرُّج (Saudi Arabia), شَهادة التَّخَرُّج (Tunisia, Oman). Repetition is the norm, not a fault. Legal texts repeat the same noun phrase (‘the Company’, never ‘the Firm’) and list every contingency (‘war, hostilities, invasion, acts by foreign enemies, rebellion …’), with phrases like ‘including but not limited to’. Do not tidy this away. Collocations decide meaning. رَفَعَ دَعْوَى ضِدَّ … أَمامَ … is ‘to file a complaint against … in …’ or simply ‘to sue’; أَقامَ دَعْوَى also works. ‘Commit a crime’ is ارْتَكَبَ / اقْتَرَفَ جَرِيمة, but back-translating ‘carry out’ as نَفَّذَ or أَنْجَزَ fails: those go with مَشْرُوع, اخْتِبار, بَرْنامَج. With حُكْم: نَفَّذَ (execute), صادَقَ عَلَى (confirm), صَدَرَ (be issued), أَصْدَرَ (pass), اسْتَصْدَرَ (obtain), أَلْغَى (rescind), طَعَنَ في (appeal against), طالَبَ بِـ (demand), رَفَضَ (reject). chunks.title: Recognized translations
chunks.text: Recognized translations · الترجمات المعتمدة · 131–132 · Countries now publish their own official translations, and these set precedents that later translations must follow, even when better wording is possible. Research what is in use. Oman calls its ministry the ‘Ministry of Legal Affairs’ (وزارة الشؤون القانونية) where others say وزارة العدل; وزارة الخارجية is the Foreign Office (UK), State Department (USA) or Ministry of Foreign Affairs (elsewhere). This also applies to certificates, the freelancer’s ‘bread and butter’: follow established models or a sworn translation may be rejected.

chunks.title: Syntax: long sentences, the passive, shall and may
chunks.text: Syntax: long sentences, the passive, shall and may. التركيب: الجملة الطويلة والمبني للمجهول وshall/may · 132–141 · Legal English has the longest sentences of any genre: one official sentence ran to 516 words. Typical features include the formulaic subjunctive (‘Be it enacted’), inversion, long sub-clauses, adjectives placed after the noun (‘Lords Spiritual’), and chains of ‘and’. The Universal Declaration preamble stacks ‘Whereas …’ clauses before the main clause (‘Now, therefore, The General Assembly proclaims …’); Arabic opens each with لَمّا كانَ / وَلَمّا كانَ and resolves it with فَإِنَّ الجَمْعِيّةَ العامّةَ. The passive: legal English uses it heavily, Arabic dislikes it, and classical rules forbid naming the agent. Strategies: an Arabic passive, an active, reflexive forms (V, VII, VIII), تَمَّ / يَتِمُّ + verbal noun, or nominalization. Agent phrases (بِواسِطة, مِنْ قِبَل, مِنْ طَرَف) are calques considered substandard but now common in legal texts. Shall is never a future in legal English; it is an obligation, like ‘must’. May is permission, and ‘may not’ is a prohibition. Performative declarations use a simple present (‘This Regulation is hereby repealed’). Arabic can use عَلَى, يَجِبُ عَلَى, لا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ / أَنْ or يَنْبَغِي, but very often renders ‘shall’ with a plain imperfect. The declarative ‘do’ (‘We the People … do ordain’) works like ‘hereby’ with performative verbs; it is never translated, and the verb becomes an imperfect. The work shall be performed by the subcontractor. يَتِمُّ تَنْفِيذُ العَمَلِ بِواسِطَةِ المُقاوِلِ
